item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Dave Roberts Says ‘Starving’ Brewers Wanted World Series More Than Dodgers
item.dc:creator: Cameron Kiszla
item.description: The Milwaukee Brewers are the 2026 World Series champions, and Los Angeles Dodgers manager Dave Roberts knows why. item.content:encoded:
The Milwaukee Brewers are the 2026 World Series champions, and Los Angeles Dodgers manager Dave Roberts knows why.
Appearing on the "Baseball Tonight with Buster Olney" podcast, Roberts revealed his impression of the Brewers after being swept in the National League Championship Series, and in doing so, likely revealed why the Dodgers couldn't garner a win.
What did Dave Roberts say about the Brewers?
For much of the 2026 season, Roberts and the Dodgers roster had to answer questions about motivation.
After all, winning typically produces complacency, and back-to-back championships only increase that danger.
Despite that, the Dodgers frequently said they were motivated by chasing history, as no NL team has ever won three straight World Series titles before.
Despite that desire to craft an enduring legacy, the Dodgers ran into a team who just wanted it more, he told Olney.
"Typically, getting eliminated, it's hard to sit back and watch and feel like you should be there, so it hurts a little bit more," he said. "This year's different. I've really loved the way the Brewers have played.
"I was telling my wife after we got eliminated, I know our guys are hungry, but the Brewers were starving. And you don't know how that's going to translate into performance, whether it's anxiousness, feeling the pressure, or it's willing to die for every pitch, every at bat, every win."
As an example, Roberts cited a moment from one of the early games, when Dodgers relief pitcher Edgardo Henriquez threw a high fastball at 101 or 102 mph "at Cooper Pratt's face, on accident; it got away from him."
Pratt then stood up, got back in the batter's box and hit a line drive over the second baseman's head.
"That kind of encapsulates what the Brewers are about," Roberts said.
His own team's loss notwithstanding, Roberts has enjoyed this Brewers run to a title, during which they went 11-2 in the playoffs.
"For me, as a baseball guy, Buster, it's been fun to watch these guys play," he said.

item.content:encoded:
Freddie Freeman disputará en 2027 la última campaña de su actual contrato con los Dodgers y analizará su futuro durante la próxima temporada baja. Desde su llegada a Los Ángeles en 2022, el primera base se convirtió rápidamente en uno de los referentes del equipo y fue una pieza fundamental en los títulos de la Serie Mundial que la franquicia angelina conquistó en 2024 y 2025
Durante sus primeras cinco temporadas con los Dodgers, Freeman se ha consolidado como uno de los líderes del vestuario, una figura en la que confían tanto sus compañeros como Dave Roberts, mánager del equipo. El pelotero canadiense firmó un contrato de seis años y 162 millones de dólares en 2022, equivalente a 27 millones por temporada. Con su último año de contrato cada vez más cerca, ambas partes tendrán que evaluar sus opciones y decidir cómo proceder.
“Siempre he querido intentar jugar hasta los 40 años”, comentó en su momento Freeman. “Eso significaría tres años más después de este. No voy a fijar una fecha definitiva. Tendría que conseguir otro contrato, así que solo me centro en este año. Pero llegar a jugar 20 años en las Grandes Ligas sería algo bonito y especial”.
Futuro incierto para Freddie Freeman
La negociación de una posible renovación dependerá de lo que más convenga a cada parte, tanto en términos salariales como en la duración del acuerdo. Para los Dodgers, una eventual salida de Freeman también abriría espacio en la primera base para dar oportunidades a algunos de los prospectos de la franquicia angelina, como Josue De Paula.
Sin embargo, la importancia de Freddie Freeman dentro y fuera del terreno de juego es fundamental para los Dodgers en su objetivo de competir por la Serie Mundial cada temporada. La franquicia angelina podría seguir apostando por el primera base mientras mantenga un rendimiento acorde con las expectativas del equipo. Por ello, una extensión de contrato por dos o tres años podría ser una opción viable para ambas partes durante la próxima temporada baja.

item.content:encoded:
Los Angeles Dodgers first baseman Freddie Freeman is entering the final year of his contract, and his future will need some clarity soon.
Freeman is 37 years old and inching closer to 40. He has five years in the books with the Dodgers, and during that time he has delivered multiple big moments, while serving as the captain and helping the team win two World Series.
Dave Roberts and many players lean on Freeman’s experience and leadership to guide them through tough times.
Freddie Freeman’s contract status heading into the offseason
Freeman is in the last year of a six-year, $162 million contract that is paying him $27 million per season.
Now that his contract is coming to an end, the Dodgers and Freeman need to decide how they will proceed, in terms of how long his next deal will be and how much money he will pull in.
The California Post’s Jack Harris believes the Dodgers and Freeman will discuss a new deal this offseason and how they will handle his final few seasons.
“Then there is Freddie Freeman, whose contract situation will come to a head over the next 12 months,” Harris wrote.
“The 2027 season is the final one of Freeman’s current deal. However, the 37-year-old has indicated a desire to potentially play at least two more seasons beyond it, putting the onus on the Dodgers to make a decision on his future in Los Angeles.
“To this point, the future Hall of Fame first baseman has repeatedly sidestepped any contract talk publicly. But it’s unlikely next year begins without him and the team at least discussing his long-term status in the organization at some point.”
The Dodgers, even as their team ages, will certainly want to keep Freeman, a quality contact hitter who offers good defense at first base.
Freeman’s departure may unlock a path for some of their prospects to play, including Josue De Paula, since it is a position that a lot of players can play.
However, his value to the roster and clubhouse is so massive that they will ride it out with Freeman until he struggles.
What does Freddie Freeman want?
During the All-Star break, Freeman laid out that he wants to play antoher three more years, reaching 40 years old.
“I’ve always wanted to try and play until I’m 40 years old,” Freeman said. “That would be three more years after this. I’m not going to put a firm number on it. I would have to get another contract, so I’m only worried about this year. But 20 years in the big leagues would be kind of cool and special.”
If he does play another three years, he can possibly reach 3,000 hits, another one of his goals.
Freeman certainly wants to play and would love to play with the Dodgers. With the feeling being mutual on both sides, it is hard to see things working out any other way.
What will be interesting to see is the extact terms of the contract.

item.title: [MARCA] MLB Rumors: White Sox surprisingly join Dodgers, Mets as best fits for Tarik Skubal
item.dc:creator: David Schiavone

What we know following shock seep elimination The Chicago White Sox have already defied expectations by returning to the MLB playoffs, but their next move could be even more surprising if they decide to pursue Tarik Skubal in free agency. After finishing the 2024 season with a disastrous 41-121 record, Chicago has undergone a dramat
item.content:encoded:
- MLB. Superagent Scott Boras issues serious warning to MLB teams ahead of impending lockout on December 1
- Los Angeles Dodgers. Will the Dodgers fire Dave Roberts? What we know following shock seep elimination
The Chicago White Sox have already defied expectations by returning to the MLB playoffs, but their next move could be even more surprising if they decide to pursue Tarik Skubal in free agency.
After finishing the 2024 season with a disastrous 41-121 record, Chicago has undergone a dramatic transformation under manager Will Venable, culminating in an 84-win campaign and an appearance in the American League Division Series.
That progress has raised expectations on the South Side, with former MLB general manager Jim Bowden identifying the White Sox as a potential destination for one of baseball's most coveted pitchers.
Writing in The Athletic, Bowden placed Chicago alongside two considerably wealthier organizations when assessing Skubal's future.
"Best team fits: New York Mets, Los Angeles Dodgers, Chicago White Sox," Bowden wrote.
The assessment is surprising given Chicago's recent financial approach, although identifying the White Sox as a suitable destination does not establish that negotiations have taken place.
Chicago's remarkable improvement has changed the conversation surrounding the franchise, which won just 60 games in 2025 before securing a postseason berth this year.
The White Sox defeated the Houston Astros in the Wild Card round before surrendering a 2-0 series advantage against the Cleveland Guardians in the ALDS.
Although that elimination ended their championship hopes, it demonstrated that Venable's developing roster could compete against established contenders.
General manager Chris Getz now faces the challenge of strengthening a rotation featuring promising starters Sean Burke and Davis Martin.
Skubal would provide an immediate upgrade, bringing experience, postseason pedigree and the consistency expected from a frontline starter.
His potential arrival would also send a significant message about Chicago's willingness to invest in its recent success.
Dodgers face expensive decision
Skubal joined the Los Angeles Dodgers from the Detroit Tigers at the 2026 trade deadline, strengthening a rotation assembled to pursue a third consecutive World Series championship.
Across both teams, the 29-year-old finished the regular season with a 12-7 record, 2.72 ERA and 186 strikeouts in 158.2 innings.
He was particularly effective following his move to Los Angeles, recording a 2.61 ERA over 10 starts.
However, the Dodgers' championship ambitions ended when the Milwaukee Brewers swept them in the National League Championship Series.
Los Angeles must now decide how aggressively to pursue Skubal's long-term future, with the Mets and potentially other wealthy franchises positioned to enter the bidding.
Skubal contract projection raises major question
Bowden believes Skubal could secure a deal worth between $350 million and $500 million, potentially setting new standards for pitcher contracts.
"Anywhere from $350-$500 million depending on length of contract," Bowden predicted.
Such figures would represent an extraordinary financial commitment for Chicago, requiring owner Jerry Reinsdorf to authorize spending far beyond the franchise's usual approach.
Skubal's representation by Scott Boras adds another dimension to negotiations, with the prominent agent known for pursuing substantial long-term agreements.
Whether the White Sox are prepared to make such an investment remains uncertain.
Nevertheless, their inclusion among Skubal's potential destinations reflects how dramatically the franchise's position has changed.
Chicago has already demonstrated that it can return to postseason contention. The next question is whether its ownership will provide the financial backing necessary to pursue baseball's most expensive free agents.

Coming off his fourth unanimous MVP nod in 2025
item.content:encoded:
Ohtani, Muncy, Pages among Dodgers up for major awards
This browser does not support the video element.
This story was excerpted from Sonja Chen's Dodgers Beat newsletter. To read the full newsletter, click here. And subscribe to get it regularly in your inbox.
Shohei Ohtani was the undisputed Most Valuable Player in the National League in each of his first two seasons with the Dodgers, but that run appears over after his third year in Los Angeles.
Coming off his fourth unanimous MVP nod in 2025 -- which was also his third in a row -- Ohtani will likely have to wait another year to vie for his fifth career honor. Ongoing right biceps and left knee injuries diminished what he had hoped would be his first full two-way season since '23.
The injuries contributed to an extended season-ending slump for Ohtani, who also missed time to a minimum-length stint on the 15-day IL in September. At the same time, Pete Crow-Armstrong of the Cubs -- the presumptive NL MVP winner -- did not lose steam down the stretch, putting the finishing touches on a 40-40 campaign.
Even while limited, Ohtani put together quite the season, hitting 30 homers with an .889 OPS while recording a 1.79 ERA through 14 starts on the mound.
"Through mid-August, he was still, I think, the consensus MVP," president of baseball operations Andrew Friedman said at the Dodgers' season-ending press conference last week.
While the MVP Award appears out of Ohtani's grasp, he could still take home some other hardware this November. He should garner some consideration for the Edgar Martinez Outstanding Designated Hitter Award, which he won in each of the previous five seasons (although the Astros' Yordan Alvarez is likely to unseat him). He is also a finalist for the All-MLB Teams, which he has made five times as a DH and three times as a starting pitcher.
Here's an overview of the dates to know this awards season, as well as which Dodgers are in the running for each:
Sunday: Gold Glove winners announced
The Dodgers have two finalists: Andy Pages at center field and Max Muncy at third base. Pages had an impressive defensive season, leading MLB with 14 outfield assists, but his competition is Crow-Armstrong -- who was essentially the best defender in the Majors this year. Muncy made noticeable defensive improvements, but he was not considered a plus defender by any metrics this season.
This browser does not support the video element.
Monday: BBWAA award finalists and Silver Slugger finalists announced
We'll break down the potential finalists for the BBWAA awards and Silver Sluggers in their respective sections.
Nov. 6: Heart & Hustle Award winner and Platinum Glove winners announced
Miguel Rojas was named the Dodgers' team winner for the MLB Players Alumni Association's Heart & Hustle Award.
Nov. 9: BBWAA Jackie Robinson Rookies of the Year announced
None of the Dodgers' 2026 rookies were standouts, although in September, they got a brief look at someone who could very well contend for the award in '27: Josue De Paula, MLB Pipeline's No. 4 overall prospect.
Nov. 10: BBWAA Managers of the Year announced
Manager Dave Roberts led the Dodgers to a 100-win regular season for the sixth time in his managerial career, tying an MLB record. But whether or not it's fair, that kind of performance is expected from this team, making it unlikely that he receives serious consideration for this award.
This browser does not support the video element.
Nov. 11: BBWAA Cy Young Awards and Relievers of the Year announced; MLB Awards (includes the Hank Aaron Award winners, the Comeback Players of the Year, the Mariano Rivera and Trevor Hoffman Relievers of the Year, the Edgar Martinez Outstanding Designated Hitter, the All-MLB First and Second Teams and the MLB Executive of the Year Award)
No one is beating the Brewers' Jacob Misiorowski for the NL Cy Young Award, but Yoshinobu Yamamoto could be a finalist. Among qualified NL pitchers, his 2.53 ERA ranked third, his 185 innings were tied for fourth and his 0.87 WHIP ranked second.
The BBWAA's Reliever of the Year Award is new this year. Tanner Scott, who converted a team-leading 25 saves, could be the most likely Dodger to garner some votes for the honor.
The Dodgers also have eight nominees for the All-MLB Teams: Freddie Freeman, Mookie Betts, Muncy, Ohtani, Pages, Yamamoto, Tarik Skubal and Scott.
Nov. 12: BBWAA MVP Awards announced
In addition to Ohtani, who should be a finalist, other Dodgers -- such as Pages and Muncy -- could receive some down-ballot votes.
Nov. 17: Silver Slugger winners announced
Freeman, Muncy, Pages and Ohtani are the top candidates to be finalists at their respective positions.

item.title: [roundtable.io] Dodgers Expect Entire Coaching Staff Back in 2027
item.dc:creator: Anthony Arroyo
item.description: Andrew Friedman expects the Los Angeles Dodgers' coaching staff to return for the 2027 season. The Los Angeles Dodgers are not anticipating major changes to their coaching staff this offseason, with president of baseball operations Andrew Friedman expecting the entire group to return for the 2027 season. Friedman discussed the organization's plans during his end-of-season press conference, indicating that the Dodgers expect to maintain their existing coaching structure as they prepare for anothe
item.content:encoded:
Andrew Friedman expects the Los Angeles Dodgers' coaching staff to return for the 2027 season.
The Los Angeles Dodgers are not anticipating major changes to their coaching staff this offseason, with president of baseball operations Andrew Friedman expecting the entire group to return for the 2027 season.
Friedman discussed the organization's plans during his end-of-season press conference, indicating that the Dodgers expect to maintain their existing coaching structure as they prepare for another championship pursuit.
If the staff returns as anticipated, manager Dave Roberts will enter his 12th season leading Los Angeles with the same coaching group in place.
The Dodgers have built sustained success under Roberts, and retaining the current staff would allow the organization to move into the offseason without an expected overhaul of its coaching personnel.
While Friedman's comments provide an early indication of the club's plans, the expectation of a full return is not necessarily an official confirmation of every coach's status for next season.
Danny Lehmann has drawn managerial interest
Lehmann has previously been considered a potential managerial candidate, putting him among the coaches who could eventually receive opportunities to lead another organization.
His future remains worth monitoring as teams continue evaluating candidates for leadership positions. For the Dodgers, though, the expectation remains that their existing coaching staff will return for 2027.
Maintaining Lehmann and the rest of the group would give Roberts continuity in the dugout as the team begins preparing for the upcoming season.
The Dodgers have relied on an established coaching structure throughout Roberts' tenure, and keeping that group together would allow the organization to concentrate on other offseason priorities rather than making significant changes to its staff.
Dodgers look to maintain stability heading into 2027
Although managerial openings elsewhere could create opportunities for members of the Dodgers' organization, there is currently no public indication that Lehmann is involved in the Houston or Seattle searches.
For now, Friedman's comments suggest that Los Angeles expects to retain its existing coaching group as Roberts prepares for another season.
The Dodgers will have additional offseason decisions to make before the 2027 campaign begins, but the coaching staff does not appear to be an area where the organization anticipates significant change.
If the expectation holds, Roberts and his staff will return together as Los Angeles begins its next attempt to compete for another World Series championship.

item.content:encoded:
When Dalton Rushing can return to full-time catching for the Dodgers after elbow surgery appeared first on ClutchPoints. Add ClutchPoints as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
When news broke that Dalton Rushing suffered a partially torn UCL in his right elbow back in August, fans openly wondered if and when the Los Angeles Dodgers catcher would have surgery to fix it.
At the time, any surgery would have effectively ended his season, leaving LA without a key bat on the bench, so, after deliberation, the team opted for rehab instead, allowing Rushing to remain a pinch-hitting option for another World Series run.
Unfortunately, that World Series berth didn't materialize, and now Rushing will be unable to catch full-time for the next nine months after undergoing right elbow surgery on October 21, which Andrew Freedman revealed to reporters like Maddie Lee of the LA Times during his season-of-season press conference.
Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)
"Dodgers' Dalton Rushing is undergoing right elbow surgery today, per sources," Lee wrote. "It's expected to be a hybrid internal brace procedure. The expected timeline to return to catching full time is 9 months, with a return to hitting well before then."
On paper, the Dodgers' desire to keep Rushing's bat available made sense, as he was a quality performer at times during the season. But the emergence of Josue De Paula as a major league hitter quickly made Rushing irrelevant, to the point where he didn't take a single at-bat against the Atlanta Braves or the Milwaukee Brewers. With his catching return now set for mid-summer, the Dodgers will have to hope reserves like Hunter Feduccia can hold things down behind Will Smith, or that Rushing can find some work at first base to remain a more consistent part of Dave Roberts' offense.
Related: 2 trades Dodgers must make after disappointing NLCS loss to Brewers

item.content:encoded:
Following their disappointing elimination from World Series contention, the Los Angeles Dodgers announced an update on catcher Dalton Rushing.
Rushing, 25, was sidelined for the entire postseason with a partial tear of the ulnar collateral ligament (UCL) in his throwing arm. The Dodgers’ second catcher on the roster tried to play through the injury as a designated hitter but never appeared in the postseason.
Today, the Dodgers announced that Rushing will undergo surgery to address the elbow injury, Maddie Lee of the Los Angeles Times wrote.
“It’s expected to be a hybrid internal brace procedure. The expected timeline to return to catching full time is 9 months, with a return to hitting well before then,” Lee added.
Dalton Rushing’s Boosted Opportunity Derailed by Elbow Injury
The Dodgers’ second-year catcher got a new opportunity as the team’s primary catcher. The team gave him this chance while Will Smith was sidelined with a lingering neck injury that kept the Dodgers’ top catcher out for nearly three months.
Rushing was up for the new challenge. Before suffering the UCL tear, Rushing was batting .245/.335/.475 with 12 home runs and 36 RBIs.
Will Smith would finally return to the Dodgers lineup on Sept. 1. Meanwhile, the Dodgers’ depth at catcher remained limited as Rushing became unable to play defense.
The nine-month recovery period for Dalton Rushing goes in line with a return to catching in late July 2027. A return to batting will be significantly earlier for the 25-year-old.
Offseason Surgery ‘Not on the Table’ For Shohei Ohtani
LOS ANGELES, CALIFORNIA – OCTOBER 15: Shohei Ohtani #17 of the Los Angeles Dodgers reacts after striking out against the Milwaukee Brewers during the fifth inning in game four of the National League Championship Series at Dodger Stadium on October 15, 2026 in Los Angeles, California. (Photo by Sean M. Haffey/Getty Images)
Throughout the Dodgers’ 2026 season, the health status of superstar Shohei Ohtani was an ongoing conversation. For the first time since joining the franchise in 2024, the team sent Ohtani to the 15-day injured list at the end of the regular season.
The designation was due to right biceps inflammation, left knee discomfort, and a neck issue. The biceps and knee injuries surfaced earlier in the season, leading manager Dave Roberts to give him regular days off.
As the Dodgers won’t be the World Series Champion for the first time since 2023, the option for surgery to address the lingering setbacks is “not on the table,” says Dodgers president Andrew Friedman.
The Dodgers president also added that he fully expects Ohtani “to pitch next year.”
The 32-year-old was shut down from pitching in early July. In the limited opportunity on the mound, Ohtani finished the 2026 season as a pitcher with an 8-2 record, 1.79 ERA, and 0.95 WHIP across 85.2 innings.
After back-to-back 50-home-run, 100-RBI seasons, the injuries limited Ohtani to 30 home runs and 81 RBIs in 2026.
The Dodgers superstar said he “definitely” plans on pitching next season.
“And looking forward to having a better season next year,” Ohtani added.

item.title: [Sports Illustrated] Dodgers Have Clear Plan for Josue De Paula Amid Questions About His 2027 Role
item.dc:creator: J P Hoornstra; Unknown
item.description: The Los Angeles Dodgers need to find a position for their top prospect, Josue De Paula. When Ohtani returned, De Paula was relegated to the bench. His ability (or rather, his in
item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers need to find a position for their top prospect, Josue De Paula. After showcasing his potential as a hitter during a late-season call-up, it would surprise no one if the 21-year-old forced his way into the Dodgers' lineup in 2027.
The obvious question: where should he play?
De Paula slotted in at designated hitter when a multitude of injuries caught up with Shohei Ohtani in September. When Ohtani returned, De Paula was relegated to the bench. His ability (or rather, his inability) to improve the Dodgers' outfield defense was a major reason why.
“I think that he’s a young player," manager Dave Roberts said in September. "I mean, he’s 21 years old. His bat has certainly got him here, but it’s our job to make him value defense and get him to be a better defender.”
As a minor leaguer, De Paula saw time at all three outfield spots. But if Ohtani is healthy along with outfielders Teoscar Hernandez, Andy Pages and Kyle Tucker, there would appear to be no room for him in the Dodgers' 2027 lineup.
The Dodgers likely won't keep a rookie on their big league bench when playing time in the minor leagues is available next year. They also would be justified in finding a place for De Paula on their 26-man roster if his spring training performance mimics the .323/.500/.681 slash line he put up in 11 big league games to end the regular season.
The Dodgers worked with De Paula on his outfield defense during the regular season. That might not be possible during the offseason.
A lockout is expected to be imposed on Dec. 1, when the Collective Bargaining Agreement between MLB and the MLB Players' Association expires. Team personnel — managers, coaches, executives and others — were not able to contact 40-man roster players during the 2021-22 work stoppage. The same is likely to be true again.
That said, the plan for De Paula this offseason is clear.
"We've talked through it," Dodgers general manager Brandon Gomes said of De Paula on Wednesday at the end-of-season press conference. "His mindset, and our coaching staff and all of us is, to make him as good a defensive outfielder as possible."
President of baseball operations Andrew Friedman praised the impact of the Dodgers' clubhouse for embracing De Paula in September and October — as well as De Paula's development from 2025 to 2026.
As the Dodgers look to incorporate more prospects in the years to come, none might hold a more important place in the organization than De Paula.

J.P. Hoornstra is an On SI Contributor. A veteran of 20 years of sports coverage for daily newspapers in California, J.P. covered MLB, the Los Angeles Dodgers, and the Los Angeles Angels (occasionally of Anaheim) from 2012-23 for the Southern California News Group. His first book, The 50 Greatest Dodgers Games of All-Time, published in 2015. In 2016, he won an Associated Press Sports Editors award for breaking news coverage. item.title: [abc7.com] Where 2026 ranks among best World Series matchups since 2000
item.dc:creator: David Schoenfield
item.description: This year's World Series will have a tough act to follow. Not only was the 2025 World Series between the Los Angeles Dodgers and Toronto Blue Jays the first seven-game affair since 2019, but it featured an 18-inning game and then a Game 7 that might have been the greatest baseball game ever played. The good news is we're guaranteed that a long-starved fanbase will get to celebrate in 2026. The Milwaukee Brewers, coming off their impressive and dynamic four-game sweep of the Dodgers in the NLCS,
item.content:encoded:
This year's World Series will have a tough act to follow. Not only was the 2025 World Series between the Los Angeles Dodgers and Toronto Blue Jays the first seven-game affair since 2019, but it featured an 18-inning game and then a Game 7 that might have been the greatest baseball game ever played.
The good news is we're guaranteed that a long-starved fanbase will get to celebrate in 2026. The Milwaukee Brewers, coming off their impressive and dynamic four-game sweep of the Dodgers in the NLCS, are in the Fall Classic for the first time since 1982 and seek the first championship in franchise history, looking to put an exclamation point on their season after leading the majors with 103 wins.
The Tampa Bay Rays were a 1998 expansion franchise and reached the World Series in 2008 and 2020 (the shortened season during the COVID-19 pandemic) but are seeking their first title as well. Young power hitter Junior Caminero and unheralded staff ace Drew Rasmussen lead the way as the Rays look to finally cash in after making the playoffs six times in the past eight seasons.
The Brewers and Rays led their respective leagues in wins, always a bonus for those who want the best teams in the World Series. Of course, a lot of attention will be given to the small-market aspect of the matchup, as the cloud of the lockout looms in the offseason.
Let's rank all the World Series since 2000 to see where Brewers-Rays fits in. This ranking is based on hype, the quality of the teams and their star power heading into the World Series. It's not a ranking of the quality of the World Series itself, although we're going to include a grade on that for each matchup. Let's get to it.
The Yankees were back in the World Series for the sixth time in eight years, and the Marlins had rebuilt after their fire sale following their World Series title in 1997. Trust me when I say that nobody wanted the Yankees in the World Series yet again. And the Marlins were merely a 91-win wild-card team. Most notably, however, both teams had spoiled the ultimate World Series by knocking off the Cubs and Red Sox -- before either team had overcome its curse -- in Game 7s in the LCS.
Actual World Series: C. The Marlins won Game 4 in 12 innings, when Yankees manager Joe Torre inexplicably failed to use reliever Mariano Rivera, and then 23-year-old Josh Beckett tossed a five-hit shutout in Game 6.
In an all-wild-card series, the fifth-seeded Rangers had won 90 games and the sixth-seeded Diamondbacks won only 84, making this the lowest combined win total in World Series history (for full seasons). The Rangers were going for their first World Series title, so there was that, and there were some fun hitters -- Corey Seager, the red-hot Adolis Garcia (who had just driven in 15 runs in the ALCS) and Corbin Carroll -- but it was a soft matchup on paper.
Actual World Series: D-. The series turned on Seager's tying two-run homer off Paul Sewald in the bottom of the ninth of Game 1, which Garcia then won with a home run in the 11th. There wasn't a single lead change after that, and three of those games were blowouts.
This was the Cardinals team that got hot in September and clinched a wild-card spot on the final day of the season when the Braves blew a lead in the ninth inning and lost in extra innings. St. Louis certainly had star power with the likes of Albert Pujols, Lance Berkman and Matt Holliday but had won a World Series fairly recently (2006), and the Rangers had just been there the year before.
Actual World Series: A. The first two games were one-run games, including the Rangers pulling out a victory with two runs in the ninth. In Game 3, Pujols blasted a record-tying three home runs. Game 6 was the David Freese Game -- perhaps the single most exciting baseball game ever played. Game 7 was a bit of an anticlimactic 6-2 Cardinals win.
The second-lowest combined win total in World Series history featured two wild-card teams that won fewer than 90 games. The Royals were at least a good story -- in the playoffs for the first time since winning the World Series in 1985 -- and had gone 8-0 in the AL playoffs, including an epic win over the A's in the wild-card game. The Giants, however, had just won the World Series in 2010 and 2012, and this team didn't seem nearly as good as those two.
Actual World Series: B-. Five of the games were blowouts, but it did at least go seven. It'll be remembered for Madison Bumgarner's historic performance: a shutout in Game 5 (the last complete game shutout in World Series history) and then five scoreless innings of relief in Game 7, getting Salvador Perez to pop out with the tying run on third to end it.
The Red Sox were only three years removed from breaking the Curse of the Bambino in 2004, so although they were still a star-laden team with David Ortiz, Manny Ramirez and scrappy rookie Dustin Pedroia, they were no longer as interesting. The Rockies were a fun story, winning 14 of their final 15 games, including beating the Padres in a tiebreaker, just to win a wild-card spot. Then they went 7-0 in the NL playoffs and had won 21 of 22 entering the World Series.
Actual World Series: F.A dud. Two of the games were one-run games, but this goes down as one of the least memorable World Series of all time, with a forgettable four-game sweep.
The Tigers were the story of the season. They had lost 119 games three years before and 91 just the previous year. With rookie starter Justin Verlander winning 17 games, they led the AL Central most of the season -- only to lose their final five games and squeak into the playoffs as a wild-card team. The Cardinals won a weak NL Central with only 83 wins -- although they at least had Pujols at his absolute peak (.331/.431/.671, 49 home runs). Both teams hadn't won a World Series in a couple of decades: 1982 for the Cardinals, 1984 for the Tigers. Plus, it did feature two of the original 16 franchises.
Actual World Series: F. The Cardinals won one game in the bottom of the eighth, but it was otherwise a blur of nothing, most characterized by several fielding miscues by Tigers pitchers. David Eckstein won MVP honors without hitting a home run and while driving in only four runs.
The Braves were back in the World Series for the first time since 1999 -- they had made 12 playoff appearances in the intervening years without making it to the Fall Classic. Still, this was the weakest of the Atlanta playoff teams of recent vintage, winning only 88 games and missing Ronald Acuña Jr. for the playoffs. The Astros, meanwhile, were back in the World Series for the third time in five years -- but the first time since the 2017 sign-stealing scandal had broken in November 2019. Let's just say not everyone wanted them there.
Actual World Series: D. This was a weird World Series. The Braves ended up going with two bullpen games (who remembers that Dylan Lee and Tucker Davidson started?) after Charlie Morton broke a leg in Game 1. Astros starters kept getting knocked out early (the only starter to go more than five innings for either team was Max Fried in the finale). Four of the games were blowouts.
The Giants were back after winning in 2010, and the Tigers were back for the first time since 2006, featuring Triple Crown winner Miguel Cabrera and a strong 1-2 punch in the rotation with Verlander and Max Scherzer. This was also the last World Series with that season's MVP winners until Aaron Judge and Shohei Ohtani in 2024, with Cabrera and Buster Posey.
Actual World Series: D-. A boring sweep. Pablo Sandoval did hit three home runs in Game 1, but there were two shutouts and chilly weather in Detroit made the final two games unbearable.
This one did feature the two best teams from the regular season (both won 97 games), the last time before this year that we had that happen in a full season. It was also a classic original-16 matchup, although we had seen this in 2004 -- plus, both teams had won recently (2007 for Boston, 2011 for St. Louis). These were veteran teams, with Ortiz leading the Red Sox and the Cardinals featuring four .300 hitters, plus Carlos Beltran, who hit .296 and led the team in home runs.
Actual World Series: C+. Ortiz was absolutely locked in, hitting .688/.760/1.188 with two home runs and eight walks. The Cardinals were so scared of him by Game 6 that they intentionally walked him three times -- with two of those helping lead to rallies and a 6-1 Red Sox victory in the final game.
This one could be No. 25 -- it was during the pandemic, after all, and it was played at a neutral site in a half-empty stadium for social distancing reasons. But it was a great matchup between the teams with the best records in each league, albeit over the shortened 60-game season. You had Mookie Betts and Clayton Kershaw and Randy Arozarena in the midst of one of the best postseasons ever, plus the small-market Rays trying to beat the big-market Dodgers.
Actual World Series: C+. Because teams were allowed an expanded roster of 28 players, it was a parade of relievers -- but there were some fun games, including a bonkers ending to Game 4 and then Rays manager Kevin Cash's controversial decision to remove Blake Snell in Game 6, which backfired in a big way.
Maybe this should rate higher. After all, at the time, the White Sox were trying to break a World Series drought going back to 1917 and the Astros, born in 1962, had never won. But the White Sox's drought never had the same nationwide interest as the ones for the Cubs or Red Sox (fair or not) and these weren't particularly interesting teams. The White Sox were very good -- they won 99 games -- but lacked star power, with Paul Konerko their biggest name (Frank Thomas was on the team that year but played only 34 games and was injured for the playoffs). The Astros had Yankees transplants Roger Clemens and Andy Pettitte, but their two longtime stars, Jeff Bagwell and Craig Biggio, were at the end of their careers (Bagwell, in his final season, was relegated to DH and pinch-hitting duties).
Actual World Series: C. It's hard to give a sweep a decent grade, but all four games were exciting, including Scott Podsednik's walk-off home run in Game 2 (after not hitting a home run all season) and Geoff Blum's go-ahead home run in the 14th inning to win Game 3.
The Phillies were back in the World Series for the first time since 1993 -- and hadn't won since 1980. They featured a powerful offense with Chase Utley, Ryan Howard, Jimmy Rollins and Pat Burrell. The Rays were maybe the unlikeliest World Series team ever: In their 10 previous years of existence, they had not only never had a winning season but had lost at least 90 games in each one. They won 97 games that year behind rookie Evan Longoria and power-hitting first baseman Carlos Peña, with speedsters Carl Crawford and B.J. Upton in the outfield.
Actual World Series: D+. Three games were decided by one run, but it was a pretty uneventful World Series. The lasting memory is the cold and rain in Philly that forced the midgame postponement of Game 5, the only time that has happened in World Series history. The game was suspended in the sixth inning and resumed two days later.
A Subway Series -- the first since the Yankees and Brooklyn Dodgers met in 1956 -- was certainly fun for the Big Apple, but it was less fun for the rest of the country (it drew the worst TV ratings at the time). The Yankees were going for a third straight World Series and had officially become the Evil Empire by that point. To make it even worse, they weren't even that good that season, winning only 87 games. The Mets were back in the World Series for the first time since 1986. There was certainly plenty of star power all around with the likes of Derek Jeter, Roger Clemens and Mike Piazza.
Actual World Series: C+. It was a tight-fought five-game series with all games decided by two runs or fewer. The turning point was the bottom of the ninth of Game 1, when the Yankees tied it off Armando Benitez and went on to win in 12 innings. Game 2 featured the infamous Clemens-Piazza bat-throwing incident, and the Yankees won the clincher with two runs in the ninth off a tired Al Leiter.
I know, the Astros ... again. Boo. But this was an absolute powerhouse of a team with 106 wins and stars such asYordan Alvarez (1.019 OPS) and Verlander (18-4, 1.75 ERA), plus the old standbys Jose Altuve and Alex Bregman. The Phillies, meanwhile, snuck in as a wild-card team for their first playoff trip since 2011 but were an immensely entertaining team with Bryce Harper, Kyle Schwarber& Co., as well as a passionate fanbase cheering them on.
Actual World Series: C. The Phillies won 6-5 in Game 1 on J.T. Realmuto's home run in the 10th inning. They took a 2-1 series lead, but then their bats died. Astros pitchers tossed a combined no-hitter to even the series, and Houston won the final two games 3-2 and 4-1, with Alvarez's three-run blast in Game 6 the deciding blow.
The Brewers' drought is the big narrative here as they try to finally cash in after their past decade of success, but we're still getting the 103-win Brewers facing the 98-win Rays, the best combined win total in the World Series since the Astros and Dodgers in 2017. (Not to mention we get a first-time winner no matter the outcome.) The Brewers aren't your conventional powerhouse team -- relying on speed, defense, timely hitting and a dominant bullpen -- but they do have one of the biggest stars of the 2026 season in Jacob Misiorowski, plus a rising star in young Jackson Chourio. The Rays might lack big names, although Junior Caminero is just the second player with two 40-homer seasons by age 22, and like the Brewers, they're trying to finally win it all after years of success.
Actual World Series: To be determined.
The Royals proved their 2014 World Series appearance was no fluke, winning 95 games with a better team that included trade deadline additions Ben Zobrist and Johnny Cueto. The Mets won the NL East behind a young, powerful rotation that featured Matt Harvey, Noah Syndergaard and Jacob deGrom. It was a fun matchup of teams trying to avoid lengthy title droughts -- 30 years for the Royals, 29 for the Mets.
Actual World Series: C+. It went only five games, but the Royals won the opener in 14 innings, won Game 5 with a three-run eighth inning and then won the clincher in 12 innings -- after Mets manager Terry Collins' ill-fated decision to leave in Harvey to start the ninth with a 2-0 lead.
This was a super entertaining showdown at the time. The Giants had yet to win a World Series in San Francisco and featured Tim Lincecum ("The Freak," for his small stature and overpowering stuff) and two rookies named Posey and Bumgarner. The Rangers had never won a championship and featured AL MVP Josh Hamilton and veteran DH Vladimir Guerrero. Both teams had pulled off upsets in the LCS, with the Giants beating the Phillies and the Rangers beating the Yankees.
Actual World Series: D. Meh. The Giants won the opener in a blowout as the Rangers made four errors and then tossed shutouts in Games 2 (behind Matt Cain) and 4 (behind Bumgarner). You can test Giants fans by asking them who won World Series MVP honors that year. Answer: Edgar Renteria (he hit .412 with two home runs and six RBIs).
Remember, this happened before the sign-stealing scandal changed how we view this era of the Astros. They had won 107 games behind the pitching duo of Verlander and Gerrit Cole and four players who mashed 30-plus home runs (which didn't even include Alvarez, a rookie that year). The Nationals were a wild-card team that had overcome a 19-31 season start to win 93 games and featured a starting pitching trio of Scherzer, Stephen Strasburg and Patrick Corbin (and 20-year-old sensation Juan Soto, who hit 34 home runs).
Actual World Series: B-. It went seven games -- the road team would win all seven -- although five of the games weren't close. The best game was the last one: The Nationals went ahead 3-2 in the seventh inning on Anthony Rendon's home run and then Howie Kendrick's go-ahead home run just inside the right-field foul pole.
This matchup began with a lot of hype: Shohei Ohtani, coming off his all-time game in the NLCS in which he hit three home runs and struck out 10 batters as the starting pitcher, against Vladimir Guerrero Jr., who had hit .442 with six home runs through the first two rounds of the playoffs. The Dodgers were looking to become the first team with back-to-back titles since the 2000 Yankees and the first NL team since the 1976 Reds. The Blue Jays were back in the World Series for the first time since Joe Carter walked off the Phillies in 1993. Dodgers manager Dave Roberts stirred things up after the NLCS when he said during the postgame celebration, "Let's get four more wins and really ruin baseball" -- a reference to the criticism of the Dodgers' high payroll.
Actual World Series: A+. The Dodgers won Game 3 in 18 innings on Freddie Freeman's walk-off home run, which followed an unlikely four-inning relief performance from Will Klein, the last guy on the Dodgers' staff. The Dodgers went back to Toronto trailing 3-2 but won Game 6 behind Yoshinobu Yamamoto and a crazy game-ending double play.
Game 7 featured two future Hall of Famers starting in Ohtani and Max Scherzer, more on-the-edge-of-your-seat plays than any game in World Series history, Miguel Rojas' unlikely home run in the ninth to tie it, as well as Will Smith's go-ahead one in the 11th -- and finally, Yamamoto pitching in relief to close out the game by inducing a double play with two runners on to win it for the Dodgers. It wasn't quite the greatest World Series overall, but two all-time games made it a classic.
The Angels, who joined the majors in 1961, were making their first World Series appearance, while the Giants, in the Bay Area since 1958, were trying to win their first title since moving from New York. You had Barry Bonds at the height of his unstoppable powers -- and trying to erase his own postseason demons -- while the Angels had a loaded lineup (Troy Glaus, Tim Salmon, Garret Anderson), the Rally Monkey and those deafening ThunderStix (let us pray they never return).
Actual World Series: A. Bonds was a beast, hitting .471/.700/1.294 (yes, that's a 1.994 OPS), but it wasn't enough. This series featured four one-run games, including a wild 11-10 contest and the classic Game 6, when the Angels rallied late from a 5-0 deficit to win 6-5. Game 7 was a drab 4-1 contest (Bonds went a harmless 1-for-3).
The Yankees had missed the playoffs in 2008 for the first time since 1993, so they went out and signed free agents CC Sabathia, Mark Teixeira and A.J. Burnett to add to an already stacked roster that included Jeter, Alex Rodriguez, Robinson Cano, Hideki Matsui, Jorge Posada and Johnny Damon. Whoa. Yes, they were still the Evil Empire. The Phillies, trying to defend their title, had traded for Cliff Lee and then signed Pedro Martinez in July to bolster their rotation.
Actual World Series: C. It could have been a classic battle, but there were no one-run games and Game 6 -- Martinez's final start of his career -- was over early. The crucial contest was Game 4, when the Yankees scored three runs in the ninth off Phillies closer Brad Lidge to win 7-4.
This one presented conflicting emotions. The Yankees were going for an unthinkable fourth straight title, but in the wake of 9/11, there was a "Win it for New York" angle that the Yankees had never encountered. The Diamondbacks, meanwhile, had the big, bad duo of Randy Johnson and Curt Schilling. When asked on the eve of the World Series about the Yankees' mystique and aura, Schilling provided one of the great quips in World Series history: "Mystique and Aura? Those are dancers at a nightclub." The Diamondbacks were not going to be intimidated.
Actual World Series: A+. Four one-run games, including three of the most memorable World Series moments ever: Jeter's Mr. November home run to win Game 4, Scott Brosius' walk-off home run to win Game 5 and then Luis Gonzalez's bloop single to beat the invincible Mariano Rivera in Game 7.
Two of baseball's most historic franchises had never met in a World Series, creating the classic showdown with games in Fenway Park and Dodger Stadium. It doesn't get any better than that. The Red Sox were a 108-win powerhouse -- with AL MVP Mookie Betts leading the way, backed up by J.D. Martinez, who hit .330 with 43 home runs that season. Chris Sale and David Price headlined the rotation. The Dodgers actually had a bit of a down year with 92 wins, but they also weren't lacking in big names, with Manny Machado (a trade deadline acquisition), Yasiel Puig, Matt Kemp, Cody Bellinger and Justin Turner, with Kershaw and rookie Walker Buehler on the pitching side.
Actual World Series: C-. A letdown. The first two games in Fenway were cold and windy. Game 3 was an 18-inning affair -- the longest in World Series history -- but was more of a slog than a game to remember. Game 4 was the best of the series as the Red Sox rallied with nine runs over the final three innings to win 9-6.
This series had it all: dominant teams (both won over 100 games), long World Series title droughts (never for the Astros, 1988 for the Dodgers) and superstars galore (Altuve, Verlander, Carlos Correa, Kershaw, Seager, Bellinger, Yu Darvish). We didn't know at the time that both franchises were just kicking off 100-win dynasties -- let alone what the Astros were doing behind the scenes -- but the anticipation level was off the charts for the first matchup of 100-win teams in the World Series since 1970.
Actual World Series: A-. Game 1, with a start-time temperature of 103 degrees at Dodger Stadium, was a Kershaw 11-strikeout gem. The Astros tied Game 2 in the ninth on Marwin Gonzalez's home run off Kenley Jansen (1.32 ERA that season), both teams scored twice in the 10th, the Astros scored twice in the 11th on George Springer's home run and held on for a 7-6 win. Game 4 featured a five-run rally in the ninth by the Dodgers to win. Game 5 was completely bananas, with the Astros finally winning 13-12 in 10 innings. Game 7 was a letdown though, as the Astros won a 5-1 snoozer in which they scored five runs off Darvish in the first two innings.
As mentioned, what's not to like? Aside from Ohtani and Judge each playing in their first World Series and trying to put a final stamp on their legacy-defining seasons, we hadJuan Soto and Mookie Betts, a suddenly rejuvenated Giancarlo Stanton and a hobbled Freddie Freeman (only raising the drama if he hit well), Gerrit Cole and Yoshinobu Yamamoto. Aside from the history between the clubs, we had both clubs needing to rewrite their recent history: The Yankees, back in the World Series for the first time since 2009, and the Dodgers trying to add a more legitimate championship to the one they won in the COVID-shortened season.
Actual World Series:C+. The Judge-Ohtani showdown was a flop, as Judge hit .222 with one home run and Ohtani hit .105 without a home run or RBI. The series also went just five games, with the Dodgers winning the first three. The series did produce two forever moments, however: Freeman's walk-off, Kirk Gibson-esque grand slam in Game 1 and the Yankees' fifth-inning defensive meltdown in Game 5.
The Red Sox were coming off their never-done-before comeback from down 3-0 to beat the Yankees in the ALCS -- and still had to beat a 105-win Cardinals team that featured Pujols (.331, 46 home runs), Jim Edmonds (.301, 42 home runs) and Scott Rolen (.314, 34 home runs), plus in-season pickup Larry Walker, who had an OPS over 1.000 that year. The Red Sox had their own ridiculous lineup with Ortiz (.301, 41 home runs), Ramirez (.308, 43 home runs) and Damon (.304, 20 home runs) plus a rotation with Schilling and Martinez. It seems inevitable now that Boston was going to win, but that wasn't the case at the time, so the buildup was intense.
Actual World Series: D. Blah. I mean, Red Sox fans will rightfully call it the best World Series ever, but after a sloppy 11-9 Game 1 played in a drizzle at Fenway (the Red Sox won despite committing four errors), the Cardinals never led again.
The Cubs had not only not won since 1908, but they hadn't even been in a World Series since 1945. The Guardians, meanwhile, had the second-longest drought of the original 16 teams, without a title since 1948. That was enough right there to build up the anticipation, but this also rates high because it was two good teams -- Chicago won 104 games while Cleveland won 94. Cubs third baseman Kris Bryant won MVP honors that year and Cleveland was led by 18-game winner Corey Kluber (who would start three times) and young rising stars Francisco Lindor and Jose Ramirez.
Actual World Series: B. The first six games weren't anything too special, but Game 7 was one of the greatest in World Series history. Cleveland tied it on Rajai Davis' three-run homer in the bottom of the eighth, the Cubs scored twice in the 10th -- following a stress-filled rain delay -- and escaped with an 8-7, curse-ending win when Cleveland had to bat little-used Michael Martinez with its season on the line.
]

item.title: [DodgersBeat] Roberts Says Brewers Won the At-Bats in Dodgers' Game 2 Loss
item.dc:creator: Steve Webb

item.content:encoded:
MILWAUKEE, WI — Dave Roberts gave Milwaukee credit for the work that put the Dodgers in a two-game hole. After Monday’s 7–4 loss, he pointed to the Brewers’ longer at-bats, contact and ability to create trouble on the bases. Yoshinobu Yamamoto’s early exit forced Roberts to cover more than six innings with his bullpen, and two leads slipped away. With the series heading to Los Angeles, Roberts wants length from Blake Snell and more help from the lineup.
A rare rough outing for Yamamoto
Roberts saw Yamamoto struggle to find his usual sharpness, with the third inning pushing his pitch count toward an early exit.
“He wasn’t sharp today,” Roberts said. “You can see from that Contreras at-bat in the third inning that really stressed him. You’ve got to give him a lot of credit. Then you follow that up with the Bauers at-bat, and the pitch count certainly crept up.”
“At that point, you’ve got Yelich, call it 70 pitches, and you’re trying to think about maybe getting him through it, as one of your guys, to shorten the game and give us a little bit of length.”
Yelich’s two-run single ended Yamamoto’s afternoon after 2⅔ innings.
“Once Yelich gets a hit, we’ve got to find a way to put it out and give ourselves a chance,” Roberts said. “He just didn’t have it tonight, which is very rare.”
Asked about close pitches to Brice Turang that went unchallenged, Roberts explained why those calls rest with the players.
“Will’s got a great view back there, as all catchers do,” he said. “As an offense, you try to defer to the hitter to save those challenges, defer to the catcher to save those challenges. In that spot, Will didn’t feel like it was a strike.”
“If you look back and that’s a called third strike, he doesn’t double, and that changes the outing. But I’m not back there. You’ve got to trust the players to make those decisions when they get in those spots.”
Why Sasaki pitched one inning
Roki Sasaki worked a scoreless fourth before Roberts turned to Kris Bubic in the fifth. Roberts said the run of left-handed hitters made that a spot he wanted for Bubic.
“You’re trying to cover six-plus innings,” he said. “I felt Bubic, you get four out of five left-handed hitters, and that’s a perfect spot for him. I knew they weren’t going to hit for them.”
“You’ve got Roki for an inning, and then you still have a guy where, in my opinion, you’ve got a great spot for Bubic. He tries to go with the fastball up to Contreras, and then he hits a homer.”
“That’s a decision I made. That’s his lane, to be able to go out there and throw up a zero.”
Contreras’ homer tied the game. In the sixth, Roberts stayed with Brock Stewart to face him, hoping for a ground ball with runners at first and third.
“I felt like we had a chance to put him on the ground, get a double-play ball,” Roberts said. “Contreras didn’t hit the ball hard. He flared it out to left field, drove in a run, and that’s what they do.”
Milwaukee creates the trouble
The Brewers finished with 12 hits to the Dodgers’ three. Roberts felt the gap began with how the teams handled their at-bats.
“They saw a ton more pitches than we did. And they had much better at-bats than we did across the board, top to bottom,” he said. “They put the ball in play, created havoc. That’s the difference in the game.”
Asked about the Dodgers’ struggles against Milwaukee’s bullpen, Roberts included the starter in his assessment.
“We had three hits tonight. It was some of the starter, some of the bullpen,” he said. “They’ve got good arms. So do we. I think they’re finding ways to win pitches better than we are.”
“Sometimes you’ve got to find a way to get a base hit. There were a lot of balls that weren’t hit hard tonight but found the outfield grass. That’s hitting.”
Snell gets the next chance
Roberts wants Snell to give the Dodgers a longer start in Game 3, allowing the bullpen to work with a lead.
“We need Snell to go out there and give us some length, give us a typical Blake Snell outing,” he said. “I know Blake has a bad taste in his mouth from that last outing against the Braves. You’re going to see a locked-in, focused Snell.”
“On the other side of things, we’ve got to support him offensively, too.”
Roberts still sees a path back into the series, starting with one win at home.
“If you look at Game 3, I like where we’re at as far as who’s pitching, where our bullpen is at, being at home,” he said. “Then you’ve got to go from there.”
“Can we do it? Absolutely. You want to get that first one.”

Have you subscribed to the Bleed Los Podcast YouTube channel? Be sure to ring the notification bell to watch player interviews, participate in shows & promotions, and stay up to date on all Dodgers news and rumors!
A lifelong baseball fan, Webb has been going to Dodger games since he moved to Los Angeles in 1987. His favorite memory was attending the insane Game 3 of the World Series in 2025 and hugging random Dodgers fans after Freddie’s walkoff homer. He has been writing for Dodgersbeat since 2020.

item.title: [Dodgers Way] The end of the Yankees dynasty could be telling for Dodgers, Dave Roberts’ future
item.dc:creator: Stephen Parello
item.description: Empires crumble, dynasties fade, and new powers emerge. Whether the sweep the Dodgers suffered at the hands of the Milwaukee Brewers was a temporary setback or the beginning of the end remains to be seen. item.content:encoded:
Empires crumble, dynasties fade, and new powers emerge. The only thing consistent through history is change, which is something that the Los Angeles Dodgers will come to learn sooner or later. Whether the sweep the Dodgers suffered at the hands of the Milwaukee Brewers was a temporary setback or the beginning of the end remains to be seen.
Regardless, the end is coming at some point, and that will put Dave Roberts in an uncomfortable position. Tyler Kepner of The Athletic covered the New York Yankees during the end of their famous dynasty in the early 2000s and put together some lessons the Dodgers will learn from history.
The first big key is the fact that the league doesn't like dynasties. MLB updated the Competitive Balance Tax during the 2002 CBA negotiations, introducing the first version of the repeat offender tax in an attempt to stop the Yankees, who clearly felt that the tax itself was no barrier to their big-spending ways. Los Angeles faces a similar, but more stringent obstacle coming down the pike, with the league now pushing for an outright salary cap.
Whether or not that actually comes to fruition and slows down the Dodgers remains to be seen. What is for sure is the fact that the run will eventually come to an end, and it will mean the end for Roberts.
Sooner or later, Dave Roberts will become a Los Angeles Dodgers scapegoat
During the late 1990s and early 2000s, New York was led by Joe Torre. Torre wasn't a legendary manager at the time. The former catcher came to the Yankees with a .471 winning percentage over 14 years as a manager and had never won a playoff game. He might have been hired because Yankees owner George Steinbrenner believed he could control the undistinguished skipper.
Torre won the World Series in his first season at the helm, with the Yankees serving as the upstart against the more established Atlanta Braves. He'd suffer an early exit from the postseason in 1997, but his club would come back and go on a rampage in 1998 with a whopping 114 wins and a second ring for Torre. He'd then win two more to complete the three-peat, while making the Fall Classic, but coming up short in 2001 and 2003.
Torre's final three years with New York featured first-round playoff exits, and while the Yankees never actually fired him, they offered him only a one-year contract with a pay cut following the 2007 season.
The dirty little secret is that Torre wasn't really the reason that New York entered a championship drought. Instead, the organization moved away from what originally made it successful. The Yankees were built on a foundation that was called the Core Four — homegrown heroes Derek Jeter, Mariano Rivera, Jorge Posada, and Andy Pettitte. The name is a misnomer because, in reality, Bernie Williams, also a homegrown star, who just happened to be a couple of years older than the others, was an integral part of their success.
Supporting that core were a bunch of savvy pickups. Paul O'Neill was a platoon bat who frequently clashed with Lou Piniella in Cincinnati, but became the fearsome No. 3 hitter in the Yankees' order. Tino Martinez was a similar sort of player who was pushed out of Seattle and became a fearsome slugger with New York. Scott Brosius became the defensive whiz with a penchant for the clutch hit after being rescued from Oakland. The list goes on.
However, after the 2001 heartbreak at the hands of the Arizona Diamondbacks, the Yankees saw two things happen. Key players aged, and rather than finding young, up-and-coming stars as they had before, they spent like a drunken sailor in free agency, bringing in guys like Jason Giambi and Gary Sheffield. What ended up happening is they paid a premium for past performance, and while many of these pickups weren't bad, they were on the decline.
Rather than have general manager Brian Cashman or Steinbrenner face the music, Torre was the easy scapegoat.
At the end of the day, the league will try to make it harder for a dynasty to continue leveraging whatever it was that gave it an advantage. Meanwhile, the rest of the teams will start emulating you, reducing the value of what originally set you apart. And while a manager has a lot of responsibility for what happens on the field, he ultimately is the low man on the totem pole in the leadership hierarchy.
Roberts can't control how players age. He can't control how Andrew Friedman adds to the roster. He can't control what MLB does to legislate the Dodgers' advantage out of the game. And he'll eventually learn the same fate that Torre learned.
The Dodgers will still win a lot of games, but these external factors will keep them from reaching the summit, and he'll get the pink slip before anyone else is held accountable for the deterioration of the Los Angeles juggernaut.

item.title: [MLB.com] What Dodgers can learn from Ohtani's injury-plagued 2026
item.dc:creator: Sonja Chen
item.description: LOS ANGELES -- As lingering injuries began to take their toll on Shohei Ohtani during the regular season, the Dodgers frequently returned to the same refrain: What mattered most was him feeling the best he could in October. Coming off extended rest from his time on the IL and the bye during the Wild Card round, Ohtani neither performed nor looked like he was feeling as good as he could during the postseason run. He broke out with his first homer in nearly two months in Game 4 of the NL Champions
item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES -- As lingering injuries began to take their toll on Shohei Ohtani during the regular season, the Dodgers frequently returned to the same refrain: What mattered most was him feeling the best he could in October.
Coming off extended rest from his time on the IL and the bye during the Wild Card round, Ohtani neither performed nor looked like he was feeling as good as he could during the postseason run. He broke out with his first homer in nearly two months in Game 4 of the NL Championship Series, but it was too little, too late as the Dodgers' season came to an abrupt end in a sweep at the hands of the Brewers last Thursday.
Ohtani was one of several L.A. hitters going through an ill-timed slump, but his ongoing right biceps and left knee injuries could have been managed better by the Dodgers, and perhaps himself. Learning from what went wrong this year will be critical as Ohtani plans to return to a full two-way role for the 2027 season.
"I haven't been able to really come to grip in terms of what I've learned overall this season," Ohtani said through interpreter Will Ireton following the Dodgers' elimination. "It's something that I'm going to kind of go back to the drawing board in terms of treatment, training program, and see what I can come up with for next season."
There is no blueprint for handling a two-way player, so the Dodgers have had to rely heavily on conversations with Ohtani to manage his workload and his health. But as is common with star players, the team had to take Ohtani's self-assessment with a grain of salt.
"The communication back and forth has been awesome," president of baseball operations Andrew Friedman said after Ohtani came off the IL. "The fully sharing exactly how he's feeling, maybe not as awesome."
The Dodgers were proactive with Ohtani's health at times, separating his pitching and hitting workloads or giving him a full day off after his starts on the mound. But they did not skip his pitching starts or place him on the IL until it became abundantly clear that he was physically compromised.
Here's a timeline of some of the key injury-related events from Ohtani's 2026 season, including some of the inflection points where the Dodgers could have acted differently:
June 11: Ohtani exits with left knee inflammation
Ohtani's knee injury first became public knowledge the night after a start on the mound in Pittsburgh. The Dodgers initially believed he aggravated his knee on a stolen-base attempt, but Ohtani later said that something awry with his pitching mechanics may have been the cause.
July 3: Ohtani exits with right biceps tightness
Ohtani made a quality start on the mound, but he was later pinch-hit for due to biceps discomfort that he said had also bothered him "a couple months ago." This was Ohtani's final pitching start of the season. After recording a 0.74 ERA through his first 10 starts, he recorded a 4.38 ERA through his last four starts, which all came while he was dealing with the knee injury.
July 19: Ohtani out of rotation indefinitely
Citing his ongoing knee irritation, the Dodgers scratched Ohtani from his scheduled final first-half start on July 10. They were hopeful that he would make his first start after the All-Star break after receiving a lubricating Orthovisc injection, but they changed their plans after he continued to experience knee discomfort.
July 25: Ohtani shut down from throwing
Three days after Ohtani threw a full bullpen session in Philadelphia -- which seemed to take some Dodgers personnel by surprise -- he was indefinitely shut down from throwing due to regression with his knee.
Aug. 8: Ohtani starts throwing progression
After going more than two weeks without throwing, Ohtani started playing catch to begin a ramp up to get back on the mound. He seemed to be making linear progress, advancing to a bullpen session on Aug. 14 and facing hitters on Aug. 23. But this is when his production as a hitter began to drop off, as he hit .205 with a .666 OPS through his final 29 regular-season games beginning on Aug. 8.
Aug. 29: Ohtani's return to mound pushed back
Sept. 3: Ohtani misses the first of four straight games
After a game where Ohtani looked particularly physically compromised at the plate, the Dodgers decided to rest him indefinitely. They went back and forth about whether putting him on the IL made sense, with general manager Brandon Gomes saying it "hasn't even been something that we've discussed" on Sept. 3. When Ohtani returned to the lineup on Sept. 7, he said he would focus exclusively on hitting for the rest of the season, the first definitive comments from him or the team on whether he would pitch again in 2026.
Sept. 11: Ohtani placed on 15-day IL
After missing six of the Dodgers' previous seven games, Ohtani was placed on the IL. Manager Dave Roberts admitted that, with the benefit of hindsight, he would have preferred to have put him on the IL earlier. Ohtani was sidelined for a minimum-length stint and returned for the final five games of the regular season.
Oct. 13: Dodgers discuss sitting Ohtani in NLCS Game 3
Ohtani went 3-for-20 with no extra-base hits through his first six postseason games, leading the top Dodgers brass to have a conversation with Ohtani about whether he should play in NLCS Game 3. Ohtani convinced them that he felt good enough to play -- and indeed, looked better in Games 3 and 4. But his brief turnaround did not change things for the Dodgers.
If anything could have changed how the season ended for Ohtani, it may have been more proactivity back when his injury saga began.

item.title: [The Korea Herald] Dodgers swept out of NLCS, management under fire
item.dc:creator: Edwin Choi
item.description: The Los Angeles Dodgers' bid for a third straight World Series title ended abruptly with a four-game sweep by the Milwaukee Brewers in the National League Championship Series, putting manager Dave Roberts back under scrutiny despite one of the most successful managerial runs in baseball. Milwaukee advanced to the World Series for the first time since 1982 after winning all four games of the NLCS. Los Angeles, widely viewed as a championship favorite entering the season, struggled to turn early l
item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers' bid for a third straight World Series title ended abruptly with a four-game sweep by the Milwaukee Brewers in the National League Championship Series, putting manager Dave Roberts back under scrutiny despite one of the most successful managerial runs in baseball.
Milwaukee advanced to the World Series for the first time since 1982 after winning all four games of the NLCS. Los Angeles, widely viewed as a championship favorite entering the season, struggled to turn early leads into wins and was eliminated without taking a game in the series.
Roberts drew criticism for several decisions during the series, including his use of pinch hitters and his willingness to stay with players who were struggling offensively.
Brewers manager Pat Murphy, however, said the expectations surrounding the Dodgers make Roberts' job unusually demanding.
"Anything short of a championship is considered a failure," Murphy said, according to DodgerBlue.
Murphy said the Dodgers remain a team he respects, pointing to their star power and consecutive World Series championships in 2024 and 2025. He said beating a club of that stature made Milwaukee's own run more meaningful.
He also noted that Roberts operates under constant pressure because of the Dodgers' payroll, roster and recent success.
"I don't think there's anyone in a tougher or lonelier position than Dave Roberts," Murphy said. "When anything other than winning it all is viewed as failure, that is a very difficult standard to live with."
Roberts has nevertheless built a lengthy record of success in Los Angeles.
The Dodgers have reached the postseason in each of his 11 seasons as manager, winning 10 division titles. They have recorded six 100-win seasons, finished with the National League's best regular-season record five times and won three World Series championships during his tenure.
Roberts also has 72 postseason victories, the second-most by a manager in major league history. His .621 career winning percentage is the highest among managers since Jackie Robinson broke Major League Baseball's color barrier in 1947, according to DodgerBlue.
The Brewers' sweep was notable because Los Angeles scored first in every game but failed to hold those advantages. Milwaukee repeatedly rallied and ultimately controlled the series both offensively and defensively.
Murphy said that persistence was central to Milwaukee's success.
He described his roster as a group that continued to compete regardless of the Dodgers' reputation or collection of star players, and said the Brewers entered the series determined to prove they could beat the two-time defending champions.
For Roberts, the result means another offseason in which his decisions will be examined closely. But Murphy argued that the Dodgers' loss should not erase the consistency Roberts has maintained over more than a decade in charge.
(This article was produced with the assistance of AI. — Ed.)

item.title: [Dodger Blue] Kyle Tucker makes promise to Dodgers fans
item.dc:creator: Matt Borelli
item.description: Kyle Tucker struggled for the better part of his first season with the Los Angeles Dodgers, but he was able to finish the year on a strong note. The four-time All-Star emerged as arguably the team’s most productive hitter in October, batting .333/.419/.519 with two doubles, one home run and two RBI across 31 plate appearances. He reached base safely in all eight postseason games and recorded at least one hit in seven of them. Tucker finally looked like the player the Dodgers expected when they s
item.content:encoded:
Kyle Tucker struggled for the better part of his first season with the Los Angeles Dodgers, but he was able to finish the year on a strong note.
The four-time All-Star emerged as arguably the team’s most productive hitter in October, batting .333/.419/.519 with two doubles, one home run and two RBI across 31 plate appearances. He reached base safely in all eight postseason games and recorded at least one hit in seven of them.
Tucker finally looked like the player the Dodgers expected when they signed him to a four-year, $240 million contract ahead of the 2026 season. He largely underperformed up until the playoffs, batting just .233/.330/.385 with 23 doubles, four triples, 17 home runs and 70 RBI in 154 regular-season games.
Tucker thanked Dodgers fans for their support in an Instagram post and vowed to come back stronger next season.
Tucker’s first season with the Dodgers was nothing short of disappointing, but he found some success when it mattered most and will now look to build on that momentum in 2027.
While the Dodgers’ roster could undergo some changes during the offseason, Tucker remains an important part of their potential success going forward. He is unlikely to be traded this offseason due to his contract and uncertainty over the looming MLB lockout.
However, Tucker could potentially reach free agency after the 2027 season by exercising a player option. That may only be feasible if he is able to bounce back and have a year that’s more up to his standards.
Kyle Tucker made key adjustments
Tucker first started showing some signs of a turnaround on Sept. 4, when he crushed a home run on a 99 mph fastball at the top of the strike zone. He continued to have success down the stretch, which Dodgers manager Dave Roberts attributed to figuring out his swing mechanics.
“I’m not a person that’s talking about mechanics too often, but I do think in this particular situation, he’s cleaned up his bat path and he’s staying in the hitting zone a lot longer,” Roberts said at the time. “Whereas before, breaking balls, he wasn’t staying on. Fastballs, he was underneath.
“But I think right now, he’s in a great spot mechanically and with the confidence he has in his swing.”
