item.title: [rafu.com] 'We Just Got Beat:' Roberts, Ohtani Give Credit to Brewers After NLCS Sweep - Rafu Shimpo
item.dc:creator: Michael Culross
item.description: By MIKEY HIRANO CULROSS Rafu Sports Editor Shohei Ohtani flung his bat into the air, exulted toward the sky, and for one shining moment, the improbable seemed more than merely possible. The ball hadn’t yet landed in the right-field pavilion, but the Dodgers and their fans were in full-tilt celebration. Not just because their superstar had hit a home run, but it was a sign that the team’s offensive malaise might finally be breaking, that for the first time in the series, the ball would be bouncin
item.content:encoded:
By MIKEY HIRANO CULROSS
Rafu Sports Editor
Shohei Ohtani flung his bat into the air, exulted toward the sky, and for one shining moment, the improbable seemed more than merely possible.
The ball hadn’t yet landed in the right-field pavilion, but the Dodgers and their fans were in full-tilt celebration. Not just because their superstar had hit a home run, but it was a sign that the team’s offensive malaise might finally be breaking, that for the first time in the series, the ball would be bouncing their way.
The notion of a three-peat for the back-to-back world champs was still alive, regardless of the long odds. At this moment, the team many expected to return to the World Series – and win it – appeared to be returning to form.
The joy was a distant memory by the time Kiké Hernandez’ fly ball settled into left-fielder Jackson Chourio’s glove for the final out of the ninth inning on Thursday, as the Milwaukee Brewers swept the Dodgers in the National League Championship Series and booked their first trip to the World Series since 1982.
In perhaps returning the favor from last year, when the Dodgers won four straight against the Brewers, Milwaukee was the better team in essentially every aspect of the game: starting pitching, relief pitching, batting, situational hitting … they simply played winning baseball.
“They played flawless. They really did,” Dodger manager Dave Roberts said in the postgame press conference, after the visiting Brewers overcame a 4-0 deficit and scored six unanswered runs to complete the sweep.
“I think for me, it never feels good to lose, but when you get beat, you can handle it a little bit better,” Roberts said after addressing his team following the loss. “I had a good conversation with the guys in there, and just told them how proud I was. I’m not used to those speeches, those consolation speeches.”
The Brewers had the best record in the major leagues this season, winning 103 games, while L.A. was runner-up with 100 victories.
“For us, it was just pitting two really good ball clubs against one another, and they won out,” Roberts added.
Ohtani’s three-run shot in the second inning was the sole home run of the series for the Dodgers, who had relied heavily on the long ball for wins late in the regular season and into the playoffs.
“I’m very disappointed, but the Brewers are a very good team; you have to give them credit,” Ohtani said through an interpreter in the home clubhouse. “They were able to expose some of our weaknesses.”
For Ohtani, the weaknesses weren’t just stats on a page. He’s been dealing with power-sapping infirmities for months, including a sore right shoulder and gimpy left knee. His last home run came nearly two months prior to Thursday’s shot, and the team shut down his pitching game at the end of July.
He said he is completely committed to returning as a two-way player in 2027, using the off-season to focus on rest, rehab and recovery.
In this year’s NLCS, Ohtani finished batting a paltry .192 with only one home run and 10 strikeouts in 26 at-bats. He had struggled atthe plate to the point there was talk of the unthinkable – Roberts not him starting in Game 4.
After some serious conversation, the manager went with his superstar in the lineup, and early on, at least, it paid off.
“I’ll always trust Shohei. I think he’s the best player on the planet, and he’s not completely healthy,” Roberts explained. “I just give him a lot of respect for not running from it, still wanting to participate, still wanting to play when he’s not 100 percent.”
Roberts noted the rare display of emotion from the Japanese star once the Game 4 home run ball left his bat.
“It was something that you don’t see very often from Shohei. I think it was a lot of pent-up anger, frustration. It was the best ball he hit in probably two, three months, and it was a big hit.
“So I think that for him to look at the dugout, show that emotion, it just shows how much he cares. He’s still human. He still cares and wants to help his team win a baseball game. That was a big hit.”
As gracious as Roberts, Ohtani and the rest of the Dodgers were in defeat, the sting was clear in their voices.
“I’m tremendously grateful for the time we have spent as a team, even though we fell short this year,” Ohtani said. “I want to use this feeling as a catalyst for next season.”
Max Muncy, whose frustrations were laid bare in Game 4 after he struck out with a tying run at third base and slammed his bat to the ground, said he and the Dodgers gave it their best.
“We left it all out there, but the train finally ran out of steam,” Muncy conceded.
The Dodgers were vying to become the first National League team to win three straight World Series titles. The New York Yankees achieved from 1998 to 2000, following the Oakland A’s from 1972 to 1974.
“I certainly think that I wish it was us going to the World Series and defending our crown, but those guys, they earned it, and it’s going to be a heck of a World Series,” Roberts said.
Heading into Game 3 in the American League Championship Series, the Cleveland Guardians held a 2-1 lead over the Tampa Bay Rays. The game scheduled for Friday has been pushed back to Saturday due to weather.
The Brewers and Rays are among the five MLB teams that have never won a World Series, along with the San Diego Padres, Seattle Mariners and Colorado Rockies.

item.title: [aol.com] Shohei Ohtani's health and a possible lockout loom over an uncertain offseason for the Dodgers - AOL
item.dc:creator: BETH HARRIS
item.description: LOS ANGELES (AP) — After their earliest postseason exit in three years, the Los Angeles Dodgers head into the offseason facing uncertainty over next year. Shohei Ohtani was dogged by injuries to his left knee and right biceps over the second half and into the playoffs that rendered him ineffective at the plate. The two-way superstar also didn't pitch after the All-Star break. Whether Ohtani needs offseason surgery remains to be seen, although he acknowledged it's possible after Thursday's loss t
item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES (AP) — After their earliest postseason exit in three years, the Los Angeles Dodgers head into the offseason facing uncertainty over next year.
Shohei Ohtani was dogged by injuries to his left knee and right biceps over the second half and into the playoffs that rendered him ineffective at the plate. The two-way superstar also didn't pitch after the All-Star break.
Whether Ohtani needs offseason surgery remains to be seen, although he acknowledged it's possible after Thursday's loss to the Brewers that completed Milwaukee's sweep of the NL Championship Series. If he does, would the recovery bleed into the start of next season?
A potential MLB lockout is looming with the current collective bargaining agreement set to expire on Dec. 1. Team owners have proposed a salary cap — something the sport has never had — and the players' union has adamantly rejected the idea.
A work stoppage would give Ohtani extra time to heal, although during such time the Dodgers would be cut off from communicating with any player, leaving Ohtani to rehab either from possible surgery or from his injuries on his own.
Communication between Ohtani and the team on his health during the season was “awesome,” Andrew Friedman, president of baseball operations, said last month, but he added: “The fully sharing exactly how he's feeling, maybe not so awesome.”
Ohtani said he plans to resume pitching next year, when he'll turn 33 in July. He's already had two Tommy John surgeries.
“What he’s doing is unprecedented, and it takes a real toll,” Friedman said. “And as you get older, I think us just being very dialed is going to be really important.”
Roster turnover is likely, even without big changes in MLB spending rules
The Dodgers had baseball's second-highest opening day payroll this year at $323.3 million, behind the New York Mets at $358.4 million. If a salary cap were to be imposed, the Dodgers' spending would be constrained when play resumes.
Some of the roster could look different next year, too, with nine players set to become free agents after the World Series, led by two-time Cy Young Award winner Tarik Skubal, who is expected to command a huge deal.
The Dodgers acquired Skubal from Detroit just before the trade deadline in August. The left-hander was 5-2 with a 2.61 ERA and 70 strikeouts in 10 regular-season games for his new team. In the postseason, he was 1-1 with a 2.45 ERA and 14 Ks. Skubal didn't want to discuss his future Thursday, although he expressed enthusiasm for the organization, his teammates and the fans.
Advertisement
Other impending free agents are infielder Miguel Rojas, utility player Kiké Hernández, and relievers Kris Bubic, Brusdar Graterol, Eric Lauer, Evan Phillips, Blake Treinen and Alex Vesia.
As expected, Rojas announced his retirement Thursday, saying, “This is it, guys. That was my last game played.” He'll still be around, though, to work in a player development role.
Dodgers add a bit of youth with De Paula
The Dodgers got a glimpse of the future when they promoted Josue De Paula directly from Double-A to the majors in September. His energy and at-bats at designated hitter during Ohtani's stint on the injured list made an impression, and the 21-year-old was added to the postseason roster as a pinch-hitter.
The team will look to De Paula to further improve as an outfielder in 2027, although finding playing time for him will be challenging given the trio of veteran starters: Teoscar Hernández, Andy Pages and Kyle Tucker. De Paula is also blocked at DH by Ohtani.
“I think the experience he got being up here and watching what our guys do on a daily basis just helped connect some dots for him,” Friedman said. “And so, physically, he is capable of being a good corner outfielder, and we’re going to continue to tap into that.”
Mookie Betts, Freddie Freeman, Ohtani, Tucker, Max Muncy and Will Smith will remain the Dodgers' veteran core. But some supporting players could be offloaded, like Kiké Hernández. Playing on a one-year deal, the 35-year-old was limited to 41 games while recovering from injuries and he didn't provide his usual postseason pop.
Manager Dave Roberts refused to blame an aging lineup for getting swept by the Brewers, whose 103 regular-season wins were three more than the Dodgers.
“We got beat,” he said. “There’s no because we’re too old or whatever. Every facet of the game, if you kind of unpack it, we were bested.”
There's drama off the field, too.
Owner Mark Walter was noticeably absent from the team's playoff games. He is facing multiple federal investigations into his business empire for possible financial improprieties involving insurance companies he controls. Walter has denied any wrongdoing. Since August, he sold his controlling interest in the Los Angeles Lakers and last month he unloaded his share in Chelsea of the Premier League.
___

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] As Dodgers grapple with the end of a dynasty, questions abound for Shohei Ohtani, free agency and the coming labor fight
item.dc:creator: Jake Mintz
item.description: LOS ANGELES — In the end, the unfamiliarity outshined the shock. The defeated 2026 Los Angeles Dodgers, many of them back-to-back champs, hadn't been forced to face this uncomfortable silence in a while. A four-game drubbing courtesy of the Milwaukee Brewers in a stunningly comprehensive NLCS sweep cast onto the most expensive team ever assembled a very foreign feeling: failure. Milwaukee, so often bounced early in the October melee, knows that discomfort and its soundtrack. That unsettling hush
item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES — In the end, the unfamiliarity outshined the shock.
The defeated 2026 Los Angeles Dodgers, many of them back-to-back champs, hadn't been forced to face this uncomfortable silence in a while. A four-game drubbing courtesy of the Milwaukee Brewers in a stunningly comprehensive NLCS sweep cast onto the most expensive team ever assembled a very foreign feeling: failure.
Milwaukee, so often bounced early in the October melee, knows that discomfort and its soundtrack. That unsettling hush that comes with the humbling unmooring of a premature postseason exit. Hugs, daps, thank yous, low-volume answers, goodbyes, regrets. But here it was, here the Dodgers were, in the tricked-out home clubhouse grappling with the end of something.
On one side of the room, Shohei Ohtani stood in front of his locker before a massive semicircle of reporters and TV cameras. For the first time in his MLB career, he'd lost a postseason series. His signing with L.A. ahead of the 2024 season sparked this era of supercharged dominance. And for eight October series his Dodgers were untouchable. Usually, during this spot in the calendar, Ohtani is getting drenched in imitation champagne as Latin rap and joyous roars echo in the background.
The scene Thursday night was a drier, quieter experience.
Join or create a Yahoo Fantasy Basketball league for the 2026-27 NBA season
This seemingly indomitable baseball behemoth donned street clothes and a New Balance backward cap, small beads of sweat still pooling on his face, trying to explain what went wrong and where he goes from here.
"I haven't been able to really come to grips in terms of what I've learned overall this season," Ohtani said via interpreter Will Ireton. "I'm going to go back to the drawing board in terms of treatment, training program and see what I can come up with next season."
The postmortem on Los Angeles' crash-out can be as extensive as you choose to make it. But simply put, they were the inferior team. Slower, older, colder and less fearsome than the hard-charging Brewers. Baseball's most aged offense failed to slug and didn't perform with runners in scoring position. One of the most talented rotations ever assembled wasn't dominant enough to make up the difference.
All season, the Dodgers touted their experience as a calling card. Perhaps, if the series had been closer, that might have mattered. As it stands, it's less necessary to assign blame when so much went wrong.
"I think for me, it never feels good to lose, but when you get beat, you can handle it a little bit better," manager Dave Roberts said after his team's 6-4 loss in Game 4.
The morning after, fans across the baseball universe are celebrating the Dodgers' downfall. They aren't the only ones. As Milwaukee's champagne celebration roared in the visiting clubhouse, Brewers coaches and executives were already receiving texts of appreciation and congratulations on slaying the mighty dragon.
But don't expect the upcoming small-market Fall Classic to remedy baseball's impending labor struggle. With the current collective bargaining agreement set to expire on Dec. 1, the league and the owners have been pushing hard for the adoption of a salary cap. Certainly, that argument becomes at least somewhat trickier to make with the half-billion-dollar boogeyman Dodgers on vacation, but the league won't suddenly change course after four games. The showdown over a cap was always going to be drawn-out and messy, no matter which team is the last one standing.
For the Dodgers organization, the uncertainty about baseball's future further complicates what was always going to be a critical offseason. One October exit won't kill off this juggernaut. Neither will a new economic landscape. The Dodgers remain advantageously positioned to compete for championships over the next decade and beyond. That's a testament to both their player-development prowess and their imposing spending power.
But the questions are already piling on Andrew Friedman's desk. Surely, the president of baseball operations is already considering the future and how this winter will shape the 2027 Dodgers.
No task is more important than figuring out what went wrong with Ohtani's season. For three months, the two-way star was, for the first time as a Dodger, doing full two-way stardom. Another MVP felt like an inevitability. Then his biceps started barking. A start on the mound was pushed back, then scratched, then so was another. Ohtani didn't throw a single in-game pitch after July 3.
His attempts to get back on the mound then appeared to compromise his offensive talents. He got ice-cold in late August into September. His physicality began to fray. His body wasn't right. Eventually, the Dodgers had no choice but to place him on the injured list. Only over the last two days of the Dodgers' postseason did Ohtani look anything like himself.
Communication with the four-time MVP has rarely been perfect. Some of that is the language barrier. Some of that is Ohtani's lone ranger approach. But now both sides need to evaluate why a diminished version of Ohtani was forced to play through pain. After the Game 4 loss, Ohtani told reporters that he intends to pitch next season. In what capacity remains to be seen. It might behoove the Dodgers to slow-play his recovery timeline to ensure he's available when they need him most — in the postseason.
There are a mountain of transactional questions as well. Tarik Skubal, added in a deadline blockbuster, is now a free agent. Will the Dodgers flex their muscles to re-sign him? Or do they want to give younger arms such as Roki Sasaki, Emmet Sheehan and Justin Wrobleski some rotation runway? What about upper-level pitching prospects such as Christian Zazueta, Zach Root, Adam Serwinowski and Jackson Ferris? Could they let Skubal walk in favor of a different free-agent starter? Freddy Peralta has looked pretty good recently.
Positionally, though, is where Los Angeles' bigger roster-construction conversations will take place. They got mollywhopped by Milwaukee in part because the Dodgers' offense looked unathletic and elderly. Friedman has expressed a desire to inject more youth into the group, but that's easier said than done. A number of spots feel set in stone: Ohtani at DH, Will Smith at catcher, Freddie Freeman at first, Mookie Betts at short, Kyle Tucker in right field, Andy Pages in center.
Max Muncy (3B) and Teoscar Hernández (LF) are older players expected to reach free agency after 2027. A trade of either could be a way to reshuffle the deck, with Hernández the likelier to go. Tommy Edman had a second straight mediocre, injury-marred campaign, but he has four seasons left on his contract. Might the Dodgers seek a suitor for the switch-hitting utilityman?
Even after harvesting the farm for the Skubal trade, Los Angeles has one of the most stocked systems in the sport. Most of their prospect juice is concentrated in the outfield. Five Dodgers outfield prospects at Double-A or above — Josue De Paula, Eduardo Quintero, Mike Sirota, Charles Davalan and James Tibbs III — could find themselves on offseason top-100 lists. De Paula, who impressed in a late-season cup of coffee, Quintero and Sirota are currently ranked fourth, 15th and 17th, respectively, by MLB Pipeline.
Unfortunately for the Dodgers, you can play only three outfielders at a time. In their existing outfield, they already have the highest-paid player in the sport (Tucker) and the starting center fielder in the 2026 All-Star Game (Pages). With just one spot remaining, it'll be fascinating to see how Friedman makes use of his farm system.
For the players, none of these contingencies or scenarios will offer any short-term solace. They aimed for a three-peat and missed. That sting will take time to subside, even if the 2027 Dodgers project to be a similarly formidable force.
"We fell short, you know?" utilityman Kiké Hernández lamented postgame. "We had a good run, but here we are."

item.title: [finchannel] Miguel Rojas retires after Dodgers’ NLCS exit, with plans to remain in baseball - FINCHANNEL
item.dc:creator: The FINANCIAL
item.description: Miguel Rojas retired Thursday, October 15, at 37 after the Los Angeles Dodgers’ elimination from the National League Championship Series. The infielder’s final game ended with Milwaukee completing a four-game sweep, leaving him to discuss a planned move into another role with the organization where he began his major league career. Speaking to reporters at Dodger Stadium, Rojas confirmed that his playing career was over. True Blue LA reported that he wanted to stay with the Dodgers, with an anti
item.content:encoded:
Miguel Rojas retired Thursday, October 15, at 37 after the Los Angeles Dodgers’ elimination from the National League Championship Series. The infielder’s final game ended with Milwaukee completing a four-game sweep, leaving him to discuss a planned move into another role with the organization where he began his major league career.
Speaking to reporters at Dodger Stadium, Rojas confirmed that his playing career was over. True Blue LA reported that he wanted to stay with the Dodgers, with an anticipated emphasis on player development, although the precise role remained undetermined. His retirement was also reported by MLB.com, the Los Angeles Times and Fox’s OutKick.
Rojas finished after 13 major league seasons split between Los Angeles and the Miami Marlins. His second Dodgers stint included two World Series championships and the home run that tied Game 7 of the 2025 championship against Toronto. He returned for one final season in 2026 after signing a one-year, $5.5 million contract.
A final game without a plate appearance
Rojas played two innings at second base in Thursday’s finale but did not bat, according to True Blue LA’s account. His final two major league plate appearances had come in Game 3 on Wednesday, when he singled and walked. All seven of his plate appearances in this postseason came against left-handed pitching.
The account listed a double alongside that single and walk in his final postseason. During the 2026 regular season, he hit .293 against left-handers, with a .340 on-base percentage and .469 slugging percentage. Those figures describe his production against left-handed pitchers, rather than his overall season.
MLB’s regular-season figures show that Rojas hit .267 with four home runs and 23 runs batted in during 2026.
The Dodgers’ season ended in a 6-4 loss after they had built a four-run lead. Shohei Ohtani supplied a three-run homer in the second inning off Dustin May. Milwaukee erased the advantage by the fifth, then moved ahead on Garrett Mitchell’s sixth-inning home run against Tanner Scott.
David Hamilton added a ninth-inning solo homer. Aaron Ashby completed a three-inning save, closing a game in which Los Angeles had doubles in the sixth, seventh and eighth innings without scoring those runners. The Dodgers went 2 for 11 with runners in scoring position Thursday.
The Brewers advanced to their first World Series since 1982 and their first as a National League club. For Los Angeles, the defeat ended the pursuit of a third consecutive championship. Rojas addressed his teammates after manager Dave Roberts’s postgame meeting, according to MLB.com’s account of the clubhouse.
Returning for the last season
The decision followed a plan Rojas had discussed before the 2026 season. MLB.com’s December 2025 report on his new contract said he intended the coming year to be his last. The deal kept him in Los Angeles after an October in which he had rarely started before the final two World Series games.
True Blue LA’s report on that contract described a 2025 regular season in which he batted .262 with a .318 on-base percentage and .397 slugging percentage. He started more often at second and third base than at shortstop, the position he had played regularly earlier in his career.
His October assignment changed in Toronto. Rojas started at second base in Games 6 and 7 after starting only twice in the Dodgers’ first 15 postseason games. In Game 6, he handled the throw from left fielder Kiké Hernández to complete the double play that ended the game.
In Game 7, his solo homer with one out in the ninth tied the score. He also fielded a grounder in the bottom of that inning and threw home to prevent Toronto from scoring the winning run. The Dodgers subsequently won in extra innings.
A return trade and a changing infield role
Rojas made his Dodgers debut in 2014 before being traded to Miami that December in the larger deal involving Dee Gordon. He spent eight seasons with the Marlins, then returned to Los Angeles in January 2023 in exchange for shortstop Jake Amaya.
In eight of his first nine major league seasons, Rojas played for manager Don Mattingly. That stretch included his 2014 Dodgers debut and years in Miami, where he established himself as a regular shortstop.
The January 2023 account of the trade described a player whose defensive record offered Los Angeles experienced depth. Rojas had batted .236 in 2022, with a .283 on-base percentage and .323 slugging percentage. That season he tied Houston’s Jeremy Peña for the most Defensive Runs Saved among major league shortstops, with 15, according to the report.
He had been a National League Gold Glove finalist at shortstop in both 2020 and 2022. The Dodgers acquired him as Gavin Lux was preparing to take on a larger role at the position. Rojas also brought experience at third base and second base, giving the team alternatives across the infield.
Lux’s spring-training knee injury subsequently changed the arrangement. In a May 2024 report, True Blue LA recalled that Rojas had started 109 games during the previous season. In spring 2024, Mookie Betts was moving into an everyday shortstop role, with Rojas among those helping him make the transition.
Mentorship alongside the playing time
Roberts publicly credited Rojas, along with coaches Dino Ebel and Chris Woodward, for the work Betts had put into shortstop in 2024. The veteran’s assistance also included pregame drills and conversations during games, according to Eric Stephen’s reporting for True Blue LA.
That report described Rojas helping Lux return to second base and working with Miguel Vargas when Vargas was learning the position in 2023. Rojas invited Vargas to work out with him in Florida after being acquired by the Dodgers. He told the outlet that coaching was part of his ambition after his playing days.
In that 2024 interview, Rojas recalled Adrián González helping him as a rookie, including conversations about baseball and professional life off the field.
Three consecutive clubhouse awards
The recognition from teammates and coaches continued in September, when Rojas was voted the Dodgers’ Roy Campanella Award winner for 2026. The award honors the player judged to embody the Hall of Fame catcher’s leadership and spirit. Rojas had also won in 2024 and 2025.
According to the September account of the award, he became the first Dodger to receive it in three consecutive seasons. Justin Turner was the only other three-time recipient, with wins in 2017, 2019 and 2020.
Clayton Kershaw and Chase Utley had each won twice. Kershaw received the honor in 2013 and 2014, and Utley in 2016 and 2018.
The same report noted that Rojas had started games at second base, shortstop and third base during 2026 and had also played three innings at first. It described his plans to join the organization’s front office with a focus on developing players. Thursday’s retirement account left the precise assignment open.
Questions and answers
Did Rojas play for teams other than the Dodgers?
Yes. He spent eight major league seasons with Miami between his two periods in Los Angeles.
Was retirement already part of his plan?
He had said before the 2026 season that it would be his last as a player.
Will he stay with the Dodgers?
Rojas said he wanted to remain with the organization. Reporting described a prospective player-development role, with its precise form still undetermined.

item.title: [Sports Illustrated] What Dave Roberts Said After Dodgers Season Ended (And What it Means for This Offseason)
item.dc:creator: Gabe Smallson; Unknown
item.description: The Los Angeles Dodgers were swept by the Milwaukee Brewers in the National League Championship Series and now face a long offseason. Manager Dave Roberts recently came under fire for a few questionable decisions during Game 3's loss, and his response was reshuffling the lineup to a more familiar look than the last contest. Shohei Ohtani was back in his leadoff spot, and after an Andy Pages RBI single in the second inning, appeared to validate Roberts' move with a three-run home run to take a co
item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers were swept by the Milwaukee Brewers in the National League Championship Series and now face a long offseason.
Manager Dave Roberts recently came under fire for a few questionable decisions during Game 3's loss, and his response was reshuffling the lineup to a more familiar look than the last contest. Shohei Ohtani was back in his leadoff spot, and after an Andy Pages RBI single in the second inning, appeared to validate Roberts' move with a three-run home run to take a commanding 4-0 lead.
For just a moment, it appeared that the two-time defending champions would force a Game 5 with two-time Cy Young award winner Tarik Skubal on the mound. Unfortunately, this lasted just two frames.
Though baseball fans are able to point to many moments these past four games that reflected poorly on a Roberts decision, the offense was inexcusable all series long. During the regular season, the Dodgers hit .257 (third in MLB), but over the course of the NLCS, hit just .187.
Despite the output, nothing could change how the skipper felt about his group. Roberts spoke after the contest on how proud he is of his team.
"Extremely proud," Robert said. "It never feels good to lose and not accomplish a goal to win the World Series. It started back in the early part of February. I love this team and what we had to go through. It’s one of those things that every night we take the field, people are bringing their best to beat us."
Going into the NLCS, the Dodgers had a roster with the average age of 30.9 years old (the oldest in MLB) to the Brewers' average age of 27.3 (the 12th youngest). Roberts was asked about the factor that age played in this series, and had a response that is very telling for the team's offseason plans.
"I really appreciate the question. I just don’t think that in four games that we came up short that age was a factor," Roberts said. "What I will say is that those guys, some of the plays that [Brice] Turang made going to his right, the plays that the outfielders made, that’s certainly youth and talent.
It wasn’t that they were fatigued. We have off days going into series. I just don’t think that our age of our ball club reflected this series. We got beat.
"There’s no because we’re too old or whatever. Every facet of the game, if you kind of unpack it, we were bested."
Roberts' unwavering support of his veterans will likely enhance the trust in the clubhouse, and with a long offseason now underway, will hopefully translate into regrouping and retooling for 2027.
Sign up for our free newsletter and follow us on X/Twitter and Facebook for the latest news.
Gabe Smallson is a sportswriter based in Los Angeles with a focus in sports and entertainment content. Gabe has previously worked at Newsweek and Dodgers Nation. He graduated from San Francisco State University in 2020 and received his Masters of Science at the University of Southern California in 2025.

item.content:encoded:
Los Dodgers se fueron eliminados en la Serie del Campeonato de la Liga ante los Brewers; el equipo que comanda el bateador japonés se quedó sin la opción de pelear por el tricampeonato en la Serie Mundial luego de ser barridos por los cerveceros.
Shohei Ohtani fue pieza clave en ese bicampeonato; sin embargo, en esta temporada estuvo ausente en varias ocasiones y en los playoffs no estuvo en su mejor ritmo, del cual tiene acostumbrado hacer cosas grandes. Aunque se rumoreaba que el equipo que dirige Dave Roberts tuvo una plática sobre el momento que atravesaba Ohtani y la posibilidad de no contemplarlo para el juego 3. Aunque se dudó, el japonés pudo jugar y pelear por la remontada; sin embargo, no se pudo hacer nada ante unos Brewers imparables.
Ohtani sobre la derrota
Shohei Ohtani no ocultó su frustración después de una temporada que estuvo marcada por las dificultades físicas y un cierre complicado para los Los Angeles Dodgers.
El astro japonés reconoció su decepción y dejó claro que su objetivo es regresar con mejores sensaciones el próximo año, después de una campaña en la que tuvo que lidiar con problemas en la rodilla izquierda y el bíceps derecho, situaciones que limitaron su actividad como lanzador y condicionaron su rendimiento durante distintos momentos del calendario.
“Estoy simplemente muy decepcionado, espero tener una mejor temporada el próximo año”, expresó Ohtani, quien ahora tendrá la misión de recuperarse físicamente y preparar su regreso como jugador de dos vías para 2027.
Números de Shohei esta temporada
Aunque su campaña no fue la más productiva desde su llegada a los Dodgers, Shohei Ohtani colaboró y peleó hasta el final con su equipo, ya que conectó un batazo para darle el jonrón a su equipo.

item.title: [Dodger Blue] Miguel Rojas delivers emotional news to Dodgers clubhouse after NLCS
item.dc:creator: Matthew Moreno
item.description: When the Los Angeles Dodgers re-signed Miguel Rojas to a one-year contract it was with an expectation he would retire following the 2026 season and immediately join the front office. But Rojas began to soften on his retirement stance as the season progressed and suggested he would return in 2027 if the Dodgers completed a three-peat and were in position to again defend their title. But with that possibility ruled out following a Milwaukee Brewers sweep in the National League Championship Series,
item.content:encoded:
When the Los Angeles Dodgers re-signed Miguel Rojas to a one-year contract it was with an expectation he would retire following the 2026 season and immediately join the front office.
But Rojas began to soften on his retirement stance as the season progressed and suggested he would return in 2027 if the Dodgers completed a three-peat and were in position to again defend their title. But with that possibility ruled out following a Milwaukee Brewers sweep in the National League Championship Series, the 37-year-old closed the book on his playing career.
Miguel Rojas informs Dodgers of retirement decision
After manager Dave Roberts spoke to the clubhouse following their Game 4 loss, he turned the floor over to Rojas. He used that opportunity to thank teammates for all they’ve done and announced he was retiring.
“Now that everything is done it’s going to be really hard to take this uniform off and move on with my life,” Rojas said while speaking with media. He was still dressed in his uniform and cleats, and spoke with tears in his eyes.
“This is where I’ve been for the majority of my life. I spent 21 years in professional baseball and obviously the last four here in this clubhouse, putting this uniform on every single day has been a privilege and pleasure. It’s not the way I wanted to end it, because we always wanted to win the last game of the season. But in baseball nothing is guaranteed.”
Rojas made his MLB debut with the Dodgers in 2014 and returned to the organization in 2023.
“It’s really amazing when I think about what happened to me and my family the last few years,” he said. “I talked to the guys, it was really emotional after the game, and I told them I’m going to be loyal. I want to stay here and wear this uniform in a different capacity and continue to make the organization better. But this is it. This is it as a player.”
Primarily known as a strong defender, Rojas will forever be remembered for his game-tying home run in the ninth inning of Game 7 of the 2025 World Series. He also memorably saved Clayton Kershaw’s only no-hitter of his career with a terrific stop and throw at third base.
Have you subscribed to the Dodger Blue YouTube channel? Be sure to ring the notification bell to watch player interviews, participate in shows and giveaways, and stay up to date on all Dodgers news and rumors!

item.title: [dailyadvance.com] Brewers sweep the Dodgers in the NLCS to reach the World Series for the first time since 1982
item.dc:creator: BETH HARRIS
item.description: LOS ANGELES (AP) — Garrett Mitchell hit a go-ahead homer in the sixth inning, Milwaukee's brilliant bullpen slammed the door late and the Brewers rallied past the Los Angeles Dodgers 6-4 on Thursday in Game 4 of the National League Championship Series to earn their first World Series trip since 1982. No. 9 hitter David Hamilton's two-out solo shot off Edwin Díaz gave the Brewers a two-run cushion in the ninth. Hamilton had just four homers in the regular season. “We got down early tonight and we
item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES (AP) — Garrett Mitchell hit a go-ahead homer in the sixth inning, Milwaukee's brilliant bullpen slammed the door late and the Brewers rallied past the Los Angeles Dodgers 6-4 on Thursday in Game 4 of the National League Championship Series to earn their first World Series trip since 1982.
No. 9 hitter David Hamilton's two-out solo shot off Edwin Díaz gave the Brewers a two-run cushion in the ninth. Hamilton had just four homers in the regular season.
“We got down early tonight and we were like, it’s going to be a great story,” Brewers captain Christian Yelich said. “We’re going to come back and win this. Like, stay together, start chipping away. And that’s exactly what they did.”
Aaron Ashby pitched three scoreless innings for a save as the Brewers erased a four-run deficit to win their first NL pennant and second overall. Milwaukee was in the American League when the franchise made its only previous World Series appearance 44 years ago, a seven-game loss to the St. Louis Cardinals.
Shohei Ohtani's first home run this postseason helped put the Dodgers ahead 4-0 in the second inning before the Brewers came back to complete a four-game sweep of the two-time defending World Series champions a year after getting swept by Los Angeles in the NLCS.
“They may have a bunch of Hall of Famers, but we’ve got a bunch of gamers — and the gamers won this week,” Milwaukee manager Pat Murphy said.
The Dodgers' goal of a three-peat — not done since the New York Yankees from 1998-2000 and never by a National League team — died with their anemic offense and injuries to Ohtani and others on their aging roster.
“I'm not used to those consolation speeches,” manager Dave Roberts said. “The thing about sports that we all love is no matter how much you prepare, you want it, there’s no guarantees.”
After topping the majors with 103 wins during the regular season, Milwaukee became the first major league club to finish a postseason sweep after getting swept by that same opponent in the previous postseason.
The Brewers also are the first team to sweep a best-of-seven postseason series in which it trailed in every game.
“There was never a doubt in that dugout what was going to happen tonight. We knew we were going to win that game,” said first baseman Jake Bauers, the NLCS MVP.
With the score tied 4-all, Mitchell fell behind 0-2 before reliever Tanner Scott threw three straight balls for a full count. Mitchell’s 409-foot leadoff drive to center field — the first homer of his career on an 0-2 count — put the Brewers ahead for the first time. Mitchell also homered in their 6-2 victory Wednesday.
“It’s absolutely surreal," Mitchell said. "You talk about the battle-tested Brewers. We went down early and the belief in that dugout got stronger and stronger.”
The Brewers’ bullpen coolly turned away multiple threats when the Dodgers had the potential tying run on base.
Winning pitcher JoJo Romero struck out Max Muncy with Kyle Tucker at third to end the sixth.
With one out in the seventh and a runner on third, Ashby struck out Ohtani swinging before Mookie Betts grounded out to end the inning. Will Smith doubled to right with one out in the eighth and was safe at third when the ball got away from Sal Frelick for an error before Ashby got Tucker to fly out and Teoscar Hernández to strike out.
“Playing with that chip on our shoulder,” Ashby said. “You don’t ever know what to expect going into a series like that last year (against the Dodgers). You don’t know how bad it can be, and then it was as bad as it was. And we came out and we survived, and we came back this year, and those guys played their tails off.”
The Brewers tied it in the fifth, when the Dodgers bullpen issued four walks and Milwaukee stole two bases. Hamilton’s single chased starter Tyler Glasnow and scored Frelick, who walked and stole second, to pull Milwaukee to 4-3.
Alex Vesia came in and promptly walked Brice Turang and William Contreras to load the bases. Vesia then walked Bauers with two outs to force in Hamilton with the tying run.
Glasnow retired his first 10 batters — six on strikeouts — before the Brewers got to him in the fourth. Turang walked, Contreras hit a ground-rule double and Bauers followed with another ground-rule double that closed Milwaukee to 4-2.
Ohtani broke out of his postseason slump with a three-run homer after Andy Pages’ RBI single in the second. The four-time MVP released weeks of pent-up frustration by raising his arms and yelling and the crowd of 49,104 joined him in celebration.
But the Brewers wouldn't be denied. And when it was over, owner Mark Attanasio thought of Milwaukee's longtime owner and beloved late broadcaster.
“It’s so important for the community, the entire state of Wisconsin,” Attanasio said. “We’re standing on shoulders of Bud Selig and Bob Uecker.”

item.title: [sgvtribune.com] Dodgers’ Shohei Ohtani returns to leadoff spot for must-win Game 4
item.dc:creator: Bill Plunkett
item.description: LOS ANGELES — Desperate times call for … unexpected measures. Two days after admitting he had a conversation with Shohei Ohtani about taking him out of the lineup for Game 3 of the National League Championship Series and one day after dropping him to sixth in the order for that game, Dodgers manager Dave Roberts moved Ohtani back to the top of the lineup. Ohtani was in the leadoff spot for Game 4 against the Milwaukee Brewers on Thursday. It was his first time batting leadoff this postseason. “J
item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES — Desperate times call for … unexpected measures.
Two days after admitting he had a conversation with Shohei Ohtani about taking him out of the lineup for Game 3 of the National League Championship Series and one day after dropping him to sixth in the order for that game, Dodgers manager Dave Roberts moved Ohtani back to the top of the lineup.
Ohtani was in the leadoff spot for Game 4 against the Milwaukee Brewers on Thursday. It was his first time batting leadoff this postseason.
“Just seeing the work the last couple days, I like where his head is at,” Roberts said. “I liked the at-bats yesterday, and I felt that trying to shake it up a little bit – obviously we haven’t performed the way that we’re capable of, so to kind of shake it up a little bit but something that’s of somewhat normalcy that our guys are used to.”
Ohtani is just 4 for 22 (.182) in the postseason, but that hardly stands out in the unproductive lineup. Through the first three games of the NLCS, the Dodgers were hitting .165 (15 for 91) as a team with just two extra-base hits and no home runs. Only Mookie Betts (3 for 12) had more than two hits.
“I think getting back to what we’ve done all year and how it’s been going recently as far as on the offense, I think it warranted just a little bit of a shakeup,” said Roberts, who also started Miguel Rojas and Kiké Hernandez against Brewers left-hander Shane Drohan.
PHILLY CONNECTION
Before re-signing Don Mattingly to a contract extension as manager, the Philadelphia Phillies reached out to two members of the Dodgers’ front office with Philly connections – Chase Utley and Raul Ibañez.
Neither would confirm the contact, but neither interviewed for the job. Both have teen-aged children and Utley acknowledged family takes priority over pursuing a managerial career at this point.
Ibañez, currently the Dodgers’ vice president of baseball development and special projects, has been approached about managing on other occasions but declined. Utley is a special assistant to Dodgers president of baseball operations Andrew Friedman.
AWARDS SEASON
Despite his injuries and a prolonged slump, Ohtani is one of the National League finalists for the Hank Aaron Award given to the top offensive performer in MLB during the regular season. Ohtani finished the season with a .275 average, 30 home runs and an .889 OPS. Ohtani has won it the past three seasons (twice in the NL and once with the Angels in the American League).
The other finalists are CJ Abrams (Washington Nationals), Jake Bauers (Milwaukee Brewers), Pete Crow-Armstrong (Chicago Cubs), Elly De La Cruz and Sal Stewart (Cincinnati Reds), Matt Olson (Atlanta Braves), Kyle Schwarber (Philadelphia Phillies), Fernando Tatis Jr. (San Diego Padres) and Jordan Walker (St. Louis Cardinals).
Ohtani is also one of three finalists for the Players’ Choice Outstanding Player Award along with Crow-Armstrong and Schwarber.
Max Muncy and Andy Pages have been named finalists for Gold Glove awards at their positions. Muncy is a finalist at third base along with Alex Bregman (Cubs) and Javier Sanoja (Miami Marlins). Pages is a finalist in center field along with Crow-Armstrong and Michael Harris II (Braves).
The Gold Glove winners will be announced on ESPN on Nov. 1.
UP NEXT
NLCS Game 5 (if necessary): Brewers (RHP Jacob Misiorowski, 16-5, 1.80 ERA) at Dodgers (LHP Tarik Skubal, 12-7, 2.72 ERA), Friday, 6 p.m. FS1, 570 AM

item.title: [sgvtribune.com] Dodgers three-peat bid ends with NLCS sweep by Brewers
item.dc:creator: Bill Plunkett
item.description: LOS ANGELES — In the end, it was all too much – coming back from a 3-0 deficit, winning a third consecutive World Series championship. Shohei Ohtani came back to life after two months of ugly at-bats, unfamiliar criticism and questions about whether he even belonged in the Dodgers’ lineup. His three-run home run in the second inning on Thursday night gave the Dodgers a four-run lead – unheard of in this postseason of run suppression. item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES — In the end, it was all too much – coming back from a 3-0 deficit, winning a third consecutive World Series championship.
Shohei Ohtani came back to life after two months of ugly at-bats, unfamiliar criticism and questions about whether he even belonged in the Dodgers’ lineup. His three-run home run in the second inning on Thursday night gave the Dodgers a four-run lead – unheard of in this postseason of run suppression.
That wasn’t enough to keep their season alive against a relentless Milwaukee Brewers team that just kept coming, taking a 6-4 win in Game 4 on Thursday to complete a four-game sweep of the two-time defending champions and advance from the National League Championship Series to their first World Series in 44 years.
After falling behind on Garrett Mitchell’s home run off Tanner Scott in the sixth inning, the Dodgers put the tying run on third base with one out in the sixth, seventh and eighth innings but couldn’t move him another 90 feet. Their dreams of a three-peat were buried under another collection of failed at-bats with a runner in scoring position. They went 2 for 11 in those situations in Game 4 and 5 for 43 in the postseason.
“As a manager and anyone participating in the game, you always wonder … could we have done something different that could have changed the game?” Dodgers manager Dave Roberts said. “I think at the end of the day, we got beat. We got outplayed in all facets. Those guys played flawless defensively. They pitched better than we did. They hit better than we did. They slugged more than we did. You’ve got to sometimes just tip your cap.
“I personally told our guys that there’s no apologies, there’s no ‘Sorry’s. We gave it everything we had, and it wasn’t good enough. That’s part of life.”
The New York Yankees of 1998-2000 are still the most recent team to ‘three-peat’ as World Series champions. A National League franchise still hasn’t done it.
“It’s hard to win one. We won two,” Freddie Freeman said. “We went for three and we came up short on a third. Special stuff the past two years. We just came up short this year.”
After losing Game 3 on Wednesday night to become the 42nd team in MLB history to fall behind 3-0 in a best-of-seven series, the Dodgers said all the right things about becoming just the second to climb out of that hole and win the series.
“Four one-game winning streaks,” Dodgers utility player Kiké Hernandez said.
“We’ve won four in a row a number of times this year, ten times, I think,” Manager Dave Roberts said.
Ohtani gave them reason to believe.
With the Brewers rolling out a ‘bullpen game’ in Game 4, opener Shane Drohan was gone after a leadoff single by Kyle Tucker in the second inning. Former Dodger Dustin May replaced him and gave up another single to Teoscar Hernandez, struck out Max Muncy then gave up an RBI single to Andy Pages – the only Dodger who seemed able to hit with a runner in scoring position this postseason.
Kiké Hernandez flew out, bringing Ohtani to the plate with two outs. He struck out against Drohan in the first inning but had finished Game 3 with a 113.5 mph exit velocity on an eighth-inning single – the kind of hard contact missing from Ohtani since mid-August and one of the signs that convinced Roberts to move him back to the leadoff spot for Game 4.
May threw Ohtani a 1-and-1 cutter in at his knees and Ohtani crushed it. It left his bat at 113.1 mph and traveled 428 feet into the right field pavilion. The emotion that burst out of Ohtani was just as explosive. As the crowd roared, he bounced down the first-base line, screaming and gesturing at his teammates in the dugout.
It looked like things were finally turning the Dodgers’ way in this series.
“It’s hard to not say yeah to that,” Muncy said. “He gets that moment, it’s like that’s the swing we’ve been waiting for. We got a nice lead, we got Glas on the mound, we’re confident behind him and they just kept stringing together one good at-bat after another after another after another. They were just kind of relentless.”
The Dodgers’ first home run in the NLCS ended the longest home-run drought of Ohtani’s career at 25 games and 116 plate appearances.
The only thing that seemed longer was how long the Dodgers were going to have to work to make that four-run second inning stand up.
It began disappearing in the fourth inning.
Starter Tyler Glasnow retired the first 10 Brewers in order and struck out six of the first eight. He didn’t have another strikeout. It was nothing but contact from the Brewers after that.
A walk and back-to-back ground-rule doubles – the second by Jake Bauers – cut the Dodgers’ lead in half. An inning later, Glasnow walked the No. 8 hitter, Sal Frelick, who stole second and scored on a single by the No. 9 hitter David Hamilton.
Glasnow was replaced by Evan Phillips who walked three in a row (one intentionally after Hamilton stole second) to force in the tying run.
The four aces the Dodgers thought would give them the upper hand in this postseason did not. Tarik Skubal, Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Blake Snell and Glasnow combined for a 6.50 ERA in the series against the Brewers. Only Skubal allowed fewer than three runs in his start.
Tanner Scott came on for the sixth inning. He didn’t give up a home run to a left-handed batter all season. The Brewers’ first batter in the sixth, left-handed Garrett Mitchell, has just two home runs off left-handed pitchers in his 286 career regular-season games.
Scott left a full-count fastball over the heart of the plate and Mitchell, a former UCLA and Orange Lutheran standout, sent it over the center field wall for his second home run off a left-handed pitcher in three at-bats (Blake Snell in Game 3).
The Brewers’ bullpen took over from there. The Dodgers got Kyle Tucker to third base after his one-out double in the sixth, Pages to third after his leadoff double in the seventh and Will Smith to third when Brewers right fielder Frelick fumbled his double in the right field corner.
The six at-bats with a chance to push across the tying run ended in three strikeouts, two ground outs and a shallow pop up to center field.
Hamilton made it a two-run lead with a solo home run in the top of the ninth. It was just the fifth hit of the game for the Brewers.
More to come on this story.

item.title: [CBS Sports] Who's to blame for Dodgers' shocking NLCS loss vs. Brewers? Five places to point fingers
item.dc:creator: Mike Axisa
item.description: The Milwaukee Brewers are going to the World Series for the second time in franchise history and the first time as a National League team (the Brewers were still in the American League when they went to the World Series in 1982). This also means the Los Angeles Dodgers have been eliminated, and their shot at becoming baseball's first threepeat champion since the 1998-2000 New York Yankees ended on Thursday night. The Brewers have swept the Dodgers in four games in the NLCS, doing so one year aft
item.content:encoded:
The Milwaukee Brewers are going to the World Series for the second time in franchise history and the first time as a National League team (the Brewers were still in the American League when they went to the World Series in 1982). This also means the Los Angeles Dodgers have been eliminated, and their shot at becoming baseball's first threepeat champion since the 1998-2000 New York Yankees ended on Thursday night. The Brewers have swept the Dodgers in four games in the NLCS, doing so one year after the Dodgers swept them in the 2025 NLCS.
Who is to blame for the Dodgers going four-and-out in the NLCS? There's plenty of blame to go around, so let's assign it, shall we?
1. The Brewers
Milwaukee continues to be baseball's best team
We have to start here. The Dodgers got swept in the NLCS because the Brewers outplayed them in every phase of the game. The Brewers got better starting pitching. Their bullpen was better. Their defense and baserunning were better. Their offense was better at both stringing together hits to build a rally and launching the ball out of the park. Pat Murphy out-managed Dave Roberts as well. You name it, and the Brewers did it better than the Dodgers this series.
"It's a pretty simple answer," Dodgers infielder Max Muncy said after Game 3. "We're playing like shit. They're playing great."
As much as we want to (and will) blame various Dodgers for the sweep, the single biggest reason they got swept is that the Brewers were simply the better team. They were the better team in the regular season based on their records (103-59 vs. 100-62) and run differentials (+214 vs. +201), and they certainly played like the better team in the NLCS. The better team doesn't always win a postseason series. In the NLCS though, the better team has played like the better team, period.
2. Shohei Ohtani
MLB's brightest star was greatly dimmed ... even with Game 4 homer
The biggest star on baseball's most star-laden team was not himself the last two months of the season. Shohei Ohtani played through knee and biceps injuries and had been so unproductive than Roberts said there would at least be a "conversation" about sitting Ohtani in Game 3. That didn't come to pass, and hey, Ohtani went 1 for 2 with a walk and a hit-by-pitch in Game 3, and hit a home run in Game 4. The homer put the Dodgers up 4-0 on Thursday. The Dodgers didn't score again. The bottom line is Ohtani was a non-factor until it was too late. It's hard to win when your best player is this diminished.
Whenever a team loses in the postseason, the best player gets a disproportionate amount of the blame, and that applies to Ohtani this series. He's clearly not healthy, , and he's had multiple chances in the first three games to swing things in his team's favor, but couldn't do it. When the best player underperforms, he wears most of the blame. It has been the way of the world since the dawn of team sports.
3. Freddie Freeman
Normally clutch, Freeman has been the worst player in the series
Freddie Freeman, not Ohtani, was the worst player in the NLCS by both win probability added and championship probability added. He went 1 for 14 in the series and the one hit came in the first inning of Game 1. Freeman went 0 for 13 after his first NLCS at-bat and that 0 for 13 includes:
- Striking out after Mookie Betts worked a leadoff walk in the third inning of Game 1.
- Grounding into an inning-ending double play in the fifth inning of Game 1.
- Popping up to second on the first pitch to lead off the eighth inning of Game 1.
- Flying out with runners on first and second and no outs in the third inning of Game 2.
- Flying out with runners on first and second and one out in the third inning of Game 3.
- Grounding out with a runner on first and two outs in the fifth inning of Game 3.
That's an awful lot of empty at-bats in clutch situations for one of the best clutch hitters of this generation. Freeman had as many double plays as total bases (one each) in the NLCS, and his only RBI came on a sacrifice fly. You won't beat a team as good as the Brewers with sac flies. You need bigger swings from your best players and Freeman didn't provide them.
4. The supporting cast
Only two Dodgers hitters had consistently strong at-bats in the NLCS
Max Muncy went 2 for 12 with six strikeouts in the NLCS. Teoscar Hernández went 3 for 14. Andy Pages went 3 for 12. Tommy Edman went 1 for 7. Will Smith went 2 for 15 in the NLCS. Postseason legend Enrique Hernández went 0 for 8 with a ghasty strikeout in Game 3. The Dodgers had runners at second and third with one out in sixth, and Hernández took two pitches in the zone for strikes, then flailed at slider out of the zone. It was maybe the single worst at-bat of this NLCS.
Freeman was terrible, Ohtani was terrible, and the thing that has so often set the Dodgers apart these last few years -- an elite supporting cast -- was terrible as well. Edman, Muncy, Smith, and the Hernándezes are a combined 11 for 58 (.189) in the four games. Betts (3 for 15 with three walks) and Kyle Tucker (4 for 12 with three walks) were the only Dodgers hitters who escaped scrutiny. They were their most productive hitters and consistently had strong at-bats. Everyone else? 😴😴😴
5. Dave Roberts
Roberts did not push the right buttons
The manager can not swing the bat or throw the ball for his players, but he can put his team in the best position to succeed, and Roberts did not do that in the NLCS. Game 3, especially, was a managerial mess. Roberts burned the precocious Josue De Paula in the sixth inning when he sent him up to pinch-hit for Miguel Rojas with runners on second and third and one out, then immediately pinch-hit Enrique Hernández for De Paula when the Brewers brought in a lefty reliever.
De Paula is a rookie, I get that, but he has a track record of hitting lefties well in the minors. More accurately, he has a strong track record of making contact against lefties, which is what the Dodgers needed in that spot. A ball in play to get a run home. Instead, Roberts defaulted to the veteran Hernández, who struck out feebly. For all his career postseason success, Hernández went 1 for 14 this postseason, and a .190/.235/.317 hitter in his last 19 postseason games. Roberts never adjusted his priors.
The NLCS was a flashback to pre-2024 Roberts, when he too often showed too much faith in his veterans and had an unfortunate knack for sticking with starters too long. In 2024 and 2025, it all worked out, and Roberts looked like a genius. Those same mistakes, the ones he got away with the last two years, reared their ugly heads. The NLCS sweep is on the players, first and foremost. Roberts didn't play his cards well either. He's made things worse.

item.content:encoded:
Dodgers’ manager Dave Roberts told reporters on Thursday that he’s very unlikely to use Tarik Skubal or Yoshinobu Yamamoto out of the bullpen in Game 4 of the NLCS against the Brewers.

Even with their backs against the wall, Roberts maintained confidence when asked if his star hurlers would be available out of the bullpen on Thursday, saying, “No. ... Our bullpen is rested, very, very capable. You’ve still got to win four, but obviously you’ve got to win one first, and I completely understand that. But the short answer, no.” It’s possible that the calculus could change if the Dodgers get down early in Game 4, but for now he appears to have full faith in Tyler Glasnow and his rested bullpen.

item.title: [FOX Sports] Dodgers Move Shohei Ohtani Back To Leadoff With Season On Line In NLCS Game 4
item.description: Dodgers Move Shohei Ohtani Back To Leadoff With Season On Line In NLCS Game 4 One loss from elimination, the Los Angeles Dodgers restored Shohei Ohtani to the top of the batting order for Game 4 of the National League Championship Series on Thursday night. Ohtani batted sixth in a 6-2 loss on Wednesday
item.content:encoded:
Dodgers Move Shohei Ohtani Back To Leadoff With Season On Line In NLCS Game 4
One loss from elimination, the Los Angeles Dodgers restored Shohei Ohtani to the top of the batting order for Game 4 of the National League Championship Series on Thursday night.
The Dodgers trailed the Milwaukee Brewers 3-0 in the best-of-seven series, and needed to four straight wins to reach the World Series and keep alive their bid for a third consecutive championship.
Ohtani batted sixth in a 6-2 loss on Wednesday night, the lowest he's hit since joining the Dodgers ahead of the 2024 season. He was 1 for 2 with a walk to raise his batting average to .182.
"Just seeing the work the last couple days, I like where his head is at," manager Dave Roberts said before the game. "I liked the at-bats yesterday. Obviously we haven’t performed the way that we’re capable of, so to kind of shake it up a little bit but something that’s of somewhat normalcy that our guys are used to."
(Photo by Sean M. Haffey/Getty Images)
Ohtani typically leads off the order but has been dropped lower while struggling with injuries to his left knee and right biceps for the last few months. Roberts didn't tell Ohtani about the change before posting the lineup.
Roberts said Ohtani has given him reasons to believe in the four-time MVP, citing Ohtani staying until 9 p.m. on Tuesday to work on his swing and his improved at-bat quality.
"Baking all that in, I felt absolutely, put him at the top," he said. "I feel good about him taking five at-bats and giving us our best chance to win and produce runs."
Roberts tweaked the entire lineup after Wednesday's loss put the Dodgers on the brink of elimination. Mookie Betts, who led off in Game 3, was bumped to No. 2, while Freddie Freeman moved to No. 3.
Will Smith, whose offensive struggles mirrored Ohtani's, moved up to fourth from seventh. Smith doubled in the sixth inning, when the Dodgers briefly took a 2-1 lead.
"I thought Will took very good at-bats, big hit yesterday," Roberts said. "He’s been in big spots."
Kyle Tucker hit fifth, while Teoscar Hernandez went from third to sixth. Miguel Rojas hit seventh and Andy Pages dropped to eighth from fifth.
Kiké Hernández, who came off the bench in Game 3, hit ninth, with regular third baseman Max Muncy available to come off the bench for Rojas or Kiké Hernández.
Reporting by The Associated Press.

item.title: [Field Level Media] Struggling Shohei Ohtani back in leadoff spot as Dodgers face elimination
item.description: One day after being dropped to sixth in the batting order, Los Angeles Dodgers star Shohei Ohtani is back in the leadoff spot for Game 4 of the National League Championship Series on Thursday night. The Milwaukee Brewers won the first three games of the series and can clinch a World Series berth on Thursday night in Los Angeles. With elimination facing the Dodgers, manager Dave Roberts put Ohtani back atop the order for the first time since the final game of the regular season on Sept. 27. In We
item.content:encoded:
One day after being dropped to sixth in the batting order, Los Angeles Dodgers star Shohei Ohtani is back in the leadoff spot for Game 4 of the National League Championship Series on Thursday night.
The Milwaukee Brewers won the first three games of the series and can clinch a World Series berth on Thursday night in Los Angeles.
With elimination facing the Dodgers, manager Dave Roberts put Ohtani back atop the order for the first time since the final game of the regular season on Sept. 27. In Wednesday’s 6-2 loss, Ohtani went 1-for-2 with a walk and a hit by pitch.
“Just seeing the work the last couple days, I like where his head is at,” Roberts said prior to Game 4. “I just really — I liked the at-bats yesterday, and I felt that trying to shake it up a little bit. Obviously, we haven’t performed the way that we’re capable of, so to kind of shake it up a little bit, but something that’s of somewhat normalcy that our guys are used to.”
Ohtani, 32, has been bothered by right biceps and left knee injuries for multiple months and his productivity has slipped.
He has batted just .182 (4-for-22) with no homers and no RBIs in seven postseason games. Ohtani hasn’t homered since Aug. 18 against the Colorado Rockies and owns just one RBI since that homer.
When he batted sixth against the Brewers on Wednesday, it marked the first time he had batted so low in a starting lineup since Sept. 19, 2020 – when the Los Angeles Angels slotted him sixth as the designated hitter against the Texas Rangers.
Roberts said he didn’t tell Ohtani in advance about his return to the leadoff spot. He likes the idea of it possibly jump-starting Ohtani and his struggling troops.
“I feel good about him taking five at-bats and giving us our best chance to win and produce runs today,” Roberts said of Ohtani.
Ohtani is a four-time MVP — twice with the Angels and twice with the Dodgers — during nine big league campaigns. He hit 11 postseason homers, including eight last year, as the Dodgers won back-to-back titles.
–Field Level Media

item.content:encoded:
En las Grandes Ligas de Béisbol (MLB), pocas historias representan mejor la capacidad de resistir bajo presión que la protagonizada por los Red Sox de Boston en 2004. Hace exactamente 22 años, todo parecía perdido frente a los Yankees de Nueva York —su máximo rival—, pero los de Boston encontraron la manera de transformar una eliminación prácticamente anunciada en una de las hazañas más recordadas de la historia del béisbol.
Más de dos décadas después, aquella remontada vuelve a cobrar relevancia, siendo referencia para unos Dodgers de Los Ángeles que también se encuentran al borde del abismo en su camino al tricampeonato consecutivo.
Una remontada para la historia
La Serie de Campeonato de la Liga Americana de 2004 comenzó con un dominio contundente de los Yankees. Nueva York ganó los primeros tres encuentros y dejó a Boston contra las cuerdas, a una sola derrota de despedirse de la postemporada. El panorama parecía todavía más oscuro después del tercer partido, cuando los neoyorquinos se impusieron por un escandaloso 19-8.
Sin embargo, los Red Sox se negaron a aceptar su destino. Boston ganó el cuarto encuentro por 6-4 en entradas extras —lo que le añadió todavía más drama a la casi eliminación— y volvió a imponerse en el quinto, también en episodios adicionales, por 5-4. Con la confianza recuperada, llegó otro 4-2 a los Yankees en el sexto juego, para luego sellar la remontada con una contundente victoria de 10-3 en el séptimo, disputado incluso fuera de casa, en el Yankee Stadium.
Aquella reacción tuvo varios protagonistas inolvidables. David Ortiz apareció en los momentos decisivos y fue nombrado “Jugador Más Valioso” (MVP) de la serie. Johnny Damon también dejó su huella en el partido definitivo, con dos cuadrangulares y seis carreras impulsadas. Pero hubo otro nombre que quedó ligado para siempre al inicio de aquella transformación: nada más y nada menos que Dave Roberts.
El actual mánager de los Dodgers era entonces corredor emergente de Boston. En el noveno episodio del cuarto juego, con su equipo al borde de la eliminación, se robó la segunda base ante Mariano Rivera. Minutos después anotó la carrera del empate, en lo que fue una jugada que cambió el rumbo de la serie y le abrió la puerta a una remontada sin precedentes.
El significado de aquella reacción fue mucho más allá de una serie de playoffs. Boston terminó conquistando la Serie Mundial de 2004 barriendo a los St. Louis Cardinals, y poniendo fin a una espera de 86 años sin levantar el trofeo más importante. La llamada “Maldición del Bambino” quedó atrás y los Red Sox cambiaron para siempre la historia de su franquicia.
Veintidós años después, Roberts vuelve a encontrarse frente a un 0-3, aunque esta vez desde el banquillo. Sus Dodgers perdieron los primeros tres partidos de la Serie de Campeonato de la Liga Nacional ante los Brewers.
El golpe más reciente llegó con el triunfo de los de Milwaukee por 6-2 en el tercer encuentro, después de que Jake Bauers y Garrett Mitchell conectaran cuadrangulares consecutivos en la séptima entrada, silenciando un Dodger Stadium que segundos antes había celebrado con locura un inning de dos carreras para ponerse 2-1 al frente.
La derrota dejó a Los Ángeles sin margen de error. Pese a contar con figuras como Shohei Ohtani, Mookie Betts y Freddie Freeman, los Dodgers necesitan recuperar la producción ofensiva y encontrar respuestas ante un rival que ha sabido aprovechar sus oportunidades.
Los Brewers, por su parte, están a una victoria de regresar a la Serie Mundial por primera vez desde 1982. Milwaukee tiene la ventaja, el impulso y la oportunidad de cerrar la serie.
Los Ángeles, en cambio, ya no puede mirar más allá del siguiente partido. Necesita ganar cuatro encuentros consecutivos para sobrevivir y avanzar a la Serie Mundial, y la experiencia de Roberts convierte la comparación con 2004 en algo inevitable. Él sabe de primera mano que ir en contra 0-3 no significa una eliminación matemática, pero también conoce el tamaño del reto. Aquellos Red Sox demostraron cómo una sola victoria puede cambiar la presión de lado y transformar por completo una serie.
La comparación, sin embargo, tiene límites. Los Red Sox de 2004 ya escribieron su nombre en los libros de récords al convertirse en el único equipo que ha remontado un marcador así en una serie de postemporada al mejor de siete juegos. Los Dodgers todavía deben demostrar que pueden acompañarlos en la historia.
La pregunta ahora es si Roberts podrá convertir sus recuerdos de 2004 en una fuente de inspiración para su equipo. Hace 22 años, Dave Roberts ayudó a encender una remontada que parecía imposible. Hoy, su misión es intentar que aquella historia no sea solamente un recuerdo glorioso, sino el ejemplo de que todavía queda una última oportunidad para cambiar el destino.

item.title: [MLB.com] Back to basics: Ohtani returns to leadoff spot for NLCS Game 4
item.dc:creator: Sonja Chen
item.description: LOS ANGELES -- With their season on the line, the Dodgers are going back to their roots. Shohei Ohtani was in the leadoff spot for the first time this postseason as the Dodgers shook up their lineup ahead of Game 4 of the NL Championship Series against the Brewers on Thursday night at Dodger Stadium, a game they must win to keep their season -- and their three-peat bid -- alive. item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES -- With their season on the line, the Dodgers are going back to their roots.
Shohei Ohtani was in the leadoff spot for the first time this postseason as the Dodgers shook up their lineup ahead of Game 4 of the NL Championship Series against the Brewers on Thursday night at Dodger Stadium, a game they must win to keep their season -- and their three-peat bid -- alive.
Ohtani dropped as low as sixth in the order in NLCS Game 3, when a scuffling Will Smith also dropped to seventh. Both contributed to the Dodgers' lone run-scoring rally in the sixth inning, with Ohtani drawing a walk to load the bases before Smith cashed in with a two-run double. Two innings later, Ohtani smoked a 113.5 mph single, his hardest-hit batted ball since June 20.
The big plate appearances from Ohtani and Smith, as well as the work they have put in behind the scenes, were enough to convince manager Dave Roberts to elevate both of them back up the order.
"I think getting back to what we've done all year and how it's been going recently as far as on the offense," Roberts said, "I think it warranted just a little bit of a shakeup."
Here's the full lineup:
1. Shohei Ohtani, DH
2. Mookie Betts, SS
3. Freddie Freeman, 1B
4. Will Smith, C
5. Kyle Tucker, RF
6. Teoscar Hernández, LF
7. Miguel Rojas, 2B
8. Andy Pages, CF
9. Kiké Hernández, 3B
The Dodgers are trying to do what just one other team has done before: Come back from being down 0-3 in a best-of-seven postseason series. Of the 42 teams that have been in that position, only Roberts' 2004 Red Sox have successfully come back to win the series. Thirty-two of those series ended in sweeps.
Roberts' advice to his team is to focus solely on winning Game 4. They can't look at the big picture of needing four wins in as many games. They need to win each pitch, each inning and each day for as long as their season is alive.
Having Ohtani back atop the order, Roberts hopes, will put the Dodgers in the best position to do that. Ohtani is hitting 4-for-22 (.182) with no extra-base hits, seven strikeouts and four walks in seven games this postseason. There was a discussion about sitting him for Game 3 amid his lingering right biceps and left knee injuries, but Ohtani was adamant that he felt good enough to play and was close to figuring something out with his swing.
The reasoning for Ohtani's return to the leadoff spot a game later is twofold: He showed Roberts enough through his work and in Game 3. And if this is it for the Dodgers' postseason run, Roberts wants to go down trusting his generational talent to set the tone.
"There is something to that, absolutely," Roberts said. "But also I think the player still has to give you hope to believe in, to bet on -- where I think that the work, being here till 9 p.m. two nights ago working, the at-bats yesterday. For me baking all that in, I felt absolutely, put him at the top."

item.title: [Reviewing the Brew] Everything Brewers fans need to know about Dodgers’ Game 4 starter Tyler Glasnow
item.dc:creator: Brandon Glick
item.description: It's sort of a sick joke that, even down 3-0 and having used up their trio of all-universe aces, the Los Angeles Dodgers can trot another frontline starter out to the mound to try and stave off elimination against the Milwaukee Brewers. Alas, the Crew will have to get through Tyler Glasnow if they want to complete their revenge arc and sweep the two-time reigning champs in the NLCS. Of course, after seeing Tarik Skubal, Yoshinobu Yamamoto, and Blake Snell -- who have four Cy Youngs and a World S
item.content:encoded:
It's sort of a sick joke that, even down 3-0 and having used up their trio of all-universe aces, the Los Angeles Dodgers can trot another frontline starter out to the mound to try and stave off elimination against the Milwaukee Brewers. Alas, the Crew will have to get through Tyler Glasnow if they want to complete their revenge arc and sweep the two-time reigning champs in the NLCS.
Of course, after seeing Tarik Skubal, Yoshinobu Yamamoto, and Blake Snell -- who have four Cy Youngs and a World Series MVP between them -- there's not much that should faze the Brewers. Glasnow is a very good pitcher, but he's the closest thing to a weak link in the Dodgers' super-rotation.
Still, he's an intimidating presence on the bump and has had tons of success against most of Pat Murphy's lineup to boot. Milwaukee will counter with rookie southpaw Shane Drohan, though this will be an all-hands-on-deck effort as the Brewers try to get to where they haven't been since 1982.
To sweep Dodgers, Brewers will need to overcome intimidating history against Tyler Glasnow
Let's start with the optimistic view. Glasnow remains a perpetually injury-prone pitcher, making just 13 starts this year while dealing with back spasms and various setbacks. Though that means his arm should be fresh, he also likely isn't operating at 100%; his last start (against the Braves in the NLDS) saw him yield only one hit across 4⅔ innings, but he also walked five batters as part of a laborious outing.
That's an exploitable weakness the Crew need to take advantage of, since Glasnow has walked multiple batters in each of his past five starts. Running up his pitch count early will force Dave Roberts to dig into his stash of relievers, many of whom seemingly don't have his trust right now.
The major concern for the Brewers lies in the past, since Glasnow has had their number historically. Christian Yelich (one hit, seven strikeouts in 14 plate appearances), William Contreras (zero hits in 10 PAs), and Jackson Chourio (.286 OPS in seven PAs) have all struggled mightily in their head-to-head matchups with the right-hander.
Those numbers also don't include his dominant performance in Game 3 of last year's NLCS, when he struck out eight and held the Brewers to one run on three hits over 5⅔ innings. As such, the work of Game 3 hero Jake Bauers (.952 OPS in seven PAs) and Brice Turang (.375 OBP in eight PAs) will be key to getting the Crew ahead tonight.
Having already taken down all of the Dodgers' best arms, the Brewers should enter this one with immense confidence. With a trip to the World Series on the line, all they need to do is crush their Tyler Glasnow demons.

item.title: [reviewingthebrew.com] Brewers' best (and only) chance for historic playoff redemption in NLCS is in Shane Drohan's hands
