item.content:encoded:
Are the Dodgers really going to bench Shohei Ohtani, of all people, when the NLCS returns to Los Angeles for Game 3 on Wednesday? For, likely, a rookie in Josue De Paula who has all of 11 games of regular-season experience, at that?
We don’t have the answer to that yet, but that it’s even a consideration – and it is indeed a consideration – tells you a whole lot about how badly things have gone lately for the four-time Most Valuable Player and reigning Greatest Player Who Ever Lived. It’s not just that he’s hit a mere .150/.261/.150 in six playoff games, because plenty of great hitters can have a rough few games against outstanding playoff pitching. Matt Olson and Ronald Acuña Jr. hit about the same for Atlanta, and, for what it’s worth, Ohtani isn’t even the biggest problem spot in the Dodger lineup right now -- it’s Will Smith.
It is, instead, about the prior knowledge that Ohtani likely isn’t fully healthy, and really it’s about how bad it’s all looked. Thanks to right biceps and left knee issues, Ohtani hasn’t pitched since July 3, started to slump as a hitter in late August, then spent two weeks on the injured list in September, returning in time to play just five regular-season games, which mostly cleared up nothing.
He hasn’t hit a homer since Aug. 18, though it’s somewhat worse than even that; given that his final three homers of the regular season all came in one series at Coors Field, it’s now been more than two months since his last homer at Dodger Stadium, that against the Royals back on Aug. 12.
“I mean, obviously, it hasn’t been good,” Dodgers manager Dave Roberts said to The Athletic. “He doesn’t feel great. I think for me, it’s having a conversation with him [Tuesday], kind of try to figure out what’s best for him, what’s best for us. He certainly has earned that conversation and deserves it.”
Indeed he has. But also, through Aug. 18, he was a top-5 hitter in baseball. Since then, including the playoffs, he’s been one of the 10 weakest, finding himself hitting fifth in the lineup in the NLDS, the first time in more than six years he’d hit that low. In September, he struck out 39% of the time, the second-highest month of his entire career, in part because he’s running one of the highest chase rates he’s ever had, and his squared-up rate is as low as it’s been in years, too. It’s all going wrong, at the moment.
It seems eminently clear that Ohtani is not anywhere near his full-strength self, and if it later comes out that he’s simply too physically compromised to succeed but is trying to play through it for the sake of the team, it would surprise absolutely no one.
But as the Dodgers weigh what would generally have been an unthinkable decision -- benching the biggest star in the game while down 2-0 in the playoffs -- it’s important to go a little deeper than just outcomes. (Not that what he’s done has been anywhere near good enough, but remember that the entire Majors are hitting .213/.295/.337 in the playoffs right now. It’s really, really hard to hit in October, when the best pitchers can be used more aggressively.)
What can we find under the hood that might explain the root cause of his lack of performance?
"The physical part, he’s kind of moving past that," hitting coach Aaron Bates said at the start of the playoffs. "Now it’s just getting the timing against different speeds, when he wants to get his move off, that sort of thing -- kind of the usual stuff hitters go through as opposed to him navigating trying to achieve the physical components."
It is, from an external view, about timing, and his total lack of it right now. Maybe that’s because physical limitations prevent Ohtani from achieving his usual timing, in which case continuing to play him helps no one. Maybe he just hasn’t found it yet since his return, and more time and work will help him get there. That is the entirety of the question the Dodgers have to answer -- if this is a thing that can be solved in the next few days, or not.
What we do know for sure is that the timing of his swing seems completely off. Just look at performance against 95 mph+ pitches, something at which, from 2024-25, Ohtani was third-best in baseball. Compare the before/after since the date of his most recent homer, and including the playoffs in the “after.”
Ohtani against 95 mph+ pitches
- Through Aug. 18: .280 AVG, .441 SLG
- Since Aug. 19: .036 AVG, .071 SLG
That’s one lone hit (an admittedly impressive one, a Sept. 24 double off Mason Miller, of all people) against velocity, and all of this coming at the worst possible time. Why do the Majors, as whole, find such a drop-off in October offense? In part because velocity skyrockets in the biggest moments; the average October fastball this year is 96.2 mph.
Now, you might think that given that fact, and the known questions about his physical state, that Ohtani’s bat is simply slower. Counterintuitively, that hasn’t happened. Ohtani’s bat speed in October is as fast as it’s been all season. But he’s still late, which we know sounds like a difficult-to-grasp combination. Think about it this way: The bat is still moving through space plenty fast. It’s just that he’s either slower to get it started, or just not quite getting to that speed at the right time.
You can see that through the Statcast bat tracking data, and there’s so much not-great here that we’re just going to info dump it on you all at once before explaining what some of this means. There are 24 months, including the playoffs, during which this data is available, dating back to the middle of 2023.
For Ohtani, of those 24 months, October 2026 features his least impressive metrics in … just so many things.
Postseason 2026 superlatives, or lack thereof
- Attack angle: 24th of 24. Tied-lowest, at 8°. In previous years, it’s been closer to 13°. The Major League average is 10°.
- Intercept point: 24th of 24. This is his month where he’s letting the ball get deepest, where his intercept point is only 22 inches out front. He’s usually around 27 inches, and the Major League average is nearer 31.
That’s a lot of numbers, we understand, and it all points to “the swing is wildly out of tune right now.”
So, let’s show you what that means. It’s all related to timing, and it’s not about the speed or shape of his swing, because his swing path really hasn’t changed much; it’s not more flat or uppercut or anything like that. It’s all connected, in this way:
Late swings lead to: the ball getting too deep, which leads to: an opposite-field attack direction and a much lower attack angle. If you hit it at all in the first place.
For Ohtani, you could see it most clearly in the third inning of Game 2, when he grounded out weakly to third base on a Logan Henderson fastball that was “only” 94.9 mph, yet he essentially had to take it right out of the catcher’s mitt. It looked uncomfortable on the broadcast feed …
… and the data visualization underneath it really shows you how late he was.
Perhaps a more effective way is to find two very similar pitches this year, and show you how differently his swing timing was.
Take two fastballs from lefties, each playing for Milwaukee, each around 95 mph, each middle-in. On Aug. 13, Shane Drohan’s 95.2 mph sinker was laced by Ohtani at nearly 112 mph off the bat for a leadoff double. In Game 2, JoJo Romero’s slightly slower 94.1 mph sinker was fouled off in a way that almost looked painful to watch. He would later strike out on a low-and-away sweeper.
While we can’t account with certainty for what Ohtani may have been looking for on each pitch and therefore if he was fooled, there’s a big difference between being on time and being late.
Against Drohan, he caught the ball 26 inches out in front of his body. Against Romero, when he was so late that he barely tapped it at all, it was a mere 6 inches.
It all comes back to timing, where he’s been late, late, and later.
Which all leads back to the big decision the Dodgers must make: Can this be fixed by hard work over the next day or two? Or is there a limitation that simply can’t be resolved until the offseason?
If it’s the latter, then simply dropping him down in the lineup might not really be worth much. It would lead to the improbable decision that De Paula is better suited to helping the Dodgers win a must-have game, and that’s at least a little about how impressive he’s been in limited time, leading none other than Joey Votto to observe this kind of high praise after De Paula’s Game 1 walk.
More than 530 players this year saw at least 100 pitches outside the zone, playoffs included. Only one had a lower chase rate than De Paula, who is MLB Pipeline’s No. 4 prospect in baseball for a reason, with a scouting report that read that he drew comparisons to “a slightly smaller but more athletic version of Yordan Alvarez.”
No pressure, that.
It is, as it always seems to be, a math problem. You'd take 100% of Ohtani over 100% of De Paula, easily, but you don't have 100% of Ohtani right now. You don't have time to figure it out, either. For the first time in forever, the best Dodger lineup being one that doesn't include Ohtani is a real possibility.

item.title: [Sports Illustrated] Dodgers' Dave Roberts Has Clear Response on Potentially Benching Will Smith Amid Struggles
item.dc:creator: Ricardo Sandoval; Unknown
item.description: The Los Angeles Dodgers are heading back home down 0-2 in the best-of-seven National League Championship Series. The Dodgers were unable to come away with a win in Milwaukee, and will now have to take care of business at home. As things stand, that looks like a tall task, especially given how lackluster the offense has been. The Dodgers' offense has not produced this series. Multiple players are to blame, including catcher Will Smith. The Dodgers' All-Star catcher has been searching for his swin
item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers are heading back home down 0-2 in the best-of-seven National League Championship Series.
The Dodgers were unable to come away with a win in Milwaukee, and will now have to take care of business at home.
As things stand, that looks like a tall task, especially given how lackluster the offense has been.
The Dodgers' offense has not produced this series. Multiple players are to blame, including catcher Will Smith.
The Dodgers' All-Star catcher has been searching for his swing this entire postseason.
With that in mind, Dave Roberts was asked whether benching Smith and replacing him with Hunter Feduccia is an option.
Roberts responded by backing his catcher and expressing full confidence in him turning things around.
"Yeah, I'm not going to put Feduccia in place of Will Smith," Roberts said. "That's just not going to happen."
The Dodgers Need Will Smith to Break Out of His Slump
After batting third in the lineup in Game 1 against the Brewers, Roberts moved Smith down to fifth in Game 2.
In six postseason games, Smith is now hitting an abysmal .043 with a .126 OPS. He has just one hit and eight strikeouts in 23 at-bats.
Saying Smith is struggling at the plate is an understatement.
While his usual postseason numbers aren't off the charts, they're far better than what he's producing now.
In Smith's postseason career, he's hit .203 with a .638 OPS, 10 home runs, 37 RBIs and 59 hits in 291 at-bats.
Smith was asked whether the neck injury he sustained earlier in the season, which caused him to miss three months, is affecting his play.
The 31-year-old didn't use that as an excuse.
"Yeah, I felt really good the last month, the last couple weeks, especially," he said. "I still feel good up there, swinging at the right pitches, taking good pitches, just barely missing balls. Pitchers are making good pitches to me."
"It's been five games," he added before Game 2. "Obviously want the results to be a little better, but at the end of the day, it's five games at the plate. No panic from me. So I'll be fine."
Game 2 of the NLCS wasn't any better for Smith. He continued his brutal slump, going 0-for-4 with one strikeout.
It's been tough sledding for Smith, and if he can't turn things around by Game 3, the Dodgers' offense will be in major trouble.
However, that doesn't mean Roberts is going to put him on the bench.
"He still takes a good at-bat," Roberts said before Game 2. "It just hasn't kind of lined up yet. It's one of those things that in this moment in time, everything rightfully is more magnified and it's five games. All it takes is squaring one ball up, and it flips."
The Dodgers will hope Smith is able to make that flip as soon as Wednesday.

Ricardo Sandoval is a freelance writer with On SI. He is a graduate of California State University, Northridge, and specializes in sports writing, particularly in MLB, NBA and NFL. He previously served as an Associate Editor for Dodgers Nation and has worked with Newsweek and The Sporting News.

item.dc:creator: Matt Reed
item.description: Shohei Ohtani is enduring one of the worst slumps of his MLB career, and it couldn’t come at a worse time for the Los Angeles Dodgers. That is causing the back-to-back World Series champions to consider a drastic move that involves playing rookie Josue De Paula over the Japanese superstar. Ohtani has failed to hit a home run over the last two months in an unprecedented drought for Los Angeles. The Milwaukee Brewers lead 2-0 in their NLCS series against the Dodgers. That’s sparking some tough con
item.content:encoded:
Shohei Ohtani is enduring one of the worst slumps of his MLB career, and it couldn’t come at a worse time for the Los Angeles Dodgers. That is causing the back-to-back World Series champions to consider a drastic move that involves playing rookie Josue De Paula over the Japanese superstar.
Ohtani has failed to hit a home run over the last two months in an unprecedented drought for Los Angeles. The Milwaukee Brewers lead 2-0 in their NLCS series against the Dodgers. That’s sparking some tough conversations in the L.A. clubhouse.
That has caused speculation to grow about De Paula’s growing involvement in the team, especially with the Dodgers desperate for a comeback. De Paula is considered a top-five prospect, according to MLB’s top 100 rankings.
Ohtani remains a four-time MLB MVP, but Dodgers manager Dave Roberts has history on the line as Los Angeles seeks a championship three-peat. No National League team has ever won three consecutive crowns.
Many MLB fans are wondering, though, who exactly is Ohtani’s potential replacement?
MLB rookie could replace four-time MVP
The 21-year-old isn’t the only option the Dodgers could turn to if Roberts decides that Ohtani needs a break. The Dodgers superstar has just one hit in his seven at-bats through two NLCS games. That has the franchise thinking through all options leading into Game 3.
De Paula has been an exciting prospect throughout his rookie 2026 campaign, and he is honestly one of the most interesting young players in the game. However, De Paula’s background makes him even more of an interesting postseason conversation.
He’s a New York native, but moved to the Dominican Republic in 2020 to find more baseball opportunities. That’s because he only played one high school season due to the COVID-19 pandemic.
De Paula’s connection to pro sports goes beyond baseball. He’s a second cousin of former NBA stars Stephon Marbury and Sebastian Telfair. Perhaps the young MLB standout’s future will bring more sporting success to his family.
Dodgers need a lineup shake-up
The Dodgers signed the promising outfielder in 2022 as a teenager. Now, he has been thrust into an incredibly high-stakes postseason situation with Los Angeles’ season in the balance. It’s unclear if Ohtani will actually be sacrificed in the playoffs, especially for a player with minimal experience.
De Paula is still earning some playoff experience after serving as a pinch-hitter in Game 1 against the Brewers. He didn’t appear in Game 2’s 7-4 loss, though, which raises questions if Roberts will get him more involved during Wednesday’s NLCS matchup.
This season, the Dodgers’ rising star has 10 hits in 31 plate appearances, including one home run and seven RBIs.
Los Angeles hosts Milwaukee in Game 3 of the NLCS at 8 p.m. ET Wednesday on Fox Sports 1 on Fox One.

item.title: [Sports Illustrated] Shohei Ohtani's Postseason Struggles Could Lead to Josue De Paula's Big Moment
item.dc:creator: Justin Binkowski
item.description: Los Angeles Dodgers superstar Shohei Ohtani has not looked like his usual self at the plate so far in the 2026 MLB playoffs. As a result, the Dodgers are reportedly considering benching the four-time MVP. The Dodgers might keep Ohtani out of the starting lineup for Game 3 of the National League Championship Series, according to The Athletic's Ken Rosenthal and Katie Woo. If the six-time All-Star doesn't start against the Milwaukee Brewers on Wednesday, top prospect Josue De Paula reportedly coul
item.content:encoded:
Los Angeles Dodgers superstar Shohei Ohtani has not looked like his usual self at the plate so far in the 2026 MLB playoffs. As a result, the Dodgers are reportedly considering benching the four-time MVP.
The Dodgers might keep Ohtani out of the starting lineup for Game 3 of the National League Championship Series, according to The Athletic's Ken Rosenthal and Katie Woo. If the six-time All-Star doesn't start against the Milwaukee Brewers on Wednesday, top prospect Josue De Paula reportedly could be Los Angeles' designated hitter.
After a 0-for-4 performance in Game 2 of the NLCS, Ohtani is now 3-for-20 with no extra-base hits in the postseason. The lefty-swinging slugger dealt with injuries this year, which actually led to De Paula making his MLB debut in September. And now, the Dodgers could turn to the 21-year-old again as they head to Los Angeles down 2-0 in the NLCS.
Josue De Paula could inject new life into the Dodgers' lineup
While De Paula has only been used as a pinch hitter so far in the 2026 MLB playoffs, he's shown exactly what he could add to Los Angeles' lineup if he started at designated hitter in place of a struggling Ohtani. In three pinch-hit appearances this postseason, the 21-year-old has drawn two walks. The top prospect most recently pinch-hit with two outs in the top of the ninth inning of Game 1 of the NLCS and drew a walk against Milwaukee closer Trevor Megill. Although Mookie Betts flew out to end the game after De Paula's walk, the young outfielder helped move the tying run into scoring position and put the go-ahead run on base for Los Angeles.
During his first stint in the majors last month, De Paula hit .323 (10-for-31) and walked 11 times in 11 regular-season games. Meanwhile, Ohtani went 6-for-30 with four walks in eight September games. That means the Dodgers superstar has nine hits in his last 50 at-bats dating back to last month. And the general consensus is that the two-way star isn't just slumping but is more likely still dealing with injuries.
It's unclear whether Dodgers manager Dave Roberts will actually bench Ohtani on Wednesday. But if he does, De Paula could provide a spark as Los Angeles tries to mount a comeback in the NLCS.
Justin Binkowski is a lifelong baseball fan returning to cover the sport he loves after spending nearly a decade writing about video games. Before his time as managing editor at Dot Esports, Binkowski attended King's College in Wilkes-Barre, PA, where he was also a relief pitcher on the school's baseball team. While in college, Binkowski was a media relations intern for the Scranton/Wilkes-Barre RailRiders during the 2014 season.

item.title: [Reviewing the Brew] Dodgers reportedly considering drastic Shohei Ohtani move after slow start to NLCS rematch with Brewers
item.dc:creator: Owen Jonas
item.description: One year ago, Los Angeles Dodgers superstar Shohei Ohtani essentially single-handedly defeated the Milwaukee Brewers in Game 4 of the National League Championship Series to send his team to the World Series for the second consecutive year. Fast forward 361 days, and Dodgers manager Dave Roberts is considering benching the 4x MVP during his team's NLCS rematch against the Brewers. The report surfaced from Katie Woo and Ken Rosenthal of The Athletic after the Brewers' Game 2 victory over the Dodge
item.content:encoded:
One year ago, Los Angeles Dodgers superstar Shohei Ohtani essentially single-handedly defeated the Milwaukee Brewers in Game 4 of the National League Championship Series to send his team to the World Series for the second consecutive year. Fast forward 361 days, and Dodgers manager Dave Roberts is considering benching the 4x MVP during his team's NLCS rematch against the Brewers.
The report surfaced from Katie Woo and Ken Rosenthal of The Athletic after the Brewers' Game 2 victory over the Dodgers on Monday night, during which Ohtani went 0-for-4 with two strikeouts. According to the duo at The Athletic, Roberts said, "Obviously it hasn’t been good...He doesn’t feel great. I think for me, it’s having a conversation with him tomorrow, kind of try to figure out what’s best for him, what’s best for us."
Ohtani battled a knee injury and right biceps pain throughout the course of the 2026 regular season, and according to his manager, who noted that the superstar "doesn't feel great," those ailments have carried into the postseason. The result has been an uncharacteristically poor performance from Ohtani during the playoffs this year, during which he's collected just three hits -- all singles -- in 20 at-bats and struck out seven times. He does have three walks and a stolen base, but zero RBI and zero extra-base hits in six games is certainly cause for concern for Roberts and his coaching staff.
As a result, there's a very real chance that Ohtani is not in the lineup for Game 3 of the NLCS on Wednesday night. That said, regardless of whether or not the Dodgers' star is actually benched, the turmoil his lack of production has created for Los Angeles' lineup and the resulting difficult decision it has created for Roberts is a distraction that only works in the Brewers' favor.
Dodgers consideration of benching Shohei Ohtani works in Brewers favor regardless of what Dave Roberts decides
Los Angeles is down 0-2 in the series, the Brewers have already beaten their two best starting pitchers in Tarik Skubal and Yoshinobu Yamamoto, and now the Dodgers' manager is asking himself whether or not he should bench a 4x MVP. It's undoubtedly an admirable position to be in for the Brewers -- one that won't be compromised regardless of Roberts' decision on Ohtani.
On one hand, Ohtani certainly isn't right at the plate right now, and faces a tough matchup in Robert Gasser in Game 3. Ohtani struggles with low-slot lefties, and is 0-for-7 with four strikeouts against Gasser in his career. If Roberts elects to keep his struggling, hobbled MVP in the lineup for Game 3 the Brewers certainly have a favorable matchup with Gasser on the bump.
On the other hand, if Roberts elects to replace Ohtani with rookie outfielder Josue De Paula or another bat off the Dodgers' bench, the momentum hit of benching his superstar DH could be significant. The Dodgers' lineup certainly isn't helped when Ohtani is swinging the bat like he has been as of late, but taking him out of the order eliminates the possibility that he will regain his MVP form and come through with a big hit at some point in the series.
It's truly an impossible decision for Roberts, who seldom has to make these types of calls with his star-studded roster. Either he continues to play a clearly hurting Ohtani or he takes a 4x MVP out of the lineup in the NLCS. While he, his coaching staff, and Ohtani himself are mulling over their options, the Brewers, whose attention remains locked in on ending this series as quickly as possible, are the beneficiaries of the turmoil that is occurring in the Dodgers' lineup.

item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers drew six walks during Game 1 of the NLCS, including one from rookie sensation Josue De Paula in the top of the ninth inning.
De Paula pinch-hit for Kiké Hernández with the Dodgeres down 2-1, two outs, and a runner on first base. He drew a five-pitch walk against Milwaukee Brewers closer Trevor Megill, which prompted former Cincinnati Reds great and current NBC analyst Joey Votto to heap praise upon the Dodgers' 21-year-old-prospect.
"De Paula about to be in that upper tier quick, quick.," Votto wrote on X (formerly Twitter) during Sunday's game. In the comments of his tweet, the former MVP went on to mention De Paula's beautiful swing and elite swing-decisions.
The high-end comparison for De Paula has always been Yordan Alvarez, who the Dodgers famously once had in their pipeline. One can assume the likely 2026 AL MVP is certainly a player in Votto's so-called "upper tier" of hitters in MLB. De Paula didn't even swing the bat during his plate appearance in Game 1, but the seeds are being planted for what should be an incredibly successful career.
Dodgers' Josue De Paula is turning heads and could force tough managerial decisions in the playoffs
De Paula now has two walks in his three plate appearances during the postseason. His previous one came during the seventh inning of Game 4 of the NLDS, which allowed the Dodgers to score the go-ahead and game-winning runs to seal the series and advance to the NLCS.
Manager Dave Roberts could swap De Paula for the likes of Hernández, Tommy Edman, or Miguel Rojas. So far, during the postseason, the Dodgers are hitting .207/.282/.360/.642 in the postseason and De Paula's presence on the bench could help alleviate what has been an underwhelming postseason offensively for the reigning back-to-back World Series champions.
It takes every single player on the roster having a clutch moment for a team to win a World Series, and De Paula is showing that he is more than capable of providing an invaluable at bat if he is deployed properly.
De Paula's impressive, yet inconsequential, walk in Game 1 might already have Dodgers fans questioning Teoscar Hernandez's future this offseason. Unless De Paula can learn a new position on the fly like Mookie Betts, he'll completely blocked from the starting lineup by Hernandez, Andy Pages, Kyle Tucker, in 2027.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Dodgers’ Freddie Freeman Makes Blunt Statement After NLCS Game 2 Loss
item.dc:creator: Keith Watkins
item.description: The Los Angeles Dodgers fell 7-4 to the Milwaukee Brewers on Monday night in Game 2 of the NLCS. The offense managed just three hits on the night. The lineup went 0-for-4 with runners in scoring position and failed to hit a home run despite featuring some of the most dangerous power bats in baseball. Yoshinobu Yamamoto lasted only 2.2 innings, allowing three earned runs on four hits while walking two. The bullpen combined for four more runs after he departed. Nothing worked on either side of the
item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers fell 7-4 to the Milwaukee Brewers on Monday night in Game 2 of the NLCS. The offense managed just three hits on the night. The lineup went 0-for-4 with runners in scoring position and failed to hit a home run despite featuring some of the most dangerous power bats in baseball.
Yoshinobu Yamamoto lasted only 2.2 innings, allowing three earned runs on four hits while walking two. The bullpen combined for four more runs after he departed. Nothing worked on either side of the ball.
After the game, the Dodgers' clubhouse was left searching for answers heading into a critical series shift.
Freeman Does Not Sugarcoat It
Freddie Freeman kept his assessment direct when asked about the loss.
"It's hard to win games when you only get three hits," Freeman said.
No deflection. No pointing to one bad inning or a single turning point. Freeman identified the problem in the simplest terms available. The offense is not producing, and until it does, nothing else matters.
"Regroup tomorrow and go again Wednesday," Freeman added.
His manager Dave Roberts echoed the sentiment, acknowledging that Milwaukee's pitching staff has outperformed his lineup through two games. Roberts credited the Brewers for having a quality pitching staff but admitted he does not have a clear answer for why the bats have gone silent.
Muncy on Where the Dodgers Stand
"There's still a lot of series left," Muncy said. He acknowledged that the Dodgers would have preferred to steal at least one game in Milwaukee but gave credit to the Brewers for how well they have played through two games.
The series now shifts to Dodger Stadium. Home crowd. Home turf. The Dodgers need to win.
Final Word for the Dodgers
Two games. Six total hits. No home runs. The numbers tell the story on their own.
Freeman said it plainly. The Dodgers know what the problem is. Solving it before the deficit becomes insurmountable is the only thing that matters now.
Wednesday night at Dodger Stadium. The lineup needs to show up.
This article was originally published on HEAVY
The post Dodgers' Freddie Freeman Makes Blunt Statement After NLCS Game 2 Loss appeared first on HEAVY.

item.title: [AOL.com] Bench Shohei Ohtani? Dodgers have to consider drastic action with season in danger - AOL
item.dc:creator: Jack Harris
item.description: MILWAUKEE –– Entering Monday night, the Dodgers were not giving serious consideration to removing Shohei Ohtani from their lineup. One big loss, and four ugly at-bats later, however, that previously steadfast plan suddenly seemed capable of changing. Following a 7-4 defeat to the Milwaukee Brewers that put the Dodgers in a two-game hole in their National League Championship Series, the team was set to re-evaluate Ohtani’s status ahead of Game 3 on Wednesday. Manager Dave Roberts told The Athleti
item.content:encoded:
MILWAUKEE –– Entering Monday night, the Dodgers were not giving serious consideration to removing Shohei Ohtani from their lineup.
One big loss, and four ugly at-bats later, however, that previously steadfast plan suddenly seemed capable of changing.
Following a 7-4 defeat to the Milwaukee Brewers that put the Dodgers in a two-game hole in their National League Championship Series, the team was set to re-evaluate Ohtani’s status ahead of Game 3 on Wednesday.
Manager Dave Roberts told The Athletic that the team would have “a conversation” with Ohtani about whether or not he would be in the lineup for the contest. A source with knowledge of the situation confirmed to the California Post that the decision would come down to whether Ohtani still felt healthy enough to remain the starting designated hitter, as ESPN also reported.
The development came after Ohtani’s worst performance this postseason, in which he went 0-for-4 with two strikeouts.
Over six games in these playoffs, the four-time MVP is now just 3-for-20 with only three singles, two walks and seven strikeouts while battling ongoing right arm and left knee issues –– playing at what the team has repeatedly acknowledged is well less than 100%.
Despite all that, the Dodgers have also been holding out hope for a revival from their two-way superstar. Roberts promised Ohtani would “come to life” eventually. President of baseball operations Andrew Friedman predicted that “at some point, it’s going to click for him.”
Now, however, the Dodgers might not be able to keep waiting around for Ohtani magic.
After back-to-back losses to open the NLCS in Milwaukee this week, they return home to Los Angeles just two more defeats away from elimination –– and only one from a 3-0 deficit that just one team in MLB history (Roberts’ iconic Boston Red Sox squad in the 2004 American League Championship Series) has ever come back from.
“Can we [come back in this series]? Absolutely,” Roberts said. “But it’s just, you want to get that first [win].”
Prior to Monday, Ohtani had at least reached base safely in each of his first five playoff games.
Instead of continuing to progress with his swing, however, his 0-fer in Game 2 represented a notable step back.
Before the game, the injury-hampered 32-year-old took batting practice on the field for a third-straight day –– a drastic, and telling, change of routine for someone who normally never hits outside of the indoor batting cages.
During his BP sessions, coaches had been encouraged by the look of his swing, optimistically noting the fact he was driving the ball to the big part of the field.
“I feel good [with] where he’s at,” Roberts said Sunday. “[He is] certainly not 100 percent, but it’s good enough.”
Advertisement
That, however, was no longer the case in Tuesday’s demoralizing loss, when the Dodgers’ offense as a whole managed just three hits, made outs in all 15 of their at-bats against Brewers relievers, and suddenly looked like a unit in desperate need of a jolt.
Ohtani didn’t provide one. Instead, he looked even more lost than ever before.
He ended the first inning with a three-pitch strikeout, chasing an elevated fastball from Brewers rookie Logan Henderson. He stranded a runner at second to end the second, flailing at another high fastball for a softly hit grounder to third. Then came the sixth, when Ohtani was so fooled by a slider from left-handed reliever JoJo Romero that his bat flung out of his hands on his unsuccessful attempt to check his swing.
He would make one more out in the ninth, lifting a harmless fly ball to left field off top Brewers southpaw Aaron Ashby.
Once again, he did not address reporters postgame, still yet to speak publicly since before the start of the NLDS.
If the Dodgers were to drop Ohtani from the lineup for Game 3 –– when the Brewers will start left-hander Robert Gasser –– the team would have several potential ways to fill his void at DH.
The most obvious one: rookie sensation Josue De Paula.
The 21-year-old has only logged 45 total big-league plate appearances since being called up straight from double-A back in September, but has reached safely in more than half of them.
That includes a pair of impressive walks as a pinch-hitter in recent days; one that helped set up a game-winning rally in Game 4 of the NL Division Series, and another in an ultimately failed ninth-inning comeback bid in Game 1 of the NLCS on Sunday.
Granted, swapping even a diminished version of Ohtani for someone so inexperienced would undoubtedly be a stunning decision on the surface. And if this series weren’t 2-0 for the Brewers, the calculus would be different.
But right now, De Paula might be just as much of an on-base threat, and (given he is fully healthy) is perhaps an even more likely candidate to potentially slug the ball.
And, at this increasingly dire stage, the Dodgers can ill-afford to risk another empty performance from their biggest star.
If not De Paula, the Dodgers could also use the DH spot to potentially fit October hero, and right-handed hitter, Kiké Hernández back in the lineup, after he was dropped back to the bench for Game 2 in favor of Tommy Edman. Perhaps it could also be a way to get Miguel Rojas in as another extra righty bat, especially while he nurses a back injury he suffered in the NLDS.
None of these scenarios, of course, are what the Dodgers wanted to be contemplating so soon into their World Series three-peat bid.
But suddenly, with the stakes rising higher and Ohtani’s performance trending in the opposite direction, all options might need to be on the table.
The best player in baseball, at least in his current physical condition, might need to be benched.

item.title: [Los Angeles Times] Commentary: Dodgers' three-peat dreams are on life support as the deflated heroes return home
item.dc:creator: Bill Plaschke
item.description: - Click here to listen to this article - Bill Plaschke writes the Dodgers’ three-peat dreams are dying in the face of the potent Milwaukee Brewers. - The Dodgers’ aces have struggled to stay on the mound deep in games and key bats have gone silent. - After a humbling 7-4 loss in Game 2, the Dodgers need a miraculous rejuvenation at Dodger Stadium to extend their season. Once brimming with life, the Dodgers’ historic quest has curled up into a withered heap. The three-peat is dying. The three-pea
item.content:encoded:
- Click here to listen to this article
- Bill Plaschke writes the Dodgers’ three-peat dreams are dying in the face of the potent Milwaukee Brewers.
- The Dodgers’ aces have struggled to stay on the mound deep in games and key bats have gone silent.
- After a humbling 7-4 loss in Game 2, the Dodgers need a miraculous rejuvenation at Dodger Stadium to extend their season.
Once brimming with life, the Dodgers’ historic quest has curled up into a withered heap.
The three-peat is dying.
The three-peat is slowly, agonizingly having the life squeezed out of it by a collection of hardscrabble Midwesterners with no regard for stardom or status.
After two games of the National League Championship Series, the three-peat was formally been placed on life support Monday after the mighty Dodgers lost a second consecutive game to those little giants known as Milwaukee Brewers.
This time the final score was 7-4 after another devastating night at American Family Field, and now the Dodgers trail two-games-to-none in a best-of-seven series that appears beyond their control.
For a second consecutive game, their ace was knocked out. For a second consecutive game, their powerful offense petered out.
For a second consecutive game, they looked like a weary, aging band of fallen stars that had stumbled into a surprisingly deep pothole and had no idea how to climb out.
For the Dodgers to win this series and continue their journey toward a third consecutive championship, they must beat the Brewers in four of the next five games, the last two of which will be played in Milwaukee.
It doesn’t seem likely. It doesn’t even seem possible.
Not once in during their previous two title seasons did they trail anybody two-games- to-none, and they certainly don’t seem equipped to survive it now.
The Milwaukee Brewers dealt a blow to the Dodgers’ October psyche with their NLCS Game 1 win, but the Dodgers have shown they’re capable of bouncing back.
Look at how they lost on Monday. On second thought, don’t look, because what you’ll see bears scant resemblance to the swaggering, self-assured Dodgers of postseasons past.
They pitched their October ace Yoshinobu Yamamoto, and he’s always saved them, right? Not this time. He couldn’t make it out of the third inning, battered by scattered wildness and scathing swings.
They were handed runs on two errors by the Brewers shaky rookie starter Logan Henderson, and they’ve always capitalized, right? Not this time. They couldn’t make the Brewers pay for their clumsiness, managing just three total hits, the slumps of their superstars ever deepening, Will Smith and Shohei Ohtani now becoming absolute offensive liabilities.
Even with all this, they sent Henderson packing after four innings and took aim at a heavily used Brewer bullpen and surely they could summon the firepower to send at least one of those relievers running, right? Not this time, as four Brewer relievers set a major-league postseason record by pitching five perfect innings.
The last two innings being a sad microcosm of the previous seven.
Entering the eighth inning, the Dodgers only trailed 4-3 and had the top of their order coming up in what could have still been a trademark Dodger October comeback.
Not so fast.
Facing Abner Uribe, Mookie Betts struck out. Facing Aaron Ashby, Freddie Freeman struck out and Teoscar Hernández grounded out. Yeah, with perhaps their entire season on the line, they couldn’t even get the ball out of the infield.
The Brewers, of course, sealed the deal with two runs on three singles in the bottom of the eighth, and the Dodgers went meekly 1-2-3 in the ninth.
It was surely, truly painful for Dodger fans to witness the final out, a strikeout by … yep, last season’s World Series hero Miguel Rojas.
The three-peat is dying, and it’s almost unbearable to watch.
Having watched both of their top two aces beaten in Milwaukee, the Dodgers will now come home with Blake Snell and Tyler Glasnow starting in Game 3 and 4.
In any other scenario, both pitchers are aces as well and the Dodgers would have a huge advantage. But neither pitcher has looked great in the postseason and both will be pitching while bearing the weight of a stressed-out Dodger nation..
What could possibly stand in the way of the Dodgers becoming just the third franchise to win three World Series in a row? Plenty, it turns out.
“Yeah, it’s certainly a challenge,” said manager Dave Roberts. “I think that, if you look Game 3, I like where we’re at as far as in a vacuum, who’s pitching, where our bullpen is at, being at home. Then you’ve got to go from there.”
Roberts still has hope. But he’s not looking past Game 3.
“As far as can we do it, absolutely, but it’s just you want to get that first one,” he said.
Dodger Stadium will be filled with fans in what could be a celebration. Or a wake.

item.title: [New York Post] Shohei Ohtani, Will Smith are zeros again in Dodgers’ devastating Game 2 NLCS loss
item.dc:creator: Jack Harris
item.description: Heroes, zeros and other observations from the Dodgers’ 7–4 loss to the Milwaukee Brewers in Game 2 of the National League Championship Series: Zero: The whole Dodgers’ offense –– but especially Shohei Ohtani and Will Smith Really, the 7-4 scoreline in Monday’s Game 2 loss flattered the Dodgers. They managed just three hits. All of their scoring required the help of either a wild pitch or a throwing error from Brewers starter Logan Henderson. And once Milwaukee turned to the bullpen, their reliev
item.content:encoded:
Heroes, zeros and other observations from the Dodgers’ 7–4 loss to the Milwaukee Brewers in Game 2 of the National League Championship Series:
Zero: The whole Dodgers’ offense –– but especially Shohei Ohtani and Will Smith
Really, the 7-4 scoreline in Monday’s Game 2 loss flattered the Dodgers. They managed just three hits. All of their scoring required the help of either a wild pitch or a throwing error from Brewers starter Logan Henderson. And once Milwaukee turned to the bullpen, their relievers retired all 15 batters they faced the rest of the way.
Still, as has been the case all postseason, it was Ohtani and Smith whose struggles once again loomed largest.
From the Nos. 4-5 spots of the order –– after Smith was bumped down from the three-hole pregame –– they combined to go 0-for-8 with three strikeouts. Overall in the playoffs now, Ohtani is 3-for-20 without any extra-base hits, while Smith is now an unthinkable 1-for-23 with one walk and eight strikeouts.
Even worse for Smith, Monday included a couple of regrettable moments from behind the plate.
In both the first and third innings, Yoshinobu Yamamoto threw what should have been called third strikes against Brice Turang. But both times home plate umpire Chris Segal missed the call –– and, most crucially, Smith elected against trying to challenge.
Manager Dave Roberts didn’t want to second-guess his catcher postgame, while Yamamoto also described both pitches as being “too fine a line on the [edge of the] strike zone” to challenge.
Still, both times, they missed ABS chances backfired, with Turang doubling and later scoring in the first, then walking and later scoring in the third.
“It was kind of early in the game, we kind of had him on the ropes,” Smith said, explaining his thought process. “I figured we could get him out there [without risking the challenges].”
Hero: The Brewers’ bullpen
The Brewers’ bullpen also figured to be one of their strengths in this series.
But two games in, their dominance has shifted the scales of the series.
In Game 1, four Brewers relievers (DL Hall, Abner Uribe, Aaron Ashby and Trevor Megill) combined for 4 ⅔ scoreless innings while working out of several jams with a one-run lead.
In Game 2, the group was even more dominant, with four arms (Dustin May, JoJo Romero and Uribe and Ashby again) going 15 up, 15 down over five perfect closing innings.
The Dodgers’ hope is that, as the series wears on, their lineup will benefit from repeated looks at the group. However, they will have to find some sort of answer to the unit’s premium stuff first.
As of Monday night, Roberts was still searching for one.
“I know that they’ve got good arms,” Roberts said. “But I think they’re just finding ways to win pitches better than we are.”
Unsung hero
Fifteen months ago, the Dodgers traded May away as an excess piece of their pitching staff.
On Monday, he was the one Brewers pitcher to inherit some danger out of the bullpen, but found a way to limit damage in what would prove to be the Dodgers’ final rally.
After Henderson’s second error of the game –– on an errant throw while fielding a bunt from Tommy Edman –– allowed a tying run to score and left Edman standing on second, May retired Mookie Betts, Freddie Freeman and Teoscar Hernández in order. Betts’ grounder did move Edman to third, while Freeman’s sacrifice fly got him home for a brief 4-3 lead.
But May’s performance set the tone for the rest of Milwaukee’s bullpen dominance.
And now, he could turn around and be available to start Game 4, in what would be his first outing back at Dodger Stadium since being shipped away by the team.
Key stat: Four
As in, the number of misses Yoshinobu Yamamoto generated from 33 Brewers swings.
The resulting 12% whiff rate was tied for the second-lowest of Yamamoto’s career. More consequentially, it stressed his pitch count and prompted his eventual early exit from the game, leaving too large a workload for the Dodgers’ bullpen (which gave up four runs in its 5 ⅓ innings of work) to withstand at a raucous American Family Field.
Quote of the night
“They had much better at-bats than we did across the board, top to bottom. And then they put the ball in play, created havoc. That’s what they do, and we didn’t do that.”
That was Roberts’ overall summation of the Dodgers’ Game 2 loss. It captured the many, but ultimately simple, reasons they find themselves facing a daunting two-game deficit as the series shifts back to Los Angeles for Game 3 on Wednesday night.

item.title: [Los Angeles Times] Yoshinobu Yamamoto chased early, Dodgers fall into two-game hole after Game 2 NLCS loss
item.dc:creator: Maddie Lee
item.description: - Click here to listen to this article - Yoshinobu Yamamoto lasted just 2⅔ innings, and the Dodgers couldn’t hold multiple leads in a 7-4 loss to Milwaukee in Game 2 of the National League Championship Series. - The Brewers’ relievers shut down Los Angeles for the second straight game, putting the Dodgers in a 2-0 series hole as the NLCS shifts to Dodger Stadium. MILWAUKEE — Yoshinobu Yamamoto stood on the same mound where just a year ago he’d thrown a complete game and was pummeled by Brewers f
item.content:encoded:
- Click here to listen to this article
- Yoshinobu Yamamoto lasted just 2⅔ innings, and the Dodgers couldn’t hold multiple leads in a 7-4 loss to Milwaukee in Game 2 of the National League Championship Series.
- The Brewers’ relievers shut down Los Angeles for the second straight game, putting the Dodgers in a 2-0 series hole as the NLCS shifts to Dodger Stadium.
MILWAUKEE — Yoshinobu Yamamoto stood on the same mound where just a year ago he’d thrown a complete game and was pummeled by Brewers fans’ chants:
“Yel-li! Yel-li!”
This time, en route to the Dodgers’ 7-4 loss to Milwaukee on Monday in Game 2 of the National League Championship Series, Yamamoto had lasted only 2⅔ innings.
As American Family Field celebrated Brewers captain Christian Yelich’s two-run single for an early lead, Dodgers manager Dave Roberts emerged from the visiting dugout, ready to take the ball from the starter who’d made himself a household name with his postseason heroics.
Dodgers hitters are stymied by the Brewers bullpen, which throws five perfect innings in a 7-4 win that gives Milwaukee a 2-0 lead in the NLCS.
Yamamoto’s early exit put the onus on the Dodgers’ bullpen in a back-and-forth contest. And the Brewers’ bullpen shut down the Dodgers’ offense for the second straight game, pitching five hitless innings. The Dodgers finished with just three hits.
The NLCS heads to Los Angeles with the Brewers leading 2-0 in the best-of-seven series. The Dodgers will have home-field advantage for the next three games, needing to win four of the next five to return to the World Series.
It was the second straight highly touted pitching matchup, pitting Yamamoto against Logan Henderson, the Brewers’ 24-year-old budding star.
Yamamoto exited after giving up three runs and four hits in the shortest start of his career. Against Henderson, the Dodgers took advantage of mistakes by the Brewers’ usually fundamentally sound defense to score four runs against him, only two of which were earned.
The Dodgers’ offense started to chip away at Henderson right away. Leadoff hitter Mookie Betts worked a walk, which included a successful ABS challenge that turned a strikeout into a full count.
Betts then advanced to second on Freddie Freeman’s groundout to second and to third on a wild pitch.
The night before, Teoscar Hernández had zeroed in on the Dodgers’ at-bats with runners in scoring position in his postgame comments.
“We did a pretty good job,” he said after the Dodgers’ 2-1 loss in Game 1. “We just didn’t get the job done when we needed with guys in scoring position.”
His first at-bat Monday came with Betts 90 feet from home plate. Roberts had swapped Hernández and slumping Will Smith in the batting order, moving Hernández up to third and Smith down to fifth.
“For Teo to get three cracks at this guy, I like it,” Roberts said.
Right away, Hernández delivered. He fell into an 0-and-2 count but prolonged the at-bat and drove a fastball into right-center for a sacrifice fly.
The Brewers, however, evened the score without delay. Yamamoto struck out Jackson Chourio — whose leadoff home run last year was the lone run in Yamamoto’s NLCS complete game — to open the frame.
Then Brice Turang worked a full count and hit an opposite-field double. And William Contreras fought off a low slider, poking it into shallow left field to tie the score.
Two innings later, the Dodgers took the lead again, rewarded for hard contact as the Brewers’ defense showed its first signs of sloppy play. Tommy Edman led off with a single, and then Betts scorched a 100.9-mph one-hopper at shortstop Cooper Pratt, who mishandled it, giving Betts a single to put two runners on. Edman then advanced to third on a fly ball by Freeman.
Henderson tried to pick off Edman, but his errant throw gave the Dodgers the lead.
It didn’t last long.
In the bottom of the third, Yamamoto gave up a leadoff single and issued two walks before Yelich came up with two outs and drove a curveball into center field for two runs.
The first walk, to Turang, included a borderline ball four call. And the second, to Jake Bauers, came after 12 pitches.
As soon as Yamamoto left the game, it was clear it would be an uphill battle for the Dodgers.
The Dodgers retook the lead in the fifth with more help from the Brewers. After Kyle Tucker’s leadoff double, Edman laid down a sacrifice bunt. Henderson picked up the ball and sailed a throw to first, enabling the tying run to score.
Later in the inning, after former Dodger Dustin May replaced Henderson, Freeman hit a sacrifice fly, and Edman scored the go-ahead run.
This is postseason baseball, where the best pitchers take center stage and runs are at a premium. Would a stolen base or a sacrifice bunt every so often kill the Dodgers?
But, as had been the pattern all game, that 4-3 lead didn’t hold for long.
Roberts brought in left-hander Kris Bubic, replacing right-hander Roki Sasaki after a hitless inning, to face the left-handed-heavy heart of the order. But Bubic missed down the middle to the right-handed-hitting Contreras, who gave the fastball a ride over the center field wall, tying the score.
In the sixth, against Dodgers right-hander Brock Stewart, Contreras singled in the go-ahead run in a traffic-filled inning that included a Freeman error on a muffed pickoff attempt. Dodgers left-hander Tanner Scott came to the rescue and struck out Bauers and Yelich to end the inning, and Garrett Mitchell to kick off the seventh.
The Brewers added insurance runs in the eighth inning on RBI singles by Turang off hard-throwing right-hander Edgardo Henriquez and Bauers against left-hander Justin Wrobleski.

item.title: [Orange County Register] Dodgers shut out by Brewers’ bullpen again, fall behind 2-0 in NLCS
item.dc:creator: Bill Plunkett
item.description: MILWAUKEE — Billboards around town promote the Milwaukee Brewers with the slogan “Win Our Way.” The Dodgers tried. It didn’t work. They scored four runs without getting a hit with a runner in scoring position – or hitting a home run. But the Brewers outhit them 12-3 and the final 15 Dodgers batters were retired in order as the Brewers pulled away to a 7-4 victory on Monday in Game 2 of the National League Championship Series. “They pitched well and they hit good,” Freddie Freeman said. “That’s t
item.content:encoded:
MILWAUKEE — Billboards around town promote the Milwaukee Brewers with the slogan “Win Our Way.”
The Dodgers tried. It didn’t work.
They scored four runs without getting a hit with a runner in scoring position – or hitting a home run. But the Brewers outhit them 12-3 and the final 15 Dodgers batters were retired in order as the Brewers pulled away to a 7-4 victory on Monday in Game 2 of the National League Championship Series.
“They pitched well and they hit good,” Freddie Freeman said. “That’s the name of the game, and they did it better than us today.”
They did it twice in Milwaukee. The best-of-seven series now heads back to Los Angeles with the Dodgers trailing 2-0. Game 3 is Wednesday at 5 p.m. with Blake Snell scheduled to start for the Dodgers.
“Grind. Win one game at a time, one pitch at a time,” Mookie Betts said. “The mindset can’t really change. We can’t add more pressure. There’s already enough as it is. Keep it simple. One pitch at a time. Figure out a way to get a hit.”
They have played hard to get for the Dodgers this postseason. Through six games against the Atlanta Braves and Brewers, they are batting .193 (37 for 192) as a team and, most costly, 2 for 26 (.077) with runners in scoring position.
“I don’t have an answer why,” Dodgers manager Dave Roberts said. “I know that they’ve got good arms. So do we. I think they’re just finding ways to win pitches better than we are. Sometimes you’ve got to find a way to get a base hit and those guys — there’s a lot of balls that weren’t hit hard tonight but found the outfield grass. That’s hitting.”
The Dodgers found ways to score without hitting early in Game 2.
The pesky, opportunistic Dodgers scored a run in the first inning without a hit. Betts drew a leadoff walk, moved to second on Freddie Freeman’s slow roller then third on a wild pitch and scored on a sacrifice fly by Teoscar Hernandez.
They scored again on a pair of singles and a wild pickoff throw by Brewers starting pitcher Logan Henderson who was more effective throwing home than he was to first base.
That came up again in the fifth inning. Kyle Tucker led off with a double and Tommy Edman tried to bunt him to third – you wanted bunts. Henderson did him one better, fielding the ball and throwing wildly to first base. Tucker scored on Henderson’s second error and Edman wound up scoring on a close play at the plate (confirmed by replay) on a sacrifice fly by Freeman.
Each of the runs either gave the Dodgers the lead or tied the game as the two teams played in a phone booth, never straying more than a run apart.
That was true, in part, because Dodgers starter Yoshinobu Yamamoto was not sharp. He threw 75 pitches to get just two outs into the third inning. The Brewers swung at 33 of those pitches and only missed four times.
“He wasn’t as precise as he normally is,” Dodgers catcher Will Smith said. “I thought they did a really good job, not expanding out of the zone, taking advantage, especially up the middle.”
Two key decisions by Smith could have changed things, though.
On a 2-and-2 pitch to Brice Turang in the first inning, Yamamoto seemed to hit the outside corner with a cutter for strike three – or he didn’t. That was the call by home plate umpire Chris Segal. It might have been overturned by ABS but Smith did not challenge.
Two pitches later, Turang doubled. William Contreras drove him in with a single.
“Yeah, I went back and looked,” Smith said of the questionable call. “I don’t know if it clipped it or whatever. It was kind of early in the game. We kind of had him on the ropes where we could just get him out there.
“The walk one was a bummer but I guess it happens. It’s baseball.”
That came two innings later. The Brewers had a runner at second with one out when Yamamoto again appeared to hit the outside corner with a splitter on a full count to Turang. Segal called it a ball and Yamamoto appeared to gesture towards Smith that he wanted to challenge. Smith didn’t.
“That one was a splitter. It actually cut back a little bit,” Smith said. “I just saw it out (of the strike zone) and didn’t know if it came back enough or not.”
Two batters later, Jake Bauers won a 12-pitch battle with Yamamoto – the longest plate appearance against Yamamoto this season – fouling off six consecutive pitches before drawing a walk to load the bases.
“I was trying to work on the edge of the zone,” Yamamoto said through his interpreter. “And some pitches it was really good but he just stayed on it. He did a good job.”
Two pitches later, Christian Yelich stroked a two-run single through the middle, the first base hit off of a Yamamoto curveball since August 27 and the last pitch Yamamoto would throw in the game.
“That changed the game,” Brewers manager Pat Murphy said of Bauers’ walk, adding that he was told the confrontation lasted seven minutes. “You think about that and what it does to a pitcher. He can get through an inning in less than seven minutes and he does all the time. He’s one of the best pitchers in the land. It was a great at-bat. I think a turning point, I really do.”
It started the Dodgers’ bullpen turning.
Roberts turned to Alex Vesia to finish off the third and gave the ball to Roki Sasaki for a scoreless fourth.
But then he took it away from the converted starter after just one inning and gave it to Kris Bubic with two lefties coming up in the fifth. In between them was Contreras and he tied the game with a solo home run off Bubic. The Dodgers never regained a lead.
“For me, I felt Bubic had 4 out of 5 left-handed hitters (coming up), and that’s a perfect spot for him,” Roberts said. “I knew they weren’t going to hit for them. You have Roki for an inning, and then you still have a guy — in my opinion, you’ve got a great spot for Bubic.
“That’s a decision I made, and we just didn’t — again, that’s his lane to be able to go out there and throw up a zero.”
The Brewers finally did things their way in the sixth inning against Brock Stewart.
He hit No. 9 hitter David Hamilton with a pitch. Hamilton went to second when Freeman mishandled a pickoff throw from Stewart and third on a ground out by Jackson Chourio. After an intentional walk of Turang, Contreras collected his third RBI of the game with a single to left field.
They did it again in the eighth against Edgardo Henriquez. Hamilton led off with a single, stole second and went to third on a ground out. Turang drove him in with an RBI single, giving the Brewers the first two-run lead for either team in this series. When Bauers drove in another run with a single, it gave the Brewers their first three-run lead this postseason.
Left to their own devices, the Dodgers couldn’t create another scoring opportunity. The final 15 batters went down in order against Brewers relievers Dustin May, JoJo Romero, Abner Uribe and Aaron Ashby.
“They all throw 100 (mph) from different angles,” Freeman said.
The five perfect innings in relief are a postseason record. In winning the first two games of the NLCS, the Brewers’ bullpen has pitched 9⅔ scoreless innings.
“They attack hitters. They throw strikes. They’ve got good stuff, They throw hard,” Teoscar Hernandez said. “We just got to do a better job.
“I mean, they threw, the last two days, the same pitchers beside the starters. So we know what we’re gonna get during the games. They trust those guys. So that’s the guys that we’re gonna get.”
The Dodgers do not face elimination yet. But they must win two out of three at home in order to avoid it.
“We’ve got to find a way to get hits. That’s really it,” Betts repeated.
“They’re a really good ballclub. Really good arms. They’re swinging it. They’re playing really well. We have to come and be ready to go. There’s no secrets. We’re playing the game the same way. We’ve just got to find a way to get those hits.”

item.title: [New York Post] Dodgers’ biggest advantages are disappearing at the worst possible time
item.dc:creator: Dylan Hernandez
item.description: MILWAUKEE – One by one, their advantages are vanishing. Their edge in starting pitching? Marginalized by the Brewers’ lineup. Their superior offensive firepower? Held without a home run in the first two games of this National League Championship Series. Shohei Ohtani? Reduced to being blown away by mid-90s fastballs. item.content:encoded:
MILWAUKEE – One by one, their advantages are vanishing.
Their edge in starting pitching?
Marginalized by the Brewers’ lineup.
Their superior offensive firepower?
Held without a home run in the first two games of this National League Championship Series.
Shohei Ohtani?
Reduced to being blown away by mid-90s fastballs.
The Dodgers are behind by two games in this race to four wins, and in the wake of their 7-4 defeat in Game 2 at American Family Field, they have to be praying for the Brewers to run out of gas before they reach the finish line.
“It’s certainly a challenge,” manager Dave Roberts said.
Before the Dodgers can win this series, they will have to get back into it first. They will play at home over the next three games. They have Blake Snell and Tyler Glasnow lined up to pitch in Games 3 and 4, respectively.
“Still a pretty good scenario we’re in,” first baseman Freddie Freeman said.
Sending Snell and Glasnow to the mound won’t mean anything, however, if the Dodgers don’t start hitting. An error or wild pitch by the Brewers played a role in every run scored by the Dodgers, who collected only three hits, all of them coming against starter Logan Henderson. The four relievers deployed by Brewers manager Pat Murphy combined to pitch five no-hit innings.
The Dodgers will have to jumpstart their offense with a version of Shohei Ohtani who remains physically diminished.
Ohtani was 0 for 4 in Game 2, failing to reach base in a game for the first time this postseason. Pitching as if they didn’t think that Ohtani couldn’t hurt them, the Brewers attacked the four-time Most Valuable Player, leading to a couple of strikeouts in which he looked completely overmatched.
Henderson struck him out with three fastballs in the first inning. Left-hander Jojo Romero tricked him into waving at a sweeper that ended up in the batter’s box on the other side of home plate in the fifth.
Ohtani is batting .150 in the playoffs without a single run batted in. He’s struck out seven times in 20 at-bats. His last home run was on Aug. 18.
“It’s hard to see,” Betts said. “We know he’s working and hopefully he gets out of it. We need him. We need him for sure.”
Ohtani alone couldn’t take down the Brewers, regardless how well he was playing. In addition to a relentless bullpen, they have an unspectacular but industrious offense. They have the kind of edge that makes it obvious they believe they can take down the two-time defending World Series champions.
Game 2 was a prime example of that. If there was a game the Brewers were expected to drop, it was this one. Yoshinobu Yamamoto was pitching for the Dodgers.
The Brewers didn’t just beat Yamamoto. They wore him down, pushed him out of the game after only 2 ⅔ innings and forced Roberts to empty his bullpen. Tarik Skubal lasted only five innings against them in Game 1.
The result was an unmitigated disaster for the Dodgers, who have made it an annual tradition to have the Japanese right-hander bail them out of trouble at this time of the year.
The Dodgers were intimately familiar with the script from which the Brewers read.
Run up the pitch count of the starter.
Force him out of the game early.
Get into the other team’s bullpen.
Only this time, the Dodgers weren’t the team executing the game plan. They were the team against which the plan was being executed, and Yamamoto was the target of the attack.
Once the game morphed into a battle of the bullpens, the game was decided. The Brewers were able to play to their greatest strength. The Dodgers had to expose their greatest weakness.
To win the World Series last year, the Dodgers had to overcome a three-games-to-two deficit against the Toronto Blue Jays. Their title run the previous year started with them reversing a two-games-to-one deficit against the San Diego Padres.
The Dodgers have overcome deficits before.
But the Brewers are presenting them with the sort of problems they might not even be able to solve.

item.title: [True Blue LA] Dodgers need Brewers help to score, can’t stop William Contreras in NLCS Game 2 loss
item.dc:creator: Eric Stephen
item.description: Best laid plans went awry very early in Game 2 of the National League Championship Series, the sloppiest and wildest game of the Dodgers postseason to date. In a game with four lead changes and two ties, the Dodgers couldn’t get a big hit to save their life, while William Contreras had three different run-scoring hits in the Brewers’ 7-4 win at American Family Field on Monday afternoon in Milwaukee. The Dodgers head home to Los Angeles down two games to none, with their largest series deficit si
item.content:encoded:
Best laid plans went awry very early in Game 2 of the National League Championship Series, the sloppiest and wildest game of the Dodgers postseason to date. In a game with four lead changes and two ties, the Dodgers couldn’t get a big hit to save their life, while William Contreras had three different run-scoring hits in the Brewers’ 7-4 win at American Family Field on Monday afternoon in Milwaukee.
The Dodgers head home to Los Angeles down two games to none, with their largest series deficit since the 2023 NLDS.
Chaos to start
It took until the 23rd half-inning of the series for one of these teams to score more than once in a frame, but it wasn’t for lack of trying. Both Jacob Misiorowski and Tarik Skubal labored in big innings in Game 1, but limited the damage to just one run in the rallies.
After single runs for both teams in the first inning, Yoshinobu Yamamoto ran into trouble. David Hamilton singled and stole second base. Brice Turang, who battled back from an 0-2 count and an unchallenged potential third-strike ball call for a double to score in the first inning, worked his way back from an 0-2 count again to walk in the third.
With two outs and two on, first baseman Jake Bauers fouled off six full-count pitches before earning a walk to load the bases.
“Yamamoto — it’s such a big pitch mix,” Bauers said during his media availability before the game. “There’s a lot that you have to try and deal with, and I think you can fall into the trap of trying to guess along with him.”
It took only two more pitches for Yamamoto to hang a curveball to Christian Yelich — in easily the worst of his 14 major league seasons — who singled home two to turn a Dodgers lead into a Dodgers deficit. It also ended Yamamoto’s day, stunningly after needing 75 pitches to get only eight outs, the shortest of his 11 postseason start with the Dodgers.
The dozen pitches to Bauers were the most in any single plate appearance in Yamamoto’s three years in the majors, the entire battle taking seven minutes, 15 seconds per the Fox broadcast.
Only way the Dodgers scored
Brewers starter Logan Henderson allowed only three hits, one of them a ball booted by shortstop Cooper Pratt. Henderson also walked two, but it was three errant throws that proved his undoing. His wild pitch in the first inning put Mookie Betts on third base directly before scoring on a sacrifice fly.
Henderson in the third inning with runners on the corners threw wildly on a pickoff attempt of Betts at first base, allowing Tommy Edman to score from third base. After Kyle Tucker doubled to lead off the fifth inning, Henderson had another throwing error when Edman tried to sacrifice, not only scoring Tucker but putting Edman on second base. He would later score on another sacrifice fly, on a play so close at the plate it required replay review to confirm.
Getting the big hits, or not
Contreras, the Brewers three-time All-Star catcher, singled home a run off Yamamoto in the first inning to tie the game, homered off left-hander Kris Bubic in the fifth inning to tie the game, then singled home a run off Brock Stewart in the sixth to give the Brewers the lead.
It was the third multi-hit game in these playoffs for Contreras, who has three home runs this October.
The Dodgers’ three-time All-Star catcher, Will Smith, was dropped to fifth in the batting order on Monday and was hitless in four at-bats. Smith has one single in 23 at-bats this postseason, with eight strikeouts.
“Obviously want the results to be a little better, but at the end of the day, it’s [six] games at the plate,” Smith told reporters in Milwaukee on Monday before Game 2. “No panic from me. So I’ll be fine.”
Smith isn’t alone in struggles at the plate.
Shohei Ohtani, still batting fourth, was hitless in four at-bats with two strikeouts in Game 2, and has three singles in 19 at-bats plus three walks this postseason.
The Brewers tacked on insurance runs in the eighth inning off Edgardo Henriquez and Justin Wrobleski with three singles and a walk. That put the Brewers up 7-4, the first time either team led by more than one run in this series.
Game 2 of the NLCS was just the second of 27 games this postseason in which both teams scored at least four runs.
Against Henderson the Dodgers were hitless in all of four total at-bats with runners in scoring position, dropping them to 2-for-26 with runners in scoring position this postseason. But once he left with no outs in the fifth inning, the Brewers bullpen completely shut things down the rest of the way.
Dustin May, JoJo Romero, Abner Uribe, and Aaron Ashby faced 15 batters and retired them all. Ashby pitched in multiple innings for a second straight day, this time earning the save.
The Dodgers now face a major uphill battle once they get back home.
NLCS Game 2 particulars
Home run: William Contreras (3)
WP — JoJo Romero (1-1): 1 IP 2 strikeouts
LP — Brock Stewart (0-1): 2/3 IP, 2 hits, 1 run, 1 walk, 1 strikeout
Sv — Aaron Ashby (1): 1 2/3 IP, 2 strikeouts
Up next
The NLCS moves location to Los Angeles beginning with Game 3 on Wednesday evening (5 p.m., FS1). Blake Snell probably starts for the Dodgers, though Dave Roberts earlier Monday wasn’t willing to confirm their plans just yet. Left-hander Robert Gasser starts on the mound for the Brewers.

item.title: [New York Post] Brewers demoralize Dodgers, Yoshinobu Yamamoto to take stunning 2-0 NLCS lead
item.dc:creator: Jack Harris
item.description: MILWAUKEE –– The Dodgers were hoping to hit the reset switch on Monday. Instead, all they did was slam down on the panic button. Losing Game 1 of this National League Championship Series rematch against the Milwaukee Brewers was one thing. Dropping Game 2 on Monday, however, threatened to put their season in suddenly dire straits. This time, after all, they weren’t facing a presumptive Cy Young Award winner like Jacob Misiorowski. This time, more importantly, they had their own postseason stalwa
item.content:encoded:
MILWAUKEE –– The Dodgers were hoping to hit the reset switch on Monday.
Instead, all they did was slam down on the panic button.
Losing Game 1 of this National League Championship Series rematch against the Milwaukee Brewers was one thing. Dropping Game 2 on Monday, however, threatened to put their season in suddenly dire straits.
This time, after all, they weren’t facing a presumptive Cy Young Award winner like Jacob Misiorowski. This time, more importantly, they had their own postseason stalwart, reigning World Series MVP Yoshinobu Yamamoto, on the hill to calm the waters.
But in a 7-4 defeat at American Family Field, an unexpected thing happened.
Yamamoto, despite entering with a five-game playoff win streak and the second-lowest postseason ERA in the last 100 years, couldn’t steady the two-time defending champions.
The Brewers, who allowed Yamamoto to throw a complete game against them on the very same mound in Game 2 of last year’s NLCS sweep, turned the tables decisively with long, relentless, unforgiving offensive rallies.
“They had much better at-bats than we did across the board, top to bottom, and then they put the ball in play, created havoc,” manager Dave Roberts said. “That’s what they do, and we didn’t do that. That’s the difference in the game … They did what needed to do tonight.”
Indeed, Yamamoto would last only 2 ⅔ innings in a 75-pitch grind against Milwaukee’s pesky, opportunistic offense. Despite being handed a pair of early one-run leads, he would depart the mound with the Dodgers behind.
It was a demoralizing turn of events –– keyed by a couple missed ABS challenge opportunities for Will Smith, an epic 12-pitch battle by Brewers slugger Jake Bauers, and a go-ahead two-run single from former MVP Christian Yelich that ultimately chased Yamamoto from the game.
While the contest would go back-and-forth from there, Yamamoto’s early exit gave the Dodgers’ bullpen too tall a task to withstand, sending the team back to Los Angeles for Game 3 on Wednesday desperately needing a response to a stunning two-games-to-none deficit.
“We got a lot of experience, we’ve been through everything before,” first baseman Freddie Freeman said. “So we’ll regroup tomorrow and go get ’em on Wednesday.”
The Dodgers did open the scoring Monday, manufacturing a first-inning run after Mookie Betts drew a leadoff walk, took second on a grounder, advanced to third on a wild pitch, then scored on a Teoscar Hernández sacrifice fly.
However, the Brewers responded with a rally of their own in the bottom of the first –– one that set the tone for their plan of attack against Yamamoto on Sunday.
With one out in the inning, Yamamoto seemed to freeze Brice Turang for a called third strike. But, home plate umpire Chris Segal inaccurately ruled it a ball, and Smith declined to use an ABS challenge behind the plate. Three pitches later, it would prove costly, with Turang getting a full-count fastball in the zone and slicing into left for a double. In the next at-bat, William Contreras came up and somehow stayed on a 2-2 slider less than a foot off the dirt, lofting a line drive just over Max Muncy’s head at third for an RBI single.
“It was kind of early in the game,” Smith said of the ABS decision. “We kind of had him on the ropes where we could just [try to] get him out there [even without the challenge].”
A similar story would play out in the third, as the Brewers erased a 2-1 lead the Dodgers took on an errant pickoff throw from Brewers starter Logan Henderson in the top half of the frame.
That inning began with a David Hamilton single. Then, after he stole second, Turang would again benefit from a missed ABS challenge opportunity –– with Smith declining to appeal another potential third strike in a full count, even as Yamamoto seemingly suggested he do so by pointing at his head himself on the mound.
“In that spot, Will didn’t feel like it was a strike,” Roberts said, trying not to secong-guess his catcher. “But obviously if you look back, [if] that’s a called third strike … that changes the outing.”
Once again, it set a disaster in motion. With an extra out to get, Yamamoto failed to complete the inning.
Instead, Bauers stepped up with two outs and forced Yamamoto into the longest plate appearance of his MLB career, drawing a walk from a grueling dozen-pitch battle.
After working a full-count, Bauers fouled off the next seven pitches he saw, chopping balls off the plate, to the backstop, into the seats, and –– twice –– just out of the reach of Dodgers fielders in foul territory.
The seven-minute duel went on so long, the battery in Yamamoto’s PitchCom device died after his 11th pitch, causing a delay while he was brought a replacement from the dugout.
“It just got to a certain point where it was straight compete mode,” Bauers said. “A little bit of a blackout, just kind of in the flow a little bit competing.”
Finally, on pitch No. 12, Bauers took a curveball in the dirt, loading the bases.
In the next at-bat, a clearly fatigued Yamamoto hung a curveball to Yelich, who lined his two-run single to center to give the Brewers a 3-2 lead.
That would be the end of Yamamoto’s day, marking the shortest outing of his playoff career. It would also leave too many innings for the Dodgers’ bullpen to cover –– even after the team retook the lead with a two-run rally in the fifth that was keyed by another throwing error from Henderson.
In the bottom of the fifth, Contreras greeted left-hander Kris Bubic with a towering game-tying home run that clanged off the bottom of the center-field scoreboard.
In the sixth, it would be Contreras again to push the Brewers back in front, lining a first-pitch single to left against Brock Stewart –– who had made his own mess by hitting a batter and firing an errant pickoff throw to first –– that gave the Brewers’ star catcher his third RBI of the day.
This time, the Dodgers wouldn’t have an answer, nor be gifted another pathway back into the game.
Rather, for a second-straight night, they were completely shut down by the Brewers’ bullpen, going 15 up, 15 down without a single baserunner after Henderson’s exit to finish the game with just three hits.
The Brewers, meanwhile, tacked on two insurance runs in the eighth, removing any pretense of late-game drama before a jubilant sell-out crowd.
Now, the Dodgers face a two-game hole they would have never imagined. Alarm bells are ringing. Their season, and World Series three-peat hopes, are dangerously close to being dashed.

item.title: [DodgersBeat] Roberts Calls Yoshinobu Yamamoto's Preparation "Spectacular"
item.dc:creator: Steve Webb
item.description: MILWAUKEE, WI — Dave Roberts has watched Yoshinobu Yamamoto prepare for enough big starts to know how much work goes into his calm on the mound. Before Monday’s Game 2 in Milwaukee, Roberts called that preparation “spectacular” and compared his care for each detail with Clayton Kershaw’s.
