Ahead of Tuesday's matchup, Roberts named three players who could insert themselves into the lineup for NLDS Game
item.content:encoded:
Los Angeles Dodgers manager Dave Roberts named potential players who could get a spot in the starting lineup for NLDS Game 3.
The Dodgers' offense hasn't been its best through the first two games of the series, relying exclusively on homers to score all seven of their runs so far. A change of personnel could help the Dodgers string together some hits and bring some more runs across.
Ahead of Tuesday's matchup, Roberts named three players who could insert themselves into the lineup for NLDS Game 3.
"You've got Kiké [Hernandez], you've got [Miguel Rojas], you've got Muncy," Roberts said.
Hernandez provides plenty of positional versatility for the Dodgers, and could stand in at a number of positions if the Dodgers want to approach their matchup against the left-handed Chris Sale with a lineup full of right-handed batters.
The fan favorite's most likely role if he were to start Game 3 would be as the third baseman, keeping left-handed third baseman Max Muncy out of the lineup for a second consecutive game despite hitting homers in each of the first two games of the series, but he could also play either of the corner outfield spots if needed.
Rojas would stand in at second base for Tommy Edman in the most likely case, as Roberts isn't quite ready to move Edman into center to replace Andy Pages despite his rough postseason record.
Who Won't Start for the Dodgers on Tuesday?
In addition to those three players, Roberts revealed Josue De Paula won't have a starting spot against Sale.
"Josue De Paula I don't see being an option," Roberts said.
As a left-handed batter, De Paula's omission from the lineup makes plenty of sense, and he will be available off of the bench for the remainder of the game.
Other than De Paula, Hyeseong Kim and Hunter Feduccia almost certainly won't start, but the rest of the lineup could change as the Dodgers look to find a spark in their offense. With the series tied at one game apiece, the Dodgers need to claim victory in one of their two games in Atlanta to ensure they return home for a game if necessary.
Game 3 could swing momentum in the Dodgers' direction, and they'll do anything to take the lead in the NLDS. Tuesday's game begins at 3:00 p.m. PT.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Shohei Ohtani, Hank Aaron Award finalist, still searching at the plate
item.dc:creator: Eric Stephen
item.description: Dodgers designated hitter has won the Hank Aaron Award, the honor given annually to the top offensive player in his league, in each of the previous three seasons, in 2023 with the Angels then in 2024-25 in his first two years with the Dodgers. Ohtani won't win it this season, but he's a finalist again, and deservedly so. Now the Dodgers need Ohtani to find something, anything at the plate as they try to break a 1-1 tie in the National League Division Series against the Braves. Ohtani has two sin
item.content:encoded:
Dodgers designated hitter has won the Hank Aaron Award, the honor given annually to the top offensive player in his league, in each of the previous three seasons, in 2023 with the Angels then in 2024-25 in his first two years with the Dodgers. Ohtani won't win it this season, but he's a finalist again, and deservedly so.
Now the Dodgers need Ohtani to find something, anything at the plate as they try to break a 1-1 tie in the National League Division Series against the Braves.
Ohtani has two singles in eight at-bats during the NLDS, and since returning from the injured list on September 23 has seven hits, including a double, in 29 at-bats, with one walk and a strikeout. There was the September 24 game against the Padres in which he consistently hit the ball hard, but other than that Ohtani hasn't gotten any real results at the plate for seven weeks.
He last homered on August 18 at Coors Field, and in 94 plate appearances since is hitting a paltry .160/.277/.198.
Ohtani was clearly diminished at the plate just before landing on the injured list four weeks ago, after dealing with left knee inflammation and a right biceps injury. All sides seem to agree Ohtani is not 100 percent, but when asked if his injuries would require offseason attention, Ohtani didn't offer much in response.
"I haven't been able to get a good grasp of the root cause of all this. I think that process is going to happen during the off-season when I'm going to have a little bit more time to be able to address it," Ohtani said, through interpreter Will Ireton, last Friday on the eve of the NLDS. "But as of now, it's something I'm just going to have to manage."
We probably won't know the full extent of Ohtani's maladies this season until some Instagram post with a considered-font graphic detailing whatever procedure he might have had once the season is done. But for now, if we take Ohtani and the Dodgers at their word and he is healthy enough to play, he hasn't helped himself by chasing. Ohtani swung at seven pitches outside the strike zone in Game 2 alone on Sunday.
"I think that the amount of at-bats leading up to it, it was, I think, five games, I think you still — I felt good about having some at-bats to finish the season, the at-bats that he took in the bye week," manager Dave Roberts told reporters on Monday in Atlanta on the workout day at Truist Park. "But at the end of the day, he can still do a better job of staying in the strike zone. I don't think that that has anything to do with — he had the five games. He had the at-bats in between. I think that's something that — it's hard to have success when you're out of the zone."
Roberts in that same media session on Monday said he would even consider moving Ohtani even further down in the lineup. Ohtani batted second in two of his five regular season games after getting activated from the injured list and batted second in both NLDS games to date.
In three years with the Dodgers, Ohtani has only batted first or second, with his last time in another lineup spot coming in 2023, with 59 starts batting third for the Angels.
"I think moving him from 1 to 2 — but going further than that? I'm open to it," Roberts said Monday. "And it's something that if I do, I would obviously have the conversation with Shohei to explain why."
While most of the last month and a half focused on what Ohtani hasn't done, his overall numbers in 2026 were solid, and among the best in the sport. They just happen to pale in comparison to his 54-homer, 59-steal campaign followed by 55 home runs in his first two years with the Dodgers.
Ohtani hit .275/.377/.512 with 30 home runs, a 139 wRC+, 89 runs scored, 81 RBI, and 81 walks in 135 games. He's one of 10 finalists for the National League Aaron Award, which will almost certainly go to Pete Crow-Armstrong.
2026 NL Hank Aaron Award finalists
- CJ Abrams – Washington Nationals
- Jake Bauers – Milwaukee Brewers
- Pete Crow-Armstrong – Chicago Cubs
- Elly De La Cruz – Cincinnati Reds
- Shohei Ohtani – Los Angeles Dodgers
- Matt Olson – Atlanta Braves
- Kyle Schwarber – Philadelphia Phillies
- Sal Stewart – Cincinnati Reds
- Fernando Tatis Jr. – San Diego Padres
- Jordan Walker – St. Louis Cardinals
The Aaron Award, which has existed since 1999, is decided by a panel of "MLB legends and past recipients of the prestigious award" plus fan voting that accumulates into one vote on the panel. The Hank Aaron Award winners in each league will be announced during the MLB awards show on November 11.

item.title: [DodgersBeat] Dave Roberts Ponders Dodger Lineup Tweaks Ahead of Game 3
item.dc:creator: Steve Webb
item.description: ATLANTA, GA — Dave Roberts spent Monday weighing changes on both sides of the ball before Game 3 in Atlanta. The Dodgers manager said he is considering lineup tweaks against Chris Sale, including the possibility of moving Shohei Ohtani lower in the order. He also made it clear that Edwin Díaz has worked his way back into serious ninth-inning consideration after his sharp outing in Game 2. With the NLDS tied 1-1, Roberts sounded open to adjusting quickly. Díaz Could Close “I think that we’ve buil
item.content:encoded:
ATLANTA, GA — Dave Roberts spent Monday weighing changes on both sides of the ball before Game 3 in Atlanta.
The Dodgers manager said he is considering lineup tweaks against Chris Sale, including the possibility of moving Shohei Ohtani lower in the order. He also made it clear that Edwin Díaz has worked his way back into serious ninth-inning consideration after his sharp outing in Game 2.
With the NLDS tied 1-1, Roberts sounded open to adjusting quickly.
Díaz Could Close
“I think that we’ve built him up, regained the confidence in him and himself,” Roberts said of Díaz. “I think that it’s certainly a viable option for tomorrow night. I feel very confident with him finishing a game.”
Roberts said Díaz’s most recent outing was about as good as he has seen from him.
“That last outing was as good as we’ve seen him throw, and it’s hard to imagine throwing any better,” Roberts said. “He’s put himself in a position to be the closer.
“In October, I don’t pay too much attention to the long sample of a season in a lot of cases, because in October things happen quickly and you’ve got to be willing to read and react.”
Roberts also praised the way Díaz handled a difficult season.
“Character,” he said. “That’s the main thing. When things aren’t going the best and how players respond, that’s telling.
“The way he stayed the course, dealt with the injuries, went to OKC on a longer rehab to work things out and then took on whatever role we had for him says a lot about him.”
Lineup Changes Are on the Table
Roberts also acknowledged that the Dodgers could look different against Sale.
“I am considering it,” he said. “I think that’s a very fair question. I have to be mindful of it being two games, and then within those two games, what have I seen? Are we seeing good at-bats?”
He pointed to Will Smith as someone whose results have not matched the quality of his plate appearances.
“I think Will Smith is taking good at-bats, just missing some pitches, taking good swings, not chasing much,” Roberts said. “Versus other people maybe expanding, trying to do too much.
“Those are things that you’re trying to make bets on. Then you’re looking at tomorrow with Sale, the history, recency, how guys are prepared and will prepare for Sale. So yeah, I’m thinking through that, and there are possible changes.”
Roberts listed Kiké Hernández, Miguel Rojas and Max Muncy among the options he could work into the lineup.
“At the end of the day, our guys are our guys,” he said. “I can tweak a lineup. I can insert, take out a player or two, but we still have to go out there and play, execute and take good at-bats.”
Moving Ohtani Is Possible
Roberts said he would consider moving Ohtani further down in the order if he believes it helps the team.
“I would,” he said. “I think moving him from one to two, but going further than that, I’m open to it.
“If I do, I would obviously have the conversation with Shohei to explain why. At the end of the day, every conversation I’ve had with him is whatever is best for the team, he’s all in on. I know that undoubtedly.”
Roberts thinks some of Ohtani’s recent issues have come from trying to do too much.
“I think there’s a little bit of trying to do too much,” he said. “Everything orbits around Shohei in the sense of his talent, and the Braves are going to enter with caution. They’re going to continue to expand as long as we keep giving that to them.
“Until we show some discipline, they’re going to continue to use that playbook.”
He also said Ohtani may be pressing for power.
“Hitting homers, slugging is so much a part of his hallmark in the batter’s box,” Roberts said. “He’s very in tune with what’s being said, what he hasn’t done.
“But that base hit the other way yesterday, that’s production. Against a guy like Chris Sale, that gives you a chance. Trying to chase slug tomorrow night might not be the right plan given the starter.”
Roberts Still Believes in Pages
Andy Pages has also struggled, but Roberts said he plans to keep giving him chances.
“I’m going to continue to give Andy leash,” Roberts said. “I believe in him. I feel that for us to win the World Series this year, we’re going to need him to be an active part of our team.
“This is, for me, given how he has come into the postseason, too small of a sample. He has taken two walks. Tomorrow is not going to be the end-all, be-all because Sale is a tough matchup, but I still want to see good at-bats.”
Roberts believes the main issue is pressing.
“I think there’s trying to do too much,” he said. “When he came back, he was swinging the bat really well, had success, and now I think there’s a little bit of trying too much.”
Freeman Looks Healthier
One hitter Roberts feels especially good about is Freddie Freeman.
“I think he’s gotten into his legs a lot more,” Roberts said. “He’s moving balls in the hitting zone forward. He’s as healthy as he’s been in quite some time. I think the mechanics are sound.”
Roberts credited the five-day break with helping Freeman get his knee into better shape.
“The week off was really crucial for him,” he said. “Being able to manage that with the five days off got him back to health to be able to work through some things without having to perform in a game setting.”
Sale vs. Yamamoto
Roberts expects Sale to attack the Dodgers much the same way he did when Atlanta faced them in August.
“The fastball just sort of bullied us at the top of the zone,” Roberts said. “There was some chase down below, and with the lefties, throwing more two-seamers to keep us honest in and then expand away.”
Still, Roberts believes the Dodgers are in a better offensive place than they were then.
“I do think we are in a different spot,” he said. “The stakes are certainly higher. There is familiarity on both sides. I think we’ll see better at-bats.
“Chris is going to be tough regardless. We know that. We know we’re going to be in for a dogfight, but I just don’t see him bullying us like he did his last start.”
And Roberts feels good about the pitcher the Dodgers will send out against him.
“There should be a lot of talk about Chris Sale, but our guy’s pretty dang good,” Roberts said. “He’s been a very good pitcher in the postseason, so we feel very good about that.
“I think both pitchers are going to pitch well. It’s kind of who grinds out at-bats best.”

A lifelong baseball fan, Webb has been going to Dodger games since he moved to Los Angeles in 1987. His favorite memory was attending the insane Game 3 of the World Series in 2025 and hugging random Dodgers fans after Freddie’s walkoff homer. He has been writing for Dodgersbeat since 2020.

"It's not a season-ending thing, so that's something to be hopeful with," manager Dave Roberts said after the game. "But yeah, it's just a bu
item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES --Enrique Hernándezis probably headed to the injured list because of a strained left oblique only two days into his season debut for the Los Angeles Dodgers.
The 34-year-old utility man homered in his first at-bat Tuesday night, then doubled in his second before leaving a 15-6 win over the Colorado Rockies after his at-bat in the fourth inning.
"It's not a season-ending thing, so that's something to be hopeful with," manager Dave Roberts said after the game. "But yeah, it's just a bummer."
Hernández was off to a hot start after sitting out the first 53 games of the season while rehabbing from left elbow surgery during the offseason. He went 4-for-4 with two doubles and a homer in his first two games. Fans gave him a standing ovation when he was introduced Monday and cheered him loudly again Tuesday.
A chastened Hernández acknowledged he tweaked his oblique during batting practice Monday, shortly before telling reporters that he was pain-free.
"I was embarrassed because it didn't even happen in the game," he said. "I thought it was just weird tightness. Never done an oblique before, so I didn't really know what I was feeling. Compared to some of the things I've played through in the past, it was nothing."
He received treatment before Tuesday's game and believed he could start and bat ninth in the lineup.
"The homer swing felt awful. The next at-bat I went out there, I swung and missed on the first pitch and didn't feel great," Hernández said. "After that I went into survival mode."
Roberts talked to him in the dugout during the game, urging him to keep his head up.
"Honestly, at that point I was kind of not there, so I'm not necessarily sure everything that he said to me," Hernández said. "I feel pretty defeated right now. Hopefully, we get somewhat good news tomorrow."
Initially, he said he felt pain only when he was swinging.
"That's kind of why I thought I could play," Hernández said. "When I hit the double, it didn't just hurt to swing, it also hurt to run, so I knew that it was time to stop."
Teammate Mookie Betts sustained a right oblique strain in early April while running the bases. The 33-year-old shortstop missed 36 days before being activated on May 11.
"It sucks," Betts said. "We saw as soon as he came he brought life to us, but we'll just see how the rehab and whatnot goes. He'll be back."

With both games of this series having taken place in Los Angeles, both teams will now travel to Atlanta, where things will resume in Game 3 on Tuesday. And for the Dodgers, their highest-profile player could soon be moved in the lineup, according to manager Dave Roberts. The Los Angeles Dodgers Could Move Shohei O
item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers, who are attempting to win their third straight World Series title, were beaten by the Atlanta Braves in the second game of the National League Division Series.
With both games of this series having taken place in Los Angeles, both teams will now travel to Atlanta, where things will resume in Game 3 on Tuesday.
And for the Dodgers, their highest-profile player could soon be moved in the lineup, according to manager Dave Roberts.
The Los Angeles Dodgers Could Move Shohei Ohtani Down In The Lineup
Star Shohei Ohtani is 2-for-8 so far in the postseason, but he chased on over 50 percent of the pitches on which he swung, getting away from the kind of discipline he’s built his career on.
According to Dodgers skipper Dave Roberts, he’s open to moving Ohtani down in the lineup, and would have a conversation with him beforehand to explain the potential move.
“Going further than moving him from one to two, I’m open to it,” Roberts said. “If it’s something I do, I’d obviously have the conversation with Shohei to explain why. Every conversation I’ve had with him that’s whatever is best for the team, he’s all in on it.
“If you look at the AB’s there’s a lot of chase. It’s hard to square up, put good swings on balls out of zone. Sale is going to be tough, trying to get him back in the hitting zone.”
Additionally, Roberts said that Ohtani, who missed time this season, isn’t currently experiencing any health issues.
“I haven’t heard anything other than he feels fine. This time of year everyone doesn’t feel perfect. He’s doing the best he can.
“He’ll be in there Game 3. We just have to take good at-bats and expect the best.”
The Dodgers Were Beaten In Game 2
Following their Game 2 loss, Roberts said that he and his club have their work cut out for them.
“It’s a good team offensively,” he said. “They’re going to fight. (Michael) Harris is swinging a good bat. We knew it was going to be a battle. We knew those guys weren’t going to go down.
“We’re expecting Sale in Game 3, and we’ve got our work cut out. Now it’s a three-game series.”

item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers have faced two bullpen games to kick off their National League Division Series battle with the Atlanta Braves.
On Tuesday, things will get much more difficult.
The Dodgers are going up against 10-time All-Star and former Cy Young award winner Chris Sale. The left-hander is coming off a regular season in which he had a 2.16 ERA and 200 strikeouts over 162.2 innings. He then allowed three runs over 6.1 innings in his wild-card Game 1 start, and pitched 1.1 scoreless innings to close out Game 3.
The Dodgers know what they're up against with Sale, one of baseball's best pitchers.
"Chris is going to be tough," Roberts said. "We know we're going to be in for a dogfight."
The difficult lefty matchup also has manager Dave Roberts considering some lineup changes.
“I think so," Roberts said. "I am considering it. I think that’s a very fair question. I think that I have to be mindful of — it’s two games, and then with the two games, what have I seen?”
Roberts mentioned Enrique Hernandez and Miguel Rojas as potential options to be in the lineup. The only Dodgers with any semblance of success against Sale in their careers are Mookie Betts (7-for-18) and Freddie Freeman (5-for-16).
The Dodgers have been especially reliant on the home run this series, with all seven of their runs coming via the long ball.
In Sunday's Game 2, they went 0-for-8 with runners in scoring position.
Sale faced the Dodgers on Aug. 27, firing a complete-game shutout with 11 strikeouts and just five hits allowed.
Dave Roberts Considering Moving Shohei Ohtani Down in the Lineup
The Dodgers have plenty of players struggling in the lineup, including Will Smith (0-for-8), Andy Pages (0-for-7) and Tommy Edman (0-for-5).
At the top of the lineup, however, is Shohei Ohtani, who is 2-for-8 with two singles and two strikeouts. He's looked far from his usual self.
"I think there's, like we've talked about, he's not 100%," Roberts said on Monday. "But at the end of the day, he can still do a better job of staying in the strike zone. ... I think that's something that — it's hard to have success when you're out of the zone. ... And Shohei understands, any hitter understands that. So I think that's the thing is — then the question is how do we get him into it? I think there's a little bit of trying to do too much. I think that's a piece."
Roberts said he's open to moving Ohtani down in the lineup, especially with the tough left-hander on the mound.
However, he wouldn't commit to anything on Monday.
"Going further than [No. 2]? I'm open to it," Roberts said. "It's something that, if I do, I would obviously have the conversation with Shohei to explain why. And at the end of the day, every conversation I've had with him is, whatever is best for the team, he's all in on.”
For what it's worth, Ohtani is 3-for-15 against Sale in his career with five strikeouts.
"At the end of the day, our guys are our guys," Roberts said. "And, yeah, I can tweak a lineup. I can kind of insert, take out a player or two. But at the end of the day we still have got to go out there and play and execute and take good at-bats."

ATLANTA — As the Dodgers mull potential lineup changes for Game 3 of the National League Division Series, manager Dave Roberts said he is “open” to moving Shohei Ohtani lower in the batting order.
In his three seasons with the Dodgers, Ohtani has batted first or second in every game he has started. However, as he has admitted he is trying to “manage” in the aftermath of knee and arm injuries, and as Roberts has acknowledged Ohtani is “not 100%,” the lack of success could compel the manager to replace him at the top of the lineup with a more productive hitter at some point.
“I would,” Roberts said Monday. “I would. I think it’s something that, you know, I think moving him from 1 to 2 — but going further than that? I’m open to it.
“And it’s something that if I do, I would obviously have the conversation with Shohei to explain why. And at the end of the day every conversation I’ve had with him is whatever’s best for the team, he’s all-in on. So I know that undoubtedly.”
It would be strange for the Dodgers to bench Shohei Ohtani, but it’s clear that pretending he’s healthy enough to provide meaningful at-bats isn’t helping.
The Dodgers are batting .215 through the first two games of the NLDS, with the Atlanta Braves scheduled to pitch left-handed ace Chris Sale in Game 3 on Tuesday. If the Dodgers lose, they would need to win back-to-back elimination games to advance beyond this series.
Roberts said the lineup changes he would consider include starting Kiké Hernández and Miguel Rojas, both of whom hit well against left-handers. That could mean infielders Max Muncy (0 for 7 against Sale, with five strikeouts) and Tommy Edman (0 for 11 against Sale) might not start.
Center fielder Andy Pages, who batted so poorly last October he was benched for the final three games of the World Series, is hitless in seven at-bats in this series, with four strikeouts.
“I’m gonna continue to give Andy leash,” Roberts said. “I believe in him. I feel that for us to win the World Series this year, we’re gonna need him to be an active part of our team.
Roberts said he did not envision benching catcher Will Smith, who is 0 for 8 in the series. The Dodgers’ backup catcher, Hunter Feduccia, is a career .205 hitter with no postseason experience.
But, even with the Dodgers’ star-studded lineup, the spotlight shines brightest on Ohtani.
Ohtani has not homered since Aug. 18. He hit .157 between then and the end of the regular season, striking out in 41% of his at-bats. In this series, he has two hits and two strikeouts in eight at-bats, and his inability to refrain from swinging at pitches outside the strike zone has become a glaring weakness.
“He’s not 100%,” Roberts said. “But, at the end of the day, he can still do a better job of staying in the strike zone.”
Ohtani hasn’t given the Braves a reason to challenge him within the strike zone.
“Everything orbits around Shohei, in the sense of his talent,” Roberts said. “And the Braves are going to enter with caution. And, so, knowing that, they’re going to continue to expand as long as we keep giving that to them. So until we show some discipline, they’re going to continue to kind of use that playbook.”

item.title: [New York Post] Dodgers consider NLDS Game 3 lineup changes –– with Shohei Ohtani, Kiké Hernández included
item.dc:creator: Jack Harris
item.description: ATLANTA –– The Dodgers don’t want to overreact to a two-game sample size. But, with elimination all of a sudden just two games away, they don’t want to wait too long to make changes either. That’s what dynamic manager Dave Roberts was grappling with on Monday, as the Dodgers gathered at Truist Park in Atlanta ahead of Game 3 of their National League Division Series against the Braves. A daunting challenge awaits on Tuesday night, when the club will face Braves ace Chris Sale for the first time s
item.content:encoded:
ATLANTA –– The Dodgers don’t want to overreact to a two-game sample size.
But, with elimination all of a sudden just two games away, they don’t want to wait too long to make changes either.
That’s what dynamic manager Dave Roberts was grappling with on Monday, as the Dodgers gathered at Truist Park in Atlanta ahead of Game 3 of their National League Division Series against the Braves.
A daunting challenge awaits on Tuesday night, when the club will face Braves ace Chris Sale for the first time since he threw a complete-game shutout against them in August.
Thus, even though the team’s quest for a World Series three-peat just began, potential lineup changes were already under consideration.
And even superstar Shohei Ohtani might not be immune.
“I am considering [changes],” Roberts said. “I think that’s a very fair question.”
That didn’t mean Roberts was ready to commit to any significant alterations ahead of a pivotal Game 3, with the best-of-five series tied one game apiece.
He noted the danger of reading too far into small playoff sample sizes this early in the postseason.
Still, he said there were things he was “thinking through” and “possibly kind of some changes” that could be enacted on Tuesday.
One possibility: Inserting Miguel Rojas and/or Kiké Hernández into lineup, perhaps in place of Max Muncy and/or Tommy Edman, to give the Dodgers extra right-handed bats against a dominant left-hander in Sale.
Another, more notable potential option: Moving Ohtani even further down the order from his current No. 2 spot, after he went just 2-for-8 in the first two games of the NLDS while continuing to battle right arm and left knee injuries.
“[We already moved] him from 1 to 2 –– but going further than that? I’m open to it,” Roberts said. “It’s something that, if I do, I would obviously have the conversation with Shohei to explain why.”
The explanation, of course, wouldn’t be too complicated.
In Ohtani’s currently diminished physical state, he has simply not been the same presence at the top of the order that the Dodgers have grown accustomed to from the four-time MVP.
“Like we’ve talked about, he’s not 100%,” Roberts said.
But also, “I think there’s a little bit of [him also] trying to do too much,” Roberts added. “I think that’s a piece.”
Indeed, Ohtani has suffered from a futile combination so far in the playoffs, failing to either punish pitches over the plate or keep from chasing out of the strike zone.
“It’s hard to have success when you’re out of the zone,” Roberts said. “So I think that’s the thing, then the question is: How do we get him [attacking pitches back] into it?”
A change of mindset could help, especially against a premium pitcher like Sale (who has held Ohtani to a 3-for-15 mark with five strikeouts and only one double in their career head-to-head matchups).
“Trying to chase slug tomorrow night might not be the right plan, given the starter,” Roberts said.
Instead, Roberts pointed to the opposite-field single Ohtani slapped past a shift for his lone hit in Sunday’s Game 2 loss.
“That at-bat yesterday, the block base hit the other way, that’s something that is production,” Roberts said. “I think that’s something where, against a guy like Chris Sale, it gives you a chance.”
The Dodgers, of course, would love to get more pop from Ohtani, who led the team with eight home runs during last year’s World Series trek. Roberts also knows the slugger “feels the responsibility” to provide such power, which might be contributing to his lack of plate discipline.
Thus, for now, taking the pressure off Ohtani’s shoulders by potentially hitting him lower in the lineup might also prove to be prudent.
“At the end of the day, every conversation I’ve had with him is whatever’s best for the team,” Roberts said. “And he’s all in on [that]. I know that undoubtedly.”
While Roberts will contemplate other changes beyond Ohtani’s spot in the order, there were a few ideas he outright struck down Monday night.
The big one: Removing Andy Pages from the batting order despite his 0-for-7 start in the playoffs –– one that has felt reminiscent of his historic struggles last October, and been further marred by a consequential ABS challenge he missed in Game 1.
While Roberts said he feels Pages has been “trying to do too much” –– downplaying any lingering effects from the fractured hand that sidelined the center fielder for most of September –– he also said he wanted to give the 25-year-old slugger more leash.
“I believe in him,” Roberts said. “And I feel that for us to win the World Series this year, we’re gonna need him to be an active part of our team.”
That was all part of the balance Roberts was trying to strike with his team’s season potentially hanging in the balance. It might still feel early for drastic changes. But one more loss, and the club’s three-peat bid will be on the brink.
“Our guys are our guys,” Roberts said. “Yeah, I can tweak a lineup. I can kind of insert, take out a player or two. But at the end of the day, we still have got to go out there and play and execute and take good at-bats.”

item.title: [ABC7 Los Angeles] Dodgers lose 7th straight on D-backs' walk-off vs. Edwin Diaz
item.dc:creator: Follow ABC
item.description: PHOENIX -- The two-time defending World Series champions are in a rare funk. The Los Angeles Dodgers lost their season-high seventh game in a row in a stunning collapse Friday night after the Arizona Diamondbacks rallied for a 4-3 win when rookie Ryan Waldschmidt hit a two-run, walk-off homer against closer Edwin Diaz. item.content:encoded:
PHOENIX -- The two-time defending World Series champions are in a rare funk.
The Los Angeles Dodgers lost their season-high seventh game in a row in a stunning collapse Friday night after the Arizona Diamondbacks rallied for a 4-3 win when rookie Ryan Waldschmidt hit a two-run, walk-off homer against closer Edwin Diaz.
"A loss is a loss, but to get walked off never feels good," Dodgers manager Dave Roberts said. "We didn't play a clean game, a great game, on either side of the baseball, but we did enough to put ourselves in position to win a game.
"Unfortunately, we couldn't finish it."
It was another rough outing for Diaz, who has an 11.00 ERA over 11 outings this season. The 32-year-old is a three-time All-Star, but he hasn't helped the Dodgers much after signing a three-year, $69 million deal during the offseason.
Waldschmidt connected on Diaz's hanging slider, hitting it into the left-center field seats for his second career homer and first big league walk-off.
"It's the slider," Diaz said. "The fastball was great today, but I missed the slider right in the middle. I think I was trying to be perfect with the pitch, and I'm missing right in the middle. I've got to be better. I'm a big league pitcher, so I've got to make pitches."
The Dodgers were swept by the Boston Red Sox and Chicago Cubs coming into Friday night's game. They still have a comfortable lead in the National League West -- 7 games in front of the Diamondbacks -- despite a 10-16 record since July 5.
Roberts acknowledged that Diaz has been struggling since his return from the injured list on July 29, but the manager wasn't necessarily ready to try a new closer. His reasoning was simple: There's no clear-cut alternative.
"Honestly, you've got to look at the options," Roberts said. "The way some of these guys are throwing, they're not throwing great either."
The Dodgers still look like a formidable team, particularly after adding ace left-hander Tarik Skubal in a trade-deadline deal with the Detroit Tigers last week. Two-time Cy Young Award winner Blake Snell is slated to return Tuesday after missing most of the season because of injuries.
And the lineup still has plenty of star power with Shohei Ohtani, Freddie Freeman, Mookie Betts and Kyle Tucker.
Roberts said before Friday's game that the remedy for the recent troubles was simple.
"We've just got to play better," Roberts said. "I don't think the standings -- I mean they're important, they matter -- but I just feel like with the talent we have, we've just got to play good baseball and it'll take care of itself. It always does."br/]

item.title: [Sports Illustrated] Why Dodgers Top Prospect Josue De Paula Made NLDS Roster Over Dalton Rushing
item.dc:creator: J P Hoornstra; Unknown
item.description: Dalton Rushing's 2026 season has consisted of a few wildly different phases. After Phase 1 — an eight-game stretch ending April 20 — the Los Angeles Dodgers' backup catcher had a .444 batting average, and an almost incomprehensible seven home runs in 28 plate appearances. It was no surprise that Rushing couldn't maintain that torrid pace. What's surprising is what happened next — and how it resulted in his being left off the Dodgers' roster for the National League Division Series (and likely bey
item.content:encoded:
Dalton Rushing's 2026 season has consisted of a few wildly different phases. After Phase 1 — an eight-game stretch ending April 20 — the Los Angeles Dodgers' backup catcher had a .444 batting average, and an almost incomprehensible seven home runs in 28 plate appearances.
It was no surprise that Rushing couldn't maintain that torrid pace. What's surprising is what happened next — and how it resulted in his being left off the Dodgers' roster for the National League Division Series (and likely beyond).
Rookie Josue De Paula, not Rushing, is filling the role of manager Dave Roberts' left-handed pinch hitter off the bench against the Atlanta Braves. De Paula, 21, spent the season at Double-A Tulsa prior to his first big-league promotion in September. In 11 games with the Dodgers, he slashed .323/.500/.581.
"I think what we saw is a really good idea of the strike zone, quality of contact," Roberts said of De Paula. "I think that he's really unflappable, good heartbeat. I think that translates into the postseason."
Rushing was diagnosed with a partially torn UCL in his right (throwing) elbow in August. He tried to play through the injury, but catching was ultimately outside the realm of possibilities.
The Dodgers acquired two catchers, Hunter Feduccia and Ben Rortvedt, at the Aug. 3 trade deadline, and Feduccia is now the backup to Will Smith.
Rushing was able to avoid (or at least delay) surgery; that allowed him to hit even though he couldn't catch. However, the injury limited Rushing to only eight plate appearances after Aug. 1. His last hit was on July 30.
"Having eight at-bats in two months just put him behind the eight ball," Roberts said of Rushing. "The ability not to catch was something that also kind of worked against him. Great conversation with Dalton, great teammate, but I think those are the reasons for De Paula."
Overall, Rushing slashed .246/.328/.460. He hit only five home runs in 72 games after his early-season tear.
Even before the elbow injury, it was clear the league had adjusted to Rushing as a hitter (to say nothing of his sometimes questionable behavior between pitches).
The league hasn't adjusted to De Paula yet. How much that will matter in the postseason remains to be seen, but the Dodgers are impressed by what they've seen so far.
"The way he came up, obviously we think incredibly highly of him," president of baseball operations Andrew Friedman said, "and to see the calmness in his at-bats, the ability to look over baseball, the impact just felt like, as a bullet off the bench in big situations, just being able to trust the pulse and the ability."

A veteran of 20 years of sports coverage for daily newspapers in California, J.P. covered MLB, the Los Angeles Dodgers, and the Los Angeles Angels (occasionally of Anaheim) from 2012-23 for the Southern California News Group. He swung at 11 pitches while facing just 19, and chased on 53% of those swings. He didn’t have the same struggles in Game 1, chasing at a rate of just 17%, but his perform
item.content:encoded:
Los Angeles Dodgers manager Dave Roberts revealed he’s willing to move Shohei Ohtani further down the lineup as his struggles in the box persist.
Ohtani is 2-for-8 this postseason, but that isn’t the worrying part. During the second game of the NLDS, Ohtani struggled to find the plate discipline he’s had throughout his career. He swung at 11 pitches while facing just 19, and chased on 53% of those swings.
He didn’t have the same struggles in Game 1, chasing at a rate of just 17%, but his performance in Game 2 was enough to prompt some questions regarding his fitness. The Dodgers have already moved Ohtani down in the order following his return from injury, running him out at the No. 2 spot several times since he came back, and Roberts revealed he’s open to dropping him further in the lineup.
“Going further than moving him from one to two, I’m open to it,” Roberts said. “If it’s something I do, I’d obviously have the conversation with Shohei to explain why. Every conversation I’ve had with him that’s whatever is best for the team, he’s all in on it.
Ohtani will remain in the lineup for the Dodgers’ Game 3 matchup against the Atlanta Braves regardless of his spot in the lineup, but faces a big challenge in the form of Chris Sale.
Is Chris Sale a Good Matchup for Shohei Ohtani?
The Dodgers are showing plenty of confidence in Ohtani by starting him on Tuesday, as Sale is a difficult matchup for the reigning MVP—especially given his recent struggles.
Sale ranked in the Top 5% of MLB With a 36.5% chase rate this season, strikes out batters at an extremely high clip and also throws from the left side, making at-bats for Ohtani inherently more difficult.
Ohtani will have to perform much better than he has since his return from injury in order to keep up with Sale, who performed incredibly against the Dodgers across two starts in the regular season, and the Dodgers need him to do so if they’re to avoid falling behind in the series.
The third game of the NLDS begins Tuesday at 3:00 p.m. PT.

item.title: [Dodgers Nation] Andy Pages' October Struggles Resurfacing at Worst Time
item.dc:creator: Aaron Coloma
item.description: Los Angeles Dodgers outfielder Andy Pages struggled in the 2025 postseason, making headlines for his poor performance, and his 2026 postseason so far hasn’t unfolded much differently. The outfielder is ordinarily a key producer for the Dodgers, and had a fantastic season in 2025 prior to his October breakdown. He hit 27 homers last year, good for second on the team behind Shohei Ohtani, and drove in 86 runs with a .774 OPS. Pages played in 16 games last postseason, stepping up to the plate 55 ti
item.content:encoded:
Los Angeles Dodgers outfielder Andy Pages struggled in the 2025 postseason, making headlines for his poor performance, and his 2026 postseason so far hasn’t unfolded much differently.
The outfielder is ordinarily a key producer for the Dodgers, and had a fantastic season in 2025 prior to his October breakdown. He hit 27 homers last year, good for second on the team behind Shohei Ohtani, and drove in 86 runs with a .774 OPS.
Pages played in 16 games last postseason, stepping up to the plate 55 times, and logged just four hits throughout the entirety of the postseason for a .078/.113/.098 slash line and a .211 OPS.
Now, through two games, his struggles are resurfacing.
What Has Andy Pages Done in the Playoffs This Year?
Through his two postseason games so far, Pages is hitless with one walk in eight plate appearances with four strikeouts. The strikeouts are the most worrying part of Pages’ performances so far this postseason, as he doesn’t ordinarily go down on strikes this often.
On the year, Pages’ strikeout rate sat at 19.7%, which is above league average and better than seasons past. Additionally, his whiff rate sits at 22.1%, also above league average. In his small sample size this postseason, though, both numbers are well above his yearly average with a 50% strikeout rate and a whiff rate of 36.4%.
Three of his four strikeouts came during the first game of the series, swinging and missing to record the last strike twice while watching strike three fly over the plate before wasting a challenge in the other. After Game 1, manager Dave Roberts revealed the Dodgers took away Pages’ green light to challenge.
“We talked a lot this year about Andy’s success rate or lack thereof, and I didn’t revisit it before Game 1, so that’s my fault,” Roberts said to the media, including Dodgers Nation, ahead of Game 2 on Sunday. “I did have a conversation today, so we’ve managed that one going forward.”
He also lined out in the first game of the series, hitting a ball 96.5 mph to center with a favorable launch angle—a promising sight given his struggles.
Pages yielded better results in the second game of the series, though not by much. He struck out for the fourth time this postseason in the second inning, but followed that up with a walk. In his final two at-bats of the game, he grounded out to either side of the middle infield.
The first-time All-Star ordinarily had solid quality of contact over the course of the season, and will hope to find his regular season form as the Dodgers make their three-peat push.
What Options Do the Dodgers Have to Replace Pages if His Struggles Continue?
The Dodgers aren’t likely to move away from Pages during this postseason, but if worst comes to worst, they have options to put in center over him. Tommy Edman is fully healthy and more than capable of manning the role, as is Hyeseong Kim.
Josue De Paula is also with the team at the moment, and could push a corner outfielder into center field if the Dodgers want to give him a game.
The Dodgers will hope they won’t have to do that, though, as Pages is a key player for them both on offense and defense. His next opportunity to break out of his small slump comes in Game 3 of the NLDS on Tuesday against Chris Sale.

item.title: [Dodgers Nation] Edwin Diaz Looking Like Postseason Bullpen X-Factor
item.dc:creator: Aaron Coloma

Diaz only needed 12 pitches to navigate his inning, striking out the first two batters on seven pitches before forcing a flyout from All-Star Drake Baldwin. In six innings since returning from the injured list in September, Diaz has only allowed one hit and walk while striking out 11 batters. The Dodgers didn’t win Sunday’s game in
item.content:encoded:
Los Angeles Dodgers reliever Edwin Diaz came into Game 2 of the NLDS and continued his strong run of form, hurling a scoreless sixth inning with his team down a run.
Diaz only needed 12 pitches to navigate his inning, striking out the first two batters on seven pitches before forcing a flyout from All-Star Drake Baldwin. In six innings since returning from the injured list in September, Diaz has only allowed one hit and walk while striking out 11 batters.
The Dodgers didn’t win Sunday’s game in the end, but Diaz’s performance provided plenty of encouragement.
“Edwin was great,” manager Dave Roberts said. “If you look at tonight and try to find some silver linings, that was a silver lining and certainly a positive.”
What Kept Edwin Diaz on the Injured List This Year?
Diaz looked to be as advertised for the Dodgers through the first couple of weeks of the season, but injuries impacted his production and made 2026 a season to forget. He held opponents to just one run through his first five appearances as a Dodger, but allowed three in consecutive appearances immediately afterwards before landing on the injured list with loose bodies in his elbow.
He came back from his elbow injury in July, but his struggles stuck with him over the following couple of weeks, as he allowed 11 runs across 7.2 innings pitched.
The right-hander landed back on the injured list Aug. 18 with neck inflammation, and remaind there for about a month. Since coming back, Diaz seems to have everything under control.
“It felt amazing,” Díaz said of his Game 2 outing. “That’s why I came here — to help this team win and pitch in big spots. … I want to keep getting the ball and doing my job.”
Will Edwin Diaz Take Over as the Dodgers’ Closer?
The Dodgers’ closer situation is uncertain at the moment, especially following Tanner Scott’s rough outing in Game 1 of the NLDS.
LA is clearly being cautious with Diaz’s situation given his results in the regular season, but if he continues to produce at a high level he could very well find himself in the mix to take over high-leverage situations in the late innings.
His next opportunity to make a difference for the Dodgers comes in Game 3 of the NLDS on Tuesday at 3:00 p.m. PT.

item.title: [Dodgers Nation] Shohei Ohtani’s Alarming NLDS Trend Raises Dodgers Concerns
item.dc:creator: Nelson Espinal
item.description: Los Angeles Dodgers superstar Shohei Ohtani has gotten off to a modest start in the postseason, though questions remain about his health and whether he will be a key figure. Ohtani is still dealing with injuries to his left knee and right arm, both of which he admits will require management, but he has played both NLDS games thus far. How Ohtani has played in the first 2 NLDS games In Game 2, Ohtani went 1-for-4 with an opposite-field single. However, he also had seven whiffs and a called strike
item.content:encoded:
Los Angeles Dodgers superstar Shohei Ohtani has gotten off to a modest start in the postseason, though questions remain about his health and whether he will be a key figure.
Ohtani is still dealing with injuries to his left knee and right arm, both of which he admits will require management, but he has played both NLDS games thus far.
How Ohtani has played in the first 2 NLDS games
In Game 2, Ohtani went 1-for-4 with an opposite-field single. However, he also had seven whiffs and a called strike, with 11 swings on 19 pitches, and just one hard hit, per Baseball Savant.
He chased on 53% of pitches.
Game 1 was much better: 1-for-4 with a single, but with two hard hits, just two whiffs, and nine swings on 15 pitches. His chase rate was better, at 17%.
Overall, 2-for-8 is solid for most players, but someone like Ohtani is known for consistent hard contact and getting on base like crazy; it is below his typical standard.
When he returned from the injured list, he looked good in his first game, but a few games later, he showed the chase-and-whiff tendencies.
The main concern around Shohei Ohtani
Sportsnet LA broadcaster Stephen Nelson noted that Ohtani’s whiff is very abnormal.
“Shohei Ohtani hasn’t looked or felt like Shohei Ohtani for a minute. Had a few flashes in the SD series late in the regular season. But he’s been chasing everything in sight, with the NL’s 2nd-worst whiff rate post-ASG. Suboptimal,” Nelson wrote on X.
Manager Dave Roberts echoed that after Game 2, noting the lack of consistent hard contact comes from swing decisions.
“If you look at the AB’s there’s a lot of chase. It’s hard to square up, put good swings on balls out of zone. Sale is going to be tough, trying to get him back in the hitting zone,” Roberts told the media, including Dodgers Nation.
According to Roberts, Ohtani will be in the lineup for Game 3, against Chris Sale with the series tied 1-1, in a big vote of confidence.
In the postseason, the Dodgers will ride Ohtani until the wheels fall off; his hitting hasn’t been bad, and unless the results get alarming, he will have the chance to make adjustments and get back to slugging on a regular basis.

item.title: [Sports Illustrated] Dodgers Not Ruling Out Surprise Return From Injured Pitcher; Here's What It Could Mean
item.dc:creator: J P Hoornstra; Unknown
item.description: Los Angeles Dodgers manager Dave Roberts ruled pitcher Blake Treinen out for the postseason after the right-hander suffered a shoulder injury warming up for a relief appearance in San Francisco. Now, it sounds as if Roberts spoke prematurely. Dodgers president of baseball operations Andrew Friedman said Saturday that Treinen's status for the postseason is "not decided firmly." "It was clear for this round," Friedman said, "but we'll keep monitoring it as we go." Friedman described the injury as
item.content:encoded:
Los Angeles Dodgers manager Dave Roberts ruled pitcher Blake Treinen out for the postseason after the right-hander suffered a shoulder injury warming up for a relief appearance in San Francisco.
Now, it sounds as if Roberts spoke prematurely.
Dodgers president of baseball operations Andrew Friedman said Saturday that Treinen's status for the postseason is "not decided firmly."
"It was clear for this round," Friedman said, "but we'll keep monitoring it as we go."
Friedman described the injury as "soreness" — a vague if much less ominous problem than the one Roberts suggested when Treinen was placed on the injured list after the Dodgers' Sept. 26 game against the Giants.
“I don't know if it was a complete blowout, but really unfortunate,” Roberts said at the time.
In 12 MLB seasons — the last six with the Dodgers — Treinen is 49-42 with a 2.94 ERA and 83 saves. Although he served as the Dodgers' closer only occasionally, he was a reliable source of strikeouts, low ERAs and some big postseason moments as the Dodgers captured three World Series championships this decade.
In 2024, Treinen saved three postseason games in three opportunities, allowing only three runs across nine October appearances. He was the winning pitcher in Game 5 of the 2024 World Series, when he threw 2.1 scoreless relief innings against the New York Yankees.
If the Dodgers need Treinen this month, it won't merely mean that he is healthy. It will mean somebody else — likely a couple somebodies — are not.
The Dodgers have enough quality and capable bullpen arms that they did not roster two pitchers who figured to be October mainstays (left-handers Justin Wrobleski and Jack Dreyer) in the National League Division Series. That decision was made in large part due to the Dodgers' opponent.
For Treinen to appear in a game this month, he'd have to prove more worthy of a roster spot than Tanner Scott, Alex Vesia, Brock Stewart, Roki Sasaki, Evan Phillips, Edgardo Henriquez, Edwin Diaz and Kris Bubic — plus Wrobleski and Dreyer.
Right-handers Bobby Miller and Emmet Sheehan have lockers and figure to be ready if called upon, too. Right-hander Will Klein finished the season on the injured list, like Treinen, but his throwing progression has put him in position to rejoin the roster if needed.
Treinen's possible availability is likely a mere footnote to the Dodgers' 2026 postseason run. Considering it sounded impossible a week ago, it's at least worth noting.

item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES, CA — Edwin Díaz gave the Dodgers one of their best moments in an otherwise frustrating Game 2 loss. The right-hander worked a clean sixth inning, struck out two and showed the kind of power stuff the Dodgers hoped to see when they added him.
Díaz said afterward that the outing felt like a payoff for the work he has put in over the past couple of weeks. He also made it clear he is ready for whatever role Dave Roberts gives him.
“I Was Throwing Strikes”
“I think it was great,” Díaz said. “I was throwing strikes. I was getting strike one against the hitters. I think the shape of the slider was great. The fastball movement was really good.
“I was just trying to do my job, keep the game close and give our team a chance to win.”
Díaz said the clean inning came after a lot of work on his mechanics.
“I’ve been putting a lot of work together the last maybe two weeks, week and a half, and today it played out,” he said. “I think today was really good.
“I just have to keep doing my job, keep helping this team win. When they give me the ball, I just want to keep the game on the line and see if we can win games.”
Ready for the Big Spots
Díaz has spent plenty of his career pitching in high-leverage spots, and he said getting that chance in October with the Dodgers was exactly what he wanted.
“It feels amazing,” he said. “That’s why I came here, to help this team win. I’m pitching in big spots, so I just want to keep getting the ball and doing my job.”
Asked whether he would be ready to pitch the ninth inning if Roberts called on him, Díaz kept it simple.
“I’m always ready,” he said. “I’ve been throwing the ball really good. In any situation they give me the ball, I’m just going to try to do my job.”
The Stuff Was There
Díaz touched 100 mph several times and said the postseason setting added a little extra energy.
“I feel really good,” he said. “My arm feels really good. My body feels great. It’s the playoffs, baby. Everything changes.
“Personally, I feel great. I was throwing strikes. I was letting the ball rip, and I was doing my job.”
He also believes his recent work has him trending back toward the form he showed last season.
“I think the last week I’ve been pitching really good,” Díaz said. “Last year I pitched great all season long. This season didn’t start the way everyone wanted, but I finished the regular season strong. I’m going to keep doing it right now (in the postseason).”

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Blake Snell’s rocky outing leads to de facto bullpen game
item.dc:creator: Jacob Macofsky
item.description: The Dodgers needed one win to send the Atlanta Braves to the brink of elimination on Sunday. Instead, the Braves lineup forced an early exit from Blake Snell and scored two defining runs against the bullpen in a 3-2 win over the Dodgers, forcing the series back to Atlanta for Games 3 and 4. It wasn't the first rocky outing for Snell against Atlanta this season, as he only managed to toss three innings while allowing four runs in his 2026 debut back on May 8 before being placed on the injured lis
item.content:encoded:
The Dodgers needed one win to send the Atlanta Braves to the brink of elimination on Sunday. Instead, the Braves lineup forced an early exit from Blake Snell and scored two defining runs against the bullpen in a 3-2 win over the Dodgers, forcing the series back to Atlanta for Games 3 and 4.
It wasn't the first rocky outing for Snell against Atlanta this season, as he only managed to toss three innings while allowing four runs in his 2026 debut back on May 8 before being placed on the injured list. The southpaw had looked like his usual dominant stretch once he returned in August, but the ultimate test was to see how he would perform against the lone team that roughed him up.
Snell made quick work of Drake Baldwin for the first out, but after allowing a one-out single to Ronald Acuña Jr., he walked both Matt Olson and Ozzie Albies to load the bases. Snell managed to get Michael Harris II to fly out in foul territory for a crucial second out, but Mauricio Dubón tacked on the game's first run with an infield single. Snell faced seven hitters in the first inning, needing 27 pitches to give the Dodgers a chance to hit.
Snell's biggest flaw on Sunday was his inability to get quick innings, unlike Tarik Skubal on Saturday. Snell needed four pitches to get two quick outs in the second inning, but allowed a six-pitch walk to Baldwin and needed another eight to strike out Acuña. Snell allowed another two-out baserunner in the third inning, this time a single from Harris, needing 19 pitches after tossing 18 the inning prior.
Snell's hopes at a clean inning were dashed in the fourth inning, as he walked a pair of hitters and tossed 26 pitches before the plug was pulled on his night. The Dodgers got him off the hook in the bottom of the fourth inning with a Freddie Freeman home run, but the Dodgers employed six relievers out of the bullpen over their final 5 1/3 innings on the mound.
Snell had a postseason to remember last year, as his defining moment came in Game 1 of the NLCS against the Milwaukee Brewers, facing the minimum over eight shutout innings. Sunday's outing was the first time he failed to log four innings in a postseason start since he began the 2022 Wild Card series against the New York Mets back when he was a San Diego Padre. Out of the 90 pitches he tossed against Atlanta, 47 of them went for strikes.
Snell's final start of the regular season was limited to just one inning after he dealt with left groin inflammation. Dave Roberts was quick to deny any concern over Snell's groin issue, noting that he was battling himself on the mound.
"No, it wasn't that. He was fighting himself in his delivery all game. Today, I just think the fastball was really good, the changeup was good at times, but I think, in total, didn't have fastball command, didn't have slider command, and the changeup wasn't there. He was pulling it. I think overall it wasn't the groin, and he wasn't sharp tonight."
Roberts felt optimistic about his chances of Snell on the mound while Atlanta went with their own bullpen game, beginning with left-hander Ray Kerr. The pieces just couldn't fall into place on Sunday.
"Felt great. Anytime I feel I have Blake Snell lined up against any pitcher felt good. Going to getting Kerr out of the game and then getting [Grant] Holmes out of the game, I felt really good where we were at. I really did. We just couldn't execute as the game progressed."
Now the Dodgers will face the only pitcher to shut them out in the regular season, left-hander Chris Sale, in a crucial Game 3 at Truist Park on Tuesday. Yoshinobu Yamamoto will take the mound for the first time in the playoffs since his Herculean performance in Game 7 of the 2025 World Series.

item.content:encoded:
Dodgers hitters in the 2026 regular season rated as fine or even good in most measures of the ABS challenge system. They were 10th in overturns vs. expected (8.4), tied for eighth in success rate (51%) and tied for 13th in runs vs. expected (0.1). Those numbers came as the club used the 16th-most batter challenges in MLB (159).
Andy Pages’ challenge in Game 1 of the NLDS against the Braves, however, was not so good. With two outs and nobody on base in the second inning, Pages tapped his helmet after a 2-2 pitch that was deemed to have caught the strike zone.
Indeed, the pitch was a strike, measured at 2.6 inches above the bottom edge of the zone -- not particularly close. Pages and the Dodgers lost that challenge for the rest of the game.
Fortunately for Los Angeles, it didn’t prove costly in a 5-3 opening win. But manager Dave Roberts apparently doesn’t want a similar situation happening again this postseason, as he said before Sunday’s Braves win in Game 2 that he told Pages not to challenge anymore.
“We talked about obviously a lot this year with Andy's success rate or lack thereof. I didn't revisit it before Game 1 yesterday, so that's my fault,” Roberts said. “I did have a conversation today. So, yeah, we've managed that one going forward.”
This isn’t a new phenomenon for Pages, who ranked among MLB’s worst regular-season challengers. Among 182 batters with at least 10 challenges, Pages was 142nd in overturns vs. expected (-3.0) and 169th in runs vs. expected (-1.3). He was also using challenges frequently despite the lack of success, with his 25 total challenges ranking 33rd-most among hitters.
Roberts addressed his team, including Pages, regarding ABS usage after the Dodgers went on a seven-game losing streak in August. Notably, Pages did not challenge again in the regular season after an Aug. 12 miss in the first inning against the Royals.
“I think the team strategy, it's different,” Roberts said Sunday. “I think some guys have a better propensity, a better success rate understanding leverage, understanding their ability to know the strike zone. Because I trust Mookie on the ball away, but he was playing the long game, which I respect. So it's not a one-size-fits-all situation.”
Roberts and the Dodgers clearly don’t want to take any chances.

item.title: [DodgersBeat] Dave Roberts after Game 2 Loss: Dodgers Need to Sieze Chances
item.dc:creator: Steve Webb
item.description: LOS ANGELES, CA — Dave Roberts saw Game 2 as a reminder of how tough this series was always going to be. Atlanta pieced together a bullpen game, got key outs when the Dodgers had traffic on the bases and evened the NLDS before heading home. item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES, CA — Dave Roberts saw Game 2 as a reminder of how tough this series was always going to be. Atlanta pieced together a bullpen game, got key outs when the Dodgers had traffic on the bases and evened the NLDS before heading home.
Roberts also made it clear that Blake Snell’s rough command was not tied to his recent groin issue. Snell simply fought his delivery, while the Dodgers kept missing chances to change the game.
Snell Was Fighting His Delivery
“He just was fighting himself with his delivery all game,” Roberts said. “I think the fastball was really good. The changeup was good at times, but in total he didn’t have fastball command, didn’t have slider command, and the changeup wasn’t there. He was pulling it.
“Overall, it wasn’t the groin. He just wasn’t sharp tonight.”
Roberts said there had been no warning signs before the game.
“Not at all. I thought that he wasn’t that sharp in San Francisco, but we got him out of it. Felt great coming out of that outing. He had an inning this past week, felt great, and then going into this start there were no concerns.
“You can tell when a pitcher, certainly with the lower half, isn’t right. Tonight the fastball was 97, 98, so it wasn’t compromised.”
Too Many Chances Left on the Bases
The Dodgers had runners on throughout the middle innings but could not come up with the hit that would have changed the game.
“That’s what it is,” Roberts said. “You look at Dubón in that first inning, puts the bat on the ball to drive in a run, infield hit. You look at Harris, 3-2, puts the ball in play in the gap, Olson running. We just had opportunities.
“We couldn’t get a hit when we needed to. We didn’t throw out a bunch of hits, but there was still traffic. We didn’t need many hits tonight to have a different result. We just couldn’t get it.”
Roberts felt good about the matchup when he found out Atlanta would use a bullpen game.
“Felt great. Felt great. Anytime I have Blake Snell lined up against any pitcher, I feel good. Getting Kerr out of the game and then getting Holmes out of the game, I felt really good where we were at. I really did.
“We just couldn’t execute as the game progressed.”
He also gave credit to Didier Fuentes for shutting the Dodgers down over 3 2/3 innings.
“I think it was just the fastball. Tonight you could see the fastball, it was 99, 100, and there were a lot of balls that we were just missing as far as lazy fly balls. We just couldn’t hit the ball flat against him.
“He was mixing in his split once in a while. At one point he retired nine straight guys. Two days off and doing what he did was pretty impressive.”
Roberts Wants Ohtani Back in the Zone
Shohei Ohtani has had a quiet start to the series, and Roberts said the biggest issue has been chasing pitches out of the strike zone.
“I think with Sho, if you look at the at-bats, there’s a lot of chase,” Roberts said. “It’s hard to square up and put good swings on balls that are out of the zone. That’s kind of what it boils down to.
“Certainly Sale is going to be tough because there’s a lot of strike to ball, high velocity, but it’s just trying to get him back in the hitting zone.”
Roberts said Ohtani has not reported any health issue.
“I haven’t heard anything other than he feels fine. This time of year everyone doesn’t feel perfect. He’s doing the best he can.
“He’ll be in there Game 3. We just have to take good at-bats and expect the best.”
Díaz Could Get a Ninth-Inning Look
One of the bright spots for Roberts was Edwin Díaz, who worked a clean inning and looked sharp.
“Edwin was great,” Roberts said. “If you look at tonight and try to find some silver linings, that was a silver lining. That was certainly a positive.”
Asked whether Díaz could eventually get a chance to close, Roberts was direct.
“I’ve been very consistent in the fact that I wanted to get him an outing. This was a big spot, and he did what he needed to do. It looked great.
“Absolutely, you could see him closing. Yes, I can see him closing.”
A Three-Game Series Now
Roberts said Atlanta showed how aggressively it plans to use its pitching staff.
“They’re going to use any pitcher, try to get every matchup possible. Them pushing Fuentes to almost four innings, 40-something pitches, shows that they’re going to ride certain guys. Obviously, they use their bullpen accordingly.
“It’s a good team offensively. They’re going to fight. Harris is swinging a good bat. We knew it was going to be a battle. We knew those guys weren’t going to go down.
“We’re expecting Sale in Game 3, and we’ve got our work cut out. Now it’s a three-game series.”

item.content:encoded:
MILWAUKEE -- Los Angeles Dodgers utilitymanKiké Hernandezis expected to be activated in time to make his season debut Monday after recovering from surgery on his left elbow.
Dodgers manager Dave Roberts said Sunday that Hernández should be available for the start of their home series against the Colorado Rockies.
"There's a different energy with Kiké," Roberts said Sunday. "There's a levity. There's an intensity. There's a good worker in there, a winning player. So I'm looking forward to having that edge."
Hernández, 34, signed a one-year, $4.5 million contract in February that kept him with the Dodgers. He underwent surgery last fall that kept him from playing for Puerto Rico in the World Baseball Classic and delayed the start of his 2026 season.
He hit .214 with a .298 on-base percentage with three RBIs in 12 games while on a rehabilitation assignment with Oklahoma City. He batted .203 with a .255 on-base percentage, 10 homers and 35 RBIs in 92 games with Los Angeles last season.
Hernández often has done his best work in October while helping the Dodgers win World Series in 2020, 2024 and 2025. He has batted .272 with an .826 OPS, 16 homers and 42 RBIs in 103 postseason games.
His return comes while Dodgers third baseman Max Muncy recovers after a 95.5 mph sinker from Milwaukee's Aaron Ashby hit him in the right wrist on Friday. X-rays were negative and the Dodgers expressed optimism that Muncy avoided a major injury.
"We were resolved to not having him available this weekend," Roberts said. "My expectation is that he's getting a little bit better today and maybe swing a bat tomorrow to see. I don't expect him in the lineup tomorrow either."
Muncy is batting .258 with a .363 on-base percentage, .515 slugging percentage, 12 homers and 19 RBIs in 48 games.

item.title: [New York Post] Dodgers heroes, zeros from NLDS Game 2 loss: Shohei Ohtani concerns grow
item.dc:creator: Jack Harris
item.description: Dodgers heroes, zeros from Game 2 loss: Shohei Ohtani still looks off Heroes, zeros and the inside pitch from the Dodgers’ 3–2 loss to the Atlanta Braves in Game 2 of the National League Division Series: Zero Shohei Ohtani’s first at-bat of this NLDS looked relatively normal, as he pulled a 105 mph line drive into right for a first-inning, Game 1 single. Every subsequent trip to the plate, however, has been anything but. Granted, Ohtani has not been the Dodgers’ biggest problem offensively. Will
item.content:encoded:
Dodgers heroes, zeros from Game 2 loss: Shohei Ohtani still looks off
Heroes, zeros and the inside pitch from the Dodgers’ 3–2 loss to the Atlanta Braves in Game 2 of the National League Division Series:
Zero
Shohei Ohtani’s first at-bat of this NLDS looked relatively normal, as he pulled a 105 mph line drive into right for a first-inning, Game 1 single.
Every subsequent trip to the plate, however, has been anything but.
Granted, Ohtani has not been the Dodgers’ biggest problem offensively. Will Smith (0–for–8), Andy Pages (0–for–7, one walk) and Tommy Edman (0–for–5, one walk) are all vying for that honor.
But if there was any hope that the team’s playoff-opening bye week would fix the two-way amid his ongoing right arm and left knee injuries, these two games have been a reminder of just how far he is from his typical self.
“I haven’t heard anything other than he feels fine,” manager Dave Roberts said.
But…
“I don’t know if he’s trying to do too much because he doesn’t feel perfect,” the skipper added, in what felt more like a tacit acknowledgement.
A healthy Ohtani, after all, wouldn’t go 0–for–2 against plucky feel-good story Ray Kerr, striking out on an inside fastball in the first inning before popping out in a key spot with two aboard in the third.
A healthy Ohtani wouldn’t need to slap the ball the other way Ichiro-style just to get a base hit, as he did on his lone single in the fifth.
The most telling thing for the 32-year-old superstar the last two days?
The Braves haven’t been afraid to challenge him, throwing him nine fastballs in the middle-third of the strike zone so far. And he hasn’t been able to punish them for it, turning only one into a hit (that first-inning, Game 1 single) while also chasing more outside of the zone after failing to end his at-bats.
“He’ll be in there Game 3,” Roberts confirmed. “We’ve just got to, again, take good at-bats and expect the best.”
Hero
At least the Dodgers’ other pre-NLDS injury question mark has seemingly turned a corner.
In his final 66 games of the regular season (going back to July 5), Freddie Freeman had hit only one home run. In September, he slumped to a .184 average with only one extra-base hit while battling a right knee injury that threatened to linger into the playoffs.
However, the bye week seemingly did wonders for him, following up a one-hit, one-walk performance in Game 1 of the series with a two-hit night Sunday that included a solo homer to right field.
“I feel good, so I think we can be done with those questions,” he quipped when asked about his swing and knee injury. “Just more consistently getting myself in a good spot, being able to put good swings on it.”
Unsung hero
There were times this year when Edwin Díaz’s fastball velocity dipped as low as 92 mph.
During his scoreless appearance in the sixth inning on Sunday, the resurgent right-hander dialed it up to a season-high 100.8 mph.
That was just one impressive aspect of Díaz’s latest standout performance, in which he extended his scoreless streak to six innings (including 15 straight batters retired over his last five outings) since returning from his second injured list stint of the year on Sept. 18.
“Edwin was great,” Roberts said. “I think if you look at tonight, try to find some silver linings, that was a silver lining and certainly a positive.”
Key stat
Zero: As in 0 hits with runners in scoring position for the Dodgers on Sunday, and 0 runs scored via any method other than a home run so far in this NLDS.
Ironically, the club’s lack of power had been the bigger concern coming into the playoffs.
While they could be (extremely) up-and-down in the regular season in situational at-bats, they still rank seventh in batting average with runners in scoring position and third in OPS.
That, however, hasn’t translated to October yet.
“Got to find a way to score some runs without hitting a home run,” Freeman said. “I think that’s our biggest thing right now.”
Quote of the night
“We’ve been in tougher spots than this one,” outfielder Teoscar Hernández said, when asked how crucial the team’s past October experience (especially in back-and-forth series like the 2024 NLDS and 2025 World Series) would be in the face of what is now a best-of-three showdown. “It’s a 1–1 series. We know they’re going to have the best pitcher that they have, starting pitcher, in [Game 3 with Chris] Sale. But we’re just gonna try to be ready and just go with the best plan and just try to execute it.”

item.title: [CBS Sports] Shohei Ohtani still struggling at the plate: Can the Dodgers survive with this version of their superstar?
item.dc:creator: Dayn Perry
item.description: The Los Angeles Dodgers have some concerns as they vie for the elusive threepeat. Their means the series is now tied 1-1, which in turn means the series is now in essence a best-of-three with the Braves having home field advantage. A very much related concern is the current status of two-way superstar Shohei Ohtani. Ohtani hasn't pitched since July 3, when he was pulled from his start against the Padres because of left knee discomfort and soreness in his right biceps. Those injuries kept him out
item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers have some concerns as they vie for the elusive threepeat. Their means the series is now tied 1-1, which in turn means the series is now in essence a best-of-three with the Braves having home field advantage.
A very much related concern is the current status of two-way superstar Shohei Ohtani. Ohtani hasn't pitched since July 3, when he was pulled from his start against the Padres because of left knee discomfort and soreness in his right biceps. Those injuries kept him out of the All-Star Game and, presumably, won't allow him to pitch in the postseason.
The Dodgers have the rotation depth and frontline excellence to withstand the loss of Ohtani the pitcher, but what about Ohtani the hitter? His presence is invaluable in an L.A. lineup that's aging in some spots. Ohtani's knee inflammation landed him on the injured list in September, but he returned in time to play the final five games of the regular season. He went 5 for 21 in those games with only one extra-base hit, a double, and eight strikeouts against one walk. Taking the longer view, Ohtani in all of September batted just .200/.333/.233, and overall his OPS at the plate dropped from .953 in the first half of 2026 to .772 in the second half. He also saw a decline in underlying batted-ball authority from the first half to the second. He hasn't homered since Aug. 18 in Coors Field. Counting the current Braves series, that's a stretch of 20 games and 80 at-bats without a home run for Ohtani.
Speaking of the postseason, through the first two games of the Braves series, Ohtani is 2 for 8 with no extra-base hits or walks and a pair of strikeouts. Normally, such a minuscule sample wouldn't register, but against the much larger backdrop of Ohtani's poor production and the parallel matter of his ongoing case of knee inflammation, it's all a major concern for the Dodgers.
"I think with Shohei, it's just -- I think, if you look at the at-bats, there's a lot of chase," Dodgers manager Dave Roberts said after Sunday's 3-2 loss to Atlanta. "I think that it's like -- it's hard to square up, put good swings on balls that are out of the zone. That's kind of what it boils down to.
"Certainly (Chris) Sale is going to be tough because there's a lot of strike to ball, it's high velocity. But just trying to get him back in the hitting zone."
As for the possibility or even likelihood that Ohtani is compromised at the plate because of his knee and, to a lesser extent, his biceps, Roberts said:
"I haven't heard anything other than he feels fine. So I don't know if he's trying to do too much because he doesn't feel perfect. This time of year, everyone doesn't feel -- no one feels perfect. He's doing the best he can.
"Yeah, he'll be in there Game 3, and we've just got to, again, take good at-bats and expect the best."
The Dodgers with their rotation of aces don't easily concede any pitching match-up, but the bullpen game run to success by Braves manager Walt Weiss in Game 2 will allow Atlanta to start Sale, as dominant as ever at age 37, on full rest in Tuesday's pivotal Game 3. Sale owns the platoon advantage against Ohtani and other lefty Dodger batters and, as Roberts notes, his stuff is top of the scale. For a hitter struggling like Ohtani has been for weeks and possibly without a healthy foundation under him at the plate, facing the likes of Sale is no way to get right.
After almost a decade of baseball miracles upon baseball miracles, there's no sensible path to doubting Ohtani. The Dodgers' lineup fulcrum and leadoff hitter, though, might not be the real Ohtani thanks to those injuries. That, as much as anything else, is imperiling the Dodger dynasty right about now.
