item.content:encoded:
One of many things that makes the Los Angeles Dodgers so infuriating to competitors is how lucky they get when it comes to injuries. Over their last three seasons, their pitching staff has been riddled with shoulder inflammation and elbow impingements, and so on — but they always seem to get their key players back exactly when they need them.
They might have lost Blake Treinen in their last series of this season, but he's had a tough year and wasn't a lock for the postseason roster anyway. The real concern was for Edgardo Henriquez, who's been missing since September 14 with lower back discomfort.
Henriquez was officially activated from the IL on Tuesday, but his status ahead of the NLDS still seemed touch-and-go, given how fresh off injury he'll be with zero runway.
There are still boxes he has to check, but Dodgers GM Brandon Gomes said on Tuesday that he's trending the right direction. Katie Woo reported, "should he come out of all bye-week activities (live hitters, sim games, etc), he'll be on the NLDS roster."
The back end of the Dodgers' bullpen has no clear hierarchy right now, so Henriquez would be a welcome addition for later innings.
Edgardo Henriquez trending positively toward returning for Dodgers' NLDS
It's hard to guess what Dave Roberts' trust tree might look like heading into October. Tanner Scott, Edwin Díaz, and Tanner Scott are the obvious closing options, but Scott posted a 4.15 ERA in September, Díaz showed signs of life after his IL stint but still isn't truly trustworthy, and there's no telling if Sasaki will turn back into the lights-out closer he became last season.
The Dodgers used Henriquez as early as the third and as a late as extra innings over the course of the regular season, but he picked up two saves in nine games finished this year. His ability to throw 100+ MPH with regularity is his greatest asset, as long as he can control his pitches.
He was trending toward a more regular eighth- or ninth-inning role before he got hurt, as the Dodgers had to go with closers by committee with Díaz's absences and Scott struggling a little more. Henriquez has been effective anywhere between the seventh and ninth, with just a .191 batting average and .553 OPS against.
The Dodgers' bullpen being as shaky as it still is, the onus will be on the starters (again) to go as deep into games as possible, but Henriquez's presence should add a little more assurance.

item.title: [Dodgers Way] Projecting the Dodgers' NLDS roster with Josue De Paula, bench shuffle
item.dc:creator: Katrina Stebbins
item.description: The Los Angeles Dodgers get to kick back and watch as eight teams duke it out to move on to their respective League Division Series this week. The Atlanta Braves and Philadelphia Phillies will go head-to-head in the NL Wild Card Series before one of them moves on to try and topple LA. One would think that this Dodgers team would have everything buttoned up well ahead of the NLDS, but there are still a couple of key questions to be answered. Projecting the Dodgers' NLDS roster with Josue De Paula
item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers get to kick back and watch as eight teams duke it out to move on to their respective League Division Series this week. The Atlanta Braves and Philadelphia Phillies will go head-to-head in the NL Wild Card Series before one of them moves on to try and topple LA.
One would think that this Dodgers team would have everything buttoned up well ahead of the NLDS, but there are still a couple of key questions to be answered.
Projecting the Dodgers' NLDS roster with Josue De Paula called upon
Catchers (2): Will Smith, Hunter Feduccia
For some reason, the Dodgers decided to carry three catchers on their Wild Card and NLDS rosters last year — Smith, Dalton Rushing, and Ben Rortvedt — but adjusted ahead of the NLCS by shedding Rushing, who received just one at-bat in the NLDS but otherwise rode the bench.
Rortvedt didn't get a start or even substitution after Game 2 of the NLDS with Smith slowly coming back from injury at the beginning of the postseason. Feduccia figures to play a similar break-glass-in-case-of-emergency role. As a lefty, he could get a start and then an early pull depending on matchups but, barring disaster, it's mostly going to be Smith's show.
Designated hitters (2): Shohei Ohtani, Josue De Paula
The Dodgers clearly want to find a way to bring De Paula with them in October, even if only as a lingering threat on their bench. They're reportedly not entertaining putting him in the outfield at all, and it's not hard to see why. Even if they're confident they'll be able to fix his defense in time, they can't afford any leakage in the postseason.
Ohtani is still shaking off the cobwebs from his 15-day IL stint. He picked up a few hits with promising exit velocity in his return against the San Diego Padres and later against the San Francisco Giants, but there are still question marks around what version of him we might see this postseason.
Infielders (6): Freddie Freeman, Mookie Betts, Tommy Edman, Max Muncy, Miguel Rojas, Kiké Hernández
A notable exclusion here is Hyeseong Kim. Although he's in the running to get a spot on the bench and exclusively come into games to pinch-run or for reassurances on defense, there's still a chance he doesn't make the roster if the Dodgers are set on carrying 13 pitchers. Edman and Hernández, though lacking the same speed as Kim, can still offer the same defensive versatility.
Outfielders (3): Andy Pages, Kyle Tucker, Teoscar Hernández
Pages might've found himself in the same boat as Ohtani, but he announced his return to the Dodgers after a month-long IL stint in a big way, hitting .333 with a 1.180 OPS, two homers, and five RBI against the Padres and Giants. No doubt Dave Roberts and Andrew Friedman breathed a massive sigh of relief.
Alex Call will be the odd man out. He was on all four of LA's playoff rosters last year and received sporadic appearances throughout the month, but that was when Michael Conforto was still on the payroll. Tucker and Hernández have certainly had their ups-and-downs this season, but the Dodgers would never seriously consider leaving them out.
Starters (4): Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Blake Snell, Tarik Skubal, Tyler Glasnow
There's not much to say about what's probably the best rotation going into the postseason. Snell and Glasnow have both battled injury this season but came back when the Dodgers needed them most. It might be too much to ask that any of Yamamoto, Snell, or Glasnow replicate their dominance from last year, but they'll certainly try.
Relievers: (9): Tanner Scott, Roki Sasaki, Alex Vesia, Evan Phillips, Brock Stewart, Justin Wrobleski, Edwin Díaz, Kris Bubic, Edgardo Henriquez
Just like 2025, this is where things get dicey. The Dodgers' bullpen isn't quite as banged up or as unreliable as they were last year, but they're not the air-tight, bulletproof coterie that their combined salaries suggest they should be. Henriquez will be coming straight off of the IL to rejoin the team in the NLDS, and Díaz, Sasaki, and Scott are all woefully unpredictable.
There is some thought that the Dodgers might carry eight relievers instead of nine, to free up a spot on the position player side for a guy like Kim. In this scenario, we'll stick with them taking nine. If not, Bubic is the most obvious cut. Last one in, first one out.

item.title: [New York Post] Dodgers to get ‘huge impact’ with key reliever on track for NLDS return
item.dc:creator: Jack Harris
item.description: Over the last two months of the regular season, no team had a more productive bullpen than the Dodgers. And come the start of their postseason trek on Saturday, the team might be adding another key arm back to the group. General manager Brandon Gomes announced on Tuesday that the club expects to have hard-throwing right-handed reliever Edgardo Henriquez available for its National League Division Series, an encouraging development after Henriquez missed the final couple weeks of the regular seaso
item.content:encoded:
Over the last two months of the regular season, no team had a more productive bullpen than the Dodgers.
And come the start of their postseason trek on Saturday, the team might be adding another key arm back to the group.
General manager Brandon Gomes announced on Tuesday that the club expects to have hard-throwing right-handed reliever Edgardo Henriquez available for its National League Division Series, an encouraging development after Henriquez missed the final couple weeks of the regular season with a strain in his back.
Prior to getting hurt, Henriquez was emerging as one of the top arms in the Dodgers’ resurgent relief corps (which led all MLB bullpens in August and September with 4.3 combined wins above replacement, according to Fangraphs, and ranked fourth in that stretch in combined ERA at 3.20).
A 24-year-old former prospect who has started to routinely eclipse 103 mph with his fastball, Henriquez ranked fourth among the team’s relievers (minimum 20 appearances) with a 2.85 ERA this season. He also struck out 70 batters in 60 total innings and converted each of the ninth-inning save opportunities he received.
Henriquez had hit his stride in August and early September, allowing just one run in a 17-game stretch that featured 25 strikeouts and only two walks and seven hits allowed.
However, after giving up two runs in a Sept. 13 appearance in Miami against the Marlins, he went on the IL with his back injury –– one that initially cast doubt on his postseason availability.
Luckily for the Dodgers, Henriquez’s status has improved since then. He resumed a throwing during the team’s final regular-season homestand. He recently completed a session of live batting practice without feeling any lingering discomfort. And while Gomes said “we still got a few steps to go” before Henriquez gets the green light to return, every indication is that he should be available for the club’s best-of-five NLDS.
“If that all goes well, then yeah, the expectation is he’ll be on the roster,” Gomes said.
“Given the body of work, what he’s done, the unique skill set, that could be huge for us,” manager Dave Roberts added, before correcting himself: “Will be huge for us.”
Indeed, Henriquez would figure to occupy a high-leverage spot in the Dodgers’ postseason bullpen. He gives them not only a trustworthy right-hander option –– along with Roki Sasaki, Evan Phillips, Brock Stewart and the recently resurgent Edwin Díaz –– but also one of the biggest fastballs in the game.
Henriquez’s 100.7 mph average fastball velocity ranked second among MLB pitchers this season, behind only star Padres closer Mason Miller. The team’s next-hardest thrower is Sasaki, whose heater averaged only 97.9 mph this year (though could increase in the playoffs as he shifts to a bullpen role).
Last October, Henriquez was a mixed bag in the playoffs. In two of his appearances (Game 1 of the wild card series and Game 5 of the World Series), he failed to record an out while allowing a hit and two walks in both outings. But in the other (Game 3 of the World Series), he pitched two scoreless frames in the team’s marathon 18-inning win, becoming an unsung hero in their Fall Classic triumph.
This time, Henriquez is set for a prominent role, assuming he gets through one more session of live batting practice OK.
“[He would make a] huge impact,” Roberts said. “I think he’s one of those guys that getting the bye has really benefited.”

item.title: [Dodgers Nation] Dodgers Expect Edgardo Henriquez Back for NLDS If Final Tests Go Well
item.dc:creator: Nelson Espinal

Henriquez is still on the injured list with a lower back injury, which shut him down for the last two weeks of the regular season. Edgardo Henriquez injury status When speaking to the media, including Dodgers Nation, on Tuesday, September 29th, Gomes said Henriquez threw a live batting practice session against hitters, and it wen
item.content:encoded:
Los Angeles Dodgers reliever Edgardo Henriquez is “trending really well,” according to general manager Brandon Gomes, and he is looking likely to be on the NLDS roster.
Henriquez is still on the injured list with a lower back injury, which shut him down for the last two weeks of the regular season.
Edgardo Henriquez injury status
When speaking to the media, including Dodgers Nation, on Tuesday, September 29th, Gomes said Henriquez threw a live batting practice session against hitters, and it went well.
Henriquez also has additional activities lined up during the bye week to clear up, including simulated games and more live batting sessions.
If he clears the remaining checkmarks, Henriquez will be ready for the NLDS, per Gomes.
“We’ve still got a few steps to go, but if all that goes well, the expectation is he will be on the roster,” the general manager said.
What will Henriquez’s role be with the bullpen?
Before he got hurt, Henriquez was a set-up man for the Dodgers, and he was also a budding closer for the team thanks to his consistency.
Tanner Scott is prone to home runs, while Edwin Diaz was in a spiral, which helped Henriquez emerge as the most consistent relief pitcher.
Over the last few weeks, Scott has been steady, while Diaz has rebuilt himself from the ground up. Additionally, Roki Sasaki moved into the bullpen, leading the Dodgers into the postseason with plenty of candidates to close, Henriquez among them.
“Obviously we’ve had a lot of talent over the years,” manager Dave Roberts said. “But as far as sitting here today at the end of the season, it’s as good of shape as we’ve ever been in with the bullpen.
“That could change in a day, in a game, as we all know. But right now, feel really good about everyone out there.”
Roberts is known for making bullpen decisions based on feel in the postseason, and depending on how Henriquez looks coming back, he may close or perhaps settle into a middle relief role.
Luckily, the Dodgers have bullpen options, which hasn’t been the case for a while.

item.title: [Dodgers Way] Mets-Tarik Skubal rumors have already begun before Dodgers' playoff run has even started
item.dc:creator: Drew Koch
item.description: The MLB Postseason officially gets underway on Tuesday, but the Los Angeles Dodgers won't take the field until later this weekend thanks to their 100-62 record and a first-round bye. Dodgers' manager Dave Roberts now has plenty of time to set his rotation for the upcoming NLDS matchup; one that will almost certainly feature Tarik Skubal as LA's starter for Game 1 or 2. But it would seem that the New York Mets already have their sights set on the Dodgers' free agent to-be. Will Sammon of The Athl
item.content:encoded:
The MLB Postseason officially gets underway on Tuesday, but the Los Angeles Dodgers won't take the field until later this weekend thanks to their 100-62 record and a first-round bye. Dodgers' manager Dave Roberts now has plenty of time to set his rotation for the upcoming NLDS matchup; one that will almost certainly feature Tarik Skubal as LA's starter for Game 1 or 2.
But it would seem that the New York Mets already have their sights set on the Dodgers' free agent to-be. Will Sammon of The Athletic claims that Skubal to the Mets makes a lot of sense on paper, but stopped short of calling it no-brainer thanks in large part to the upcoming labor negotiations.
Dodgers & Mets look to be Tarik Skubal's most likely free agent suitors
Sammon cites the potential for a salary cap and the exorbitant salaries already on the Mets books — namely Juan Soto and Francisco Lindor — as the two biggest obstacles that could put a halt to New York's pursuit of Skubal. Those same barriers could force the Dodgers to hit the pause button as well. LA has a ton of hefty, long-term contracts that would impact the club if a salary cap was implemented.
Few, if any, know how the upcoming negotiations between the owners and the Player's Association are going to play out, but the economic impact and how teams could be required to spend in the future could greatly alter who pursues Skubal this winter and how much they'll be willing to offer.
Then there's the other aspect that no one is really talking about — at least not yet. The negotiating window will be extremely short. With the Collective Bargaining Agreement set to expire on December 1, teams will have a little more than three weeks to lay the groundwork for a potential landmark contract with the two-time Cy Young award-winner.
Throw in the fact that he's represented by Scott Boras — baseball's super-agent who's known for extending these negotiations well into the springtime — and the likelihood of striking a deal before the window closes looks less and less by the day. Yet, the potential salary cap, and thereby reduction in salary, could be enough to prompt Boras and Skubal to get a new deal done posthaste.
Much like the Mets, the Dodgers will undoubtedly be interested in re-signing Skubal this winter. Frankly, it may be a two-team race to determine who'll walk away with the offseason biggest prize. Few other organizations have the resources to ink the southpaw to the record-breaking deal he'll surely be seeking. Most pundits expect the deal to be worth more than $400 million.

item.title: [DodgersBeat] With Another 100 Win Season, Dave Roberts Joins Elite Company
item.dc:creator: Steve Webb
item.description: SAN FRANCISCO, CA — Dave Roberts has accomplished quite a bit during his tenure as Dodgers manager, but Sunday’s 5-1 victory over the Giants added another impressive achievement to his résumé. With the Dodgers reaching 100 victories, Roberts tied the all-time managerial record for most 100-win seasons, joining some of the most successful skippers in baseball history. Speaking with reporters following the regular-season finale, Roberts acknowledged the significance of the accomplishment while emp
item.content:encoded:
SAN FRANCISCO, CA — Dave Roberts has accomplished quite a bit during his tenure as Dodgers manager, but Sunday’s 5-1 victory over the Giants added another impressive achievement to his résumé.
With the Dodgers reaching 100 victories, Roberts tied the all-time managerial record for most 100-win seasons, joining some of the most successful skippers in baseball history.
Speaking with reporters following the regular-season finale, Roberts acknowledged the significance of the accomplishment while emphasizing the contributions of the players and organization that helped make it possible.
A Milestone Worth Celebrating
Asked whether reaching 100 wins carried significance even though the Dodgers had already secured their postseason position, Roberts made it clear that the milestone mattered.
“It does. It doesn’t change anything as far as our standing going forward in the postseason, but it’s still a nice feather in our cap to win 100 games.”
When informed that the victory tied him for the most 100-win seasons by any manager in major league history, Roberts reflected on the company he now keeps.
“Yeah, I guess I’m in some rare air, some good company. A lot of good players, a great organization, and it’s not easy, 100 games.
“There’s a lot of things that we had to go through this year, and we just continued to remain steadfast and play on. And so, yeah, that’s something to be proud of.”
Sunday’s victory provided a fitting conclusion to another successful regular season. Roberts particularly appreciated the pitching staff’s performance, with seven pitchers combining to hold San Francisco to one run while striking out 16.
“Obviously, we had a few guys that we wanted to stay away from. I thought the pitching did a remarkable job today. Bobby did a nice job picking up a couple innings, getting out of some stress there in the seventh, I think it was.
“And timely hitting. It didn’t look great early, but we hung in there as far as on the pitching side, and Alex with a big two-out hit, and then Andy finished up the season the right way.”
Preparing for Philadelphia or Atlanta
The Dodgers will now await the winner of the Phillies-Braves Wild Card Series, with Game 1 of the NLDS scheduled for Saturday at Dodger Stadium.
Roberts expects a competitive series between two familiar division rivals.
“When you start the season, those two teams were probably picked to be one-two in the East, and they’re very, very familiar with one another. So it’s going to be a good series.
“Obviously, the Phillies had to play to the end, but like I said, there’s a lot of familiarity, and all bets are off when you play within the division.
“So we’ll just sit back and take tomorrow off and have the workout on Tuesday. We’ll get to watch those guys, and then we’ll get to watch that other series during our workout.”
Getting the Big Bats Ready
Roberts also discussed the importance of the upcoming break for Freddie Freeman and Shohei Ohtani, both of whom have been working to find their offensive rhythm.
Regarding Ohtani, Roberts was encouraged by what he saw Sunday and believes the additional preparation will be valuable.
“I thought he looked fine. He looked better today. I do think that just getting some at-bats, however many he got since he came back, and then really just this week is going to be really crucial, I think, for Freddie. I think it’s going to be crucial for Sho.”
Roberts also emphasized that Ohtani emerged from his recent return to action healthy, which was the most important consideration.
“The process early was great. I thought in the middle of that he was kind of getting a little more anxious. I thought today the process was much better.
“But I think the main thing is that we feel that he came out of it healthy, and so you just expect the ensuing days he feels even better. When you look out to Saturday, I think he’ll be in a good spot.”
The Dodgers will make intrasquad games available during their preparation period, although Roberts said individual players will decide whether to participate.
For Roberts, the regular season concludes with another historic accomplishment and a chance to add to an already remarkable managerial legacy.
But the ultimate objective remains the same: 11 more wins and another World Series championship.
More Dodgers Coverage:
Have you subscribed to the Bleed Los Podcast YouTube channel? Be sure to ring the notification bell to watch player interviews, participate in shows & promotions, and stay up to date on all Dodgers news and rumors!
A lifelong baseball fan, Webb has been going to Dodger games since he moved to Los Angeles in 1987. His favorite memory was attending the insane Game 3 of the World Series in 2025 and hugging random Dodgers fans after Freddie’s walkoff homer. He has been writing for Dodgersbeat since 2020.

item.title: [mlb.com] Roberts ties record with 6th 100-win season as manager
item.dc:creator: Sonja Chen
item.description: SAN FRANCISCO -- With another 162 regular-season games in the books, Dodgers manager Dave Roberts has again found himself in rarefied air. The Dodgers' 5-1 victory over the Giants in 10 innings on Sunday afternoon at Oracle Park -- keyed by Alex Call's go-ahead double and a three-run blast from Andy Pages -- secured a 100-win campaign, their fifth in the past seven full-length seasons and their sixth with Roberts at the helm. Roberts joins Hall of Famers Bobby Cox and Joe McCarthy as the only ma
item.content:encoded:
SAN FRANCISCO -- With another 162 regular-season games in the books, Dodgers manager Dave Roberts has again found himself in rarefied air.
The Dodgers' 5-1 victory over the Giants in 10 innings on Sunday afternoon at Oracle Park -- keyed by Alex Call's go-ahead double and a three-run blast from Andy Pages -- secured a 100-win campaign, their fifth in the past seven full-length seasons and their sixth with Roberts at the helm.
Roberts joins Hall of Famers Bobby Cox and Joe McCarthy as the only managers with six 100-win seasons.
"I guess I'm in some rare air, some good company," said Roberts, who in June reached 1,000 career managerial wins faster than any other manager. "A lot of good players, a great organization, and it's not easy to win 100 games. And so there's a lot of things that we had to go through this year, and we just continue to remain steadfast and play on. And so, yeah, that's something to be proud of."
The last three seasons in which the Dodgers did not win 100 games -- 2025, '24 and the pandemic-shortened '20 campaign -- they won the World Series. In their 11 previous 100-win seasons, they failed to win a championship.
"That just means we’re due as an organization," Freddie Freeman said. "I don’t think any of us are going to be upset with winning 100 games."
The 2026 Dodgers are not just looking to win it all. They are defending their World Series title for the second year in a row, seeking to complete the Majors' first three-peat since the 1998-2000 Yankees.
After the bye week, in which they'll await the outcome of the Wild Card Series between the Braves and Phillies, the Dodgers' title defense begins in earnest in the NL Division Series, starting on Saturday at Dodger Stadium.
The Dodgers may have 100 wins in the books, but everything resets in the postseason. Moving forward, they're focused on getting the 11 wins they need to hoist the Commissioner's Trophy for a third straight year.

item.title: [MLB.com] Dodgers end season with 100th win, questions about Ohtani
item.dc:creator: Sonja Chen

Ohtani knocked a base hit in three at-bats as the Dodgers closed the book on their regular season with a 5-1 win in 10 innings over the Giants on Sunday afternoon at Oracle Park. L.A. has won 100 games for the sixth time under manager Dave Roberts, who joins Hall of Famers B
item.content:encoded:
SAN FRANCISCO -- Five games do not tell the story of Shohei Ohtani's year, but that season-ending sample holds a fair amount of weight as the Dodgers evaluate which version of their superstar they will get in the postseason.
Ohtani knocked a base hit in three at-bats as the Dodgers closed the book on their regular season with a 5-1 win in 10 innings over the Giants on Sunday afternoon at Oracle Park. L.A. has won 100 games for the sixth time under manager Dave Roberts, who joins Hall of Famers Bobby Cox and Joe McCarthy as the only managers to accomplish the feat.
The most meaningful games of the year are just around the corner for the back-to-back World Series champions, whose title defense picks up when the NL Division Series begins next Saturday at Dodger Stadium.
"It doesn't change anything as far as our standing going forward in the postseason," Roberts said, "but it's still a nice feather in our cap to win 100 games."
The Dodgers finished strong by going 18-7 in September, and they'll look to maintain that momentum through the upcoming bye week.
"I just think as a group we played better baseball again, and that’s what you want going into the postseason," Freddie Freeman said. "Our pitching staff is amazing. Guys started to swing the bat better. Some of us still need to use these five days to figure it out. But a lot of good things happened over the course of the end of the season."
As the Dodgers bid for a three-peat, which would be the first in the Majors since the 1998-2000 Yankees, they are counting on Ohtani to set the tone for their offense as he has consistently done in his three seasons in L.A. But in the five games after his 15-day injured list stint due to lingering right biceps and left knee injuries -- after more than two weeks without seeing live pitching -- Ohtani did not show much at the plate, hitting 5-for-21 (.238) with eight strikeouts against one walk.
Overall, Ohtani finished the regular season hitting .275 with an .889 OPS and 30 homers -- which all came before he went on the IL. His run of consecutive MVP seasons is set to end after three years, as the Cubs' Pete Crow-Armstrong has seemingly run away with the award.
Before Sunday's finale, Roberts described Ohtani's recent performance as showing rust rather than being a legitimate concern heading into the postseason. The Dodgers believe Ohtani feels as good physically as he has in some time, and they don't think his swing looks compromised, as it did before he went on the IL.
While better results from Ohtani would have been encouraging, the Dodgers were looking for more than just the surface numbers. They wanted to see him conduct quality at-bats, which he did in his first two games back and on Sunday, with a lapse in between. But ultimately, these games were more about health and process rather than pure performance, much like a rehab assignment.
"I thought today the process was much better," Roberts said. "But I think the main thing is that we feel that he came out of it healthy, and so you just expect the ensuing days he feels even better. So, when you look out to Saturday, I think he'll be in a good spot."
Ohtani's performance began to drop off most notably when he attempted to ramp back up as a pitcher starting on Aug. 8. In the 24 games between then and his IL stint, Ohtani hit .198 and struck out 34 times in 109 plate appearances. His average bat speed (72.5 mph) and exit velocity (92.2 mph) in that span were down compared with his first 106 games (72.9 mph bat speed and 93.4 mph exit velocity).
In Ohtani's five games back from the IL, he gained a tick of average bat speed (72.6 mph) and hit the ball notably harder (96.8 mph). Even though that did not translate to immediate results, it would seem to be a positive sign for both Ohtani's health and his swing.
The postseason is a new beginning. Ohtani will have the bye week to rest up and take live at-bats, and starting on Saturday, the Dodgers are hopeful that he will swing the bat more like his usual self. But they won't know exactly what they have in their superstar until they see him under the lights.

item.title: [Los Angeles Times] Commentary: Dodgers don't have a designated playoff closer. That isn't as bad as it sounds
item.dc:creator: Bill Shaikin
item.description: - Click here to listen to this article - - The Dodgers enter October seeking a third straight World Series title, but the club has not settled on a closer despite spending heavily on Edwin Díaz and Tanner Scott. - Andrew Friedman is confident about the Dodgers’ bullpen adapting to late-inning, high-leverage situations in the playoffs no matter who might be called upon. SAN FRANCISCO — Stop me if you’ve heard this a million times, but the Dodgers are trying to become the first team to win t
item.content:encoded:
- Click here to listen to this article
-
- The Dodgers enter October seeking a third straight World Series title, but the club has not settled on a closer despite spending heavily on Edwin Díaz and Tanner Scott.
- Andrew Friedman is confident about the Dodgers’ bullpen adapting to late-inning, high-leverage situations in the playoffs no matter who might be called upon.
SAN FRANCISCO — Stop me if you’ve heard this a million times, but the Dodgers are trying to become the first team to win three consecutive World Series championships since the New York Yankees, from 1998 to 2000.
Those Yankees had a Hall of Fame closer. In 1998, Mariano Rivera got the final four outs of the clincher. In 1999, he got the final four outs. In 2000, he got the final three outs.
These Dodgers? Their closer? Your guess is as good as theirs.
“I do not know,” said Andrew Friedman, the Dodgers’ president of baseball operations.
This might be a good time to know, no? The regular season is over. The postseason is upon us.
Alex Call hits a run-scoring double and Andy Pages follows with a three-run home run in the 10th inning of the Dodgers’ 5-1 win over the San Francisco Giants.
“I feel very confident that we’re going to be going into October with arguably the deepest and best pitching staff that we’ve had,” he said. “Exactly what their roles will be and how things will be ordered, I don’t know right now.”
Perhaps the Dodgers are overthinking this. They have done that before.
Tanner Scott converted 25 of 29 save opportunities this season, including saves Friday and Saturday.
But the strongest hitters on the Dodgers’ possible division series opponents are left-handed — Matt Olson, Drake Baldwin and Michael Harris II on the Atlanta Braves; Bryce Harper and Kyle Schwarber on the Philadelphia Phillies — and the Dodgers may not hesitate to use the left-handed Scott against those guys in the seventh or eighth inning.
In theory, these Dodgers have three candidates as closer: Scott, their marquee closer signing for 2025 and actual closer for most of 2026; Edwin Díaz, their marquee closer signing for 2026; and Roki Sasaki, their accidental closer last October.
Yet Friedman said he could envision scenarios where Evan Phillips could close, or even Brock Stewart, or perhaps Alex Vesia against a run of left-handed hitters. The Dodgers hope to activate Edgardo Henriquez for the playoffs. The starters could close, too, especially a well-rested Tyler Glasnow early in the first round.
Dave Roberts know the Dodgers’ chances of a three-peat rest on a surprise hero giving the team a timely boost. Meet Bill Plaschke’s top candidates for the job.
“We’ve got a number of guys that we really trust,” Friedman said. “Depending on who we’re playing, how deep our starter goes, there are a lot of factors that would go into it. But, more than who will be that pitcher on the mound, is the fact that we have so many candidates we feel really good about.”
That the Dodgers have improvised an October relief corps, transformed a rookie starter into a postseason closer and run bullpen games in elimination games might lead you to conclude Friedman does not really believe in the concept of a designated closer. In a world where “high leverage” is the trendy jargon, maybe a closer is more of an anachronism than a necessity.
That the Dodgers invested $72 million in Scott and $69 million in Díaz in consecutive winters would lead you to conclude Friedman does indeed believe in the concept of a designated closer. In fact, he does.
“I think it’s extremely helpful,” he said.
The Dodgers do not hold splashy news conferences to introduce closer candidates. When the Dodgers introduced Díaz last December, Friedman proudly introduced the three-time All-Star as the closer.
“For us, we have a high bar,” Friedman said then. “To name someone the closer, you have to be one of the best. You have to be elite and dominant at what you do.”
Díaz’s season went awry, limited to 18⅔ innings after elbow surgery and then a neck injury. But in five September appearances since his activation from the injured list, he gave up no runs and one hit in five innings, striking out nine of the 17 batters he faced. (In the same span, Scott has given up no runs and two hits in five innings, striking out nine of the 19 batters he faced.)
“What we’ve seen out of Díaz recently has been really encouraging,” Dodgers manager Dave Roberts said. “What that ultimately means, we don’t know yet.
“Of course, if you have a reliever who is really hot in October, that can be extremely valuable. It doesn’t mean you use him exclusively in the ninth. But, by and large, that’s how you would use him.”
Roberts saluted Díaz for working hard to get back to an uncertain assignment.
“I’m really proud of Edwin, given the deal he signed, to work it out, to go to the minors, to come back and pitch in whatever role we ask of him, that shows a lot of character,” Roberts said.
“He could have mailed this year in. That’s something that has not gone unnoticed. And we’ll see how October plays out.”
The Dodgers could be forgiven for believing it will all work out in the end. Their final pitcher in each of the World Series clinchers under Friedman, all starters: Julio Urías in 2020, Walker Buehler in 2024, Yoshinobu Yamamoto in 2025.
The pitchers to record a postseason save in those championship seasons: Kenley Jansen, Joe Kelly, Brusdar Graterol, Blake Treinen and Urias in 2020; Alex Vesia, Treinen and Buehler in 2024; Glasnow, Sasaki and Treinen in 2025.
The organizational flexibility can lead to some uncomfortable discussions within the clubhouse, as Roberts and coaches keep the relievers updated on the latest plan for how they might be used.
“It is tricky,” Roberts said. “These are constant conversations. They are ever-evolving. They are ongoing.”
If all goes right for the Dodgers, those conversations will be ongoing for another month.

item.title: [Orange County Register] Dodgers complete 100-win season with win over Giants
item.dc:creator: Bill Plunkett

The Dodgers reached the end of the compulsory phase of their year, finishing the regular season with a 5-1 win in 10 innings against the San Francisco Giants on Sunday afternoon at Oracle Park. The win was the Dodgers’ 100th of the season. It is the 12th time in franchise history that they have finished a season with 100 wins (including six of the past nine full seasons). None of the previous 100-win regular seasons were follo
item.content:encoded:
SAN FRANCISCO – Well, enough of that – now on to the important stuff.
The Dodgers reached the end of the compulsory phase of their year, finishing the regular season with a 5-1 win in 10 innings against the San Francisco Giants on Sunday afternoon at Oracle Park.
The win was the Dodgers’ 100th of the season. It is the 12th time in franchise history that they have finished a season with 100 wins (including six of the past nine full seasons). None of the previous 100-win regular seasons were followed by a World Series championship.
The Dodgers will now take Monday off before getting together for four days of simulated games, live batting practice and whatever else they deem necessary to get ready for the opening of the postseason that will determine if they can become the first National League franchise to win three consecutive World Series championships.
Game 1 of their NL Division Series will be Saturday at Dodger Stadium against the winner of the Wild Card Series between the Atlanta Braves and Philadelphia Phillies. That best-of-three series begins Tuesday in Atlanta – and the Dodgers will be watching.
“There’s going to be some watch parties at the ballpark. I thought that was something that was really good,” Dodgers manager Dave Roberts said of the bye week itinerary established in 2024. “You’re not playing in the Wild Card Series, but you’re watching it and you kind of get your juices going. There’s also a bonding piece that I think is important.
“I thought we did a good job of having enough live and game situations, simulating them. Our coaches are sort of revisiting what we did a couple years ago. If there’s things we want to improve on or what – it worked out well a couple years ago. A lot of it’s also contingent on how guys are feeling, making sure they get rested and reset.”
MLB’s easiest September schedule allowed the Dodgers to go into their bye week with positive momentum. They went 18-7 in the final month (including 6-0 against the Giants in the final 10 days). Only the San Diego Padres (19-6) had more wins in the month.
Those bye-week sim games essentially started this weekend at Oracle Park.
On Sunday, the Dodgers sent seven pitchers to the mound to get their work. They allowed one run on five hits — and survived giving up the potential game-deciding home run. Giants shortstop Christian Koss took Dodgers reliever Bobby Miller deep leading off the eighth inning — but replay review turned the home run into a foul ball.
Roki Sasaki made his third appearance out of the bullpen since returning from a blister and did nothing to undermine his status as perhaps the most important bullpen weapon the Dodgers will have this postseason. He struck out two of the three batters he faced in a 1-2-3 inning.
Over his three innings in relief, Sasaki has faced 11 batters and struck out six, allowing two hits in his first appearance and none since.
“I think the fastball’s better,” Roberts said, comparing the version of Sasaki the Dodgers got when they moved him to the bullpen last postseason. “I think the split’s better. It’s also nice that he’s already done it. Just in total, he’s just a better pitcher than he was last year and a lot more confident.”
Edwin Diaz continued to affirm his status as a rediscovered bullpen weapon with another 1-2-3 inning. And Roberts reported Edgardo Henriquez has been throwing bullpen sessions this weekend and will participate in the bye week workouts with the expectation that he will be ready to return from his lower back injury and be part of the Dodgers’ NLDS bullpen.
The Dodgers’ offense didn’t spark to life until the 10th inning when Alex Call doubled in the free runner then trotted home on a three-run home run by Andy Pages.

item.title: [True Blue LA] Dodgers find their breakthrough in extras to beat the Giants
item.dc:creator: Estevão Maximo
item.description: For nine-plus innings, the Dodgers and Giants couldn’t buy a hit with a runner in scoring position, but in the tenth, the Dodgers broke through for a 5-1 win. Alex Call and Andy Pages recorded two-out hits, a double, and a three-run shot to give the Dodgers their first lead in this game and the only one they’d need. Dodgers find their breakthrough in extras to beat the Giants Making a habit out of squandering chances through nine innings, the Dodgers scored four in extras to beat the Giants Befo
item.content:encoded:
For nine-plus innings, the Dodgers and Giants couldn’t buy a hit with a runner in scoring position, but in the tenth, the Dodgers broke through for a 5-1 win. Alex Call and Andy Pages recorded two-out hits, a double, and a three-run shot to give the Dodgers their first lead in this game and the only one they’d need.
Dodgers find their breakthrough in extras to beat the Giants
Making a habit out of squandering chances through nine innings, the Dodgers scored four in extras to beat the Giants
Before getting to that point of being tied in extras, Jack Dreyer did a reasonable job of keeping the Giants at bay as an opener, but a stolen base allowed the opportunity for just a pair of singles to open the scoring in the second. Shay Whitcomb singled and stole second, later driven in by Scott Bandura—his first RBI of the season, playing in just his 13th big league game. Bandura also tried to steal a base, but this time Dreyer was alert to the danger and picked him off.
Facing a traditional bullpen game with Carson Seymour completing just one inning to open this one, the Dodgers first threatened to score in the third, the inning marked by Tony Vitello’s ejection. With two on and a 2-2 count to Mookie Betts, a check swing in which he probably went around was called a no-swing. Vitello came out to argue what had already been a topic of frustration earlier in the game and was thrown out for the seventh time in his 2026. The Giants, however, got out of the jam, as Betts struck out on the next pitch, and Sam Hentges also punched out Freddie Freeman.
What the Dodgers offense couldn’t do in the third, it did in the following frame. Kyle Tucker got on to leadoff the inning thanks to a defensive error by the second baseman and moved to third on a Max Muncy double—his 27th of the season, setting a new career high in a single season. With two on and one out, Andy Pages evened the score with a sacrifice fly.
Through the following innings, the Dodgers kept threatening but never coming through, first with a Freddie Freeman hit with a man on being taken away by a great defensive play from Jonah Cox—somewhat redeeming himself for the error that contributed to the Dodgers’ first run. That, by the way, would be Freeman’s last action in the game, replaced after five by Kiké Hernández as Dave Roberts rotated key pieces.
In the sixth, Muncy nearly wrote another chapter in his book as a giant killer. But the deepest part of the park was just deep enough to keep him from a solo shot in a ball that would’ve gone out in 23 of 30 stadiums. Perhaps the biggest squandered chance, though, came in the seventh and eighth when the Dodgers first stranded a leadoff double by Tommy Edman with three straight groundouts—an inning later, after Muncy secured his third hit of the day, Andy Pages hit into an inning-ending double play with two on and one out.
The Dodgers’ pitching was the reason the offense kept getting these opportunities to take the lead. Justin Wrobleski was the first pitcher out of the bullpen for the Dodgers, but looking for an even distribution of workload, he only completed two scoreless innings in under 30 pitches. Roki Sasaki and Edwin Díaz combined to strike out three, each with a scoreless frame.
Although Wrobleski had a couple of scares, the Giants truly came back to threaten again in the seventh when Bobby Miller took the mound, but also without actually breaking through. With runners at the corners and no outs, Miller secured a strikeout, then lucked into Marcelo Mayer staying at third on a wild pitch quickly recovered by Hunter Feduccia, recorded another punchout, and finished off the inning with a groundout.
With both teams exhausting new ways of threatening without actually scoring, the Giants looked like they’d take the lead with a leadoff bomb in the eighth by Christian Koss. However, the call on the field of a home run was overturned when replay made it clear it was a foul ball, and the score remained 1-1 through nine innings.
Even in the tenth, it looked like the Dodgers were going to strand the ghost runner after their first two hitters were retired without him advancing to third, but Call came through, and an intentional walk later, Pages had the big hit of the game. With the four RBI he recorded in this game, Pages left Ohtani behind and isolated himself as the Dodgers’ RBI leader this season, with 85.
Sunday particulars
Home run: Andy Pages (23)
WP —Alex Vesia (3-1): 1 IP, 1 hit, 1 strikeout
LP —Duncan Davitt (0-1):1 IP, 2 hits, 4 runs, 3 earned runs, 1 walk
Up next
The Dodgers get a little under a week off before they get back on the field on Saturday at home. They’ll be playing host to the winner of the Wild Card round between the Braves and Phillies in game 1 of the NLDS. No starters have been announced for that series.

item.title: [Yardbarker] Dodgers Make Sudden Freddie Freeman Announcement
item.dc:creator: Simeon Kotto

After sitting Saturday against the San Francisco Giants, the Dodgers first baseman is in Sunday’s Game 162 lineup at Oracle Park and batting third. The card posted by Underdog MLB puts Shohei Ohtani at designated hitter, Mookie Betts at shortstop, Freeman at first, Kyle Tucker in right, Teoscar Hernández in left, Max Muncy at third, Andy Pages in center, H
item.content:encoded:
Freddie Freeman is back where the Los Angeles Dodgers like him: in the middle of a loaded order, on the last afternoon of the regular season.
After sitting Saturday against the San Francisco Giants, the Dodgers first baseman is in Sunday’s Game 162 lineup at Oracle Park and batting third.
The card posted by Underdog MLB puts Shohei Ohtani at designated hitter, Mookie Betts at shortstop, Freeman at first, Kyle Tucker in right, Teoscar Hernández in left, Max Muncy at third, Andy Pages in center, Hunter Feduccia behind the plate and Tommy Edman at second. Jack Dreyer is listed as the starter in what figures to be a bullpen game.
The off day was not a surprise. Freeman had started each of the previous 10 games and was dragging a .522 OPS over 45 plate appearances in that stretch.
Enrique Hernández filled in at first on Saturday while the club gave its 37-year-old cornerstone a breather.
That is how Dave Roberts has handled September: keep Freeman available, not exhausted, with the postseason a few days away.
Sunday’s assignment is the one Freeman has occupied for most of his career.
He has started more than 1,300 games in the three-hole across Atlanta and Los Angeles, and even after spring talk about a cleanup role behind Tucker, the Dodgers keep sliding him back between Betts and the middle of the order when they want their most reliable left-handed bat seeing traffic.
He entered the weekend hitting .290 with 167 hits, 16 homers and 70 RBIs. The power has been quieter lately — he has gone without an extra-base hit for more than two weeks — but the bat-to-ball skill is still the reason Los Angeles trusts him with runners on.
The context around the lineup is October-minded. Los Angeles is 99-62 and chasing a 100-win season in the finale. Will Smith is the only everyday starter sitting.
Blake Treinen is headed to the injured list with a shoulder issue, so the bullpen will be asked to work. First pitch is 12:05 p.m. PT / 3:05 p.m. ET on SportsNet LA.
For Freeman, the message is simple. One rest day. Then back in the three-hole, glove at first, with Ohtani and Betts in front of him and Tucker behind him.
If the Dodgers are going to finish 100-62 and carry momentum into the NLDS, they want their veteran first baseman in the middle of it — not on the bench, and not buried in the order.
Sunday is a tune-up with meaning: one more look at the group that has to win in October.

item.description:

item.content:encoded:
Field Level Media

27 Sep 2026, 21:25 GMT+10

(Photo credit: Darren Yamashita)
The Los Angeles Dodgers will look to tarnish the final game of longtime San Francisco Giants broadcaster Mike Krukow's career with a 100th regular-season win when the California rivals wrap up the regular season on Sunday afternoon.
The finale in San Francisco will send the Dodgers (99-62) on their quest for a third consecutive World Series championship and Krukow into retirement after 36 years of calling Giants games.
Also a pitcher for the Giants for the final seven of his 14 seasons in the majors, Krukow, 74, will be honored after Sunday's game, in which the home team will seek to end a four-game losing streak overall and a seven-game skid against the Dodgers.
'I'm going to tell them just how much they mean to me and my family,' Krukow promised this week about his farewell speech. 'I don't know if you can convey it in words, but it'll be conveyed in emotion. That I can guarantee.'
Krukow was in the booth when San Francisco won three World Series titles in five seasons from 2010-14, but the team has been to the postseason just twice since then (2016, 2021), losing both times in the National League Division Series. This season, the Giants (65-96) will finish with their fewest wins in a full season since going 64-98 in 2017.
Meanwhile, the Dodgers will wind up with more wins than the 98 they had in 2024 and 93 last season, regular seasons followed by World Series victories. This will be their 14th consecutive appearance in the postseason; they also won the World Series in the pandemic-shortened season in 2020.
With a first-round bye to start their three-peat effort as a result of having the second-best record in the National League, the Dodgers will need 11 wins to achieve a first in Major League Baseball since the Yankees captured the World Series in 1998, 1999 and 2000.
Los Angeles saw a lot go right in its first two games in San Francisco -- both victories -- as they got home runs from Teoscar Hernandez, Andy Pages, Enrique Hernandez and Mookie Betts, sharp starting pitching from Tarik Skubal and Blake Snell, and stellar game-closing from Tanner Scott.
The Dodgers will take the field Sunday with postseason roster spots still up for grabs and pitchers needing one more outing before a five-day break leading into a best-of-five NLDS, which will open in Los Angeles on Saturday.
'We want to finish playing good baseball,' Dodgers manager Dave Roberts told reporters. 'Our guys still got to get ready because we've got a week of not playing baseball. So (the goal is) just to finish strong, finish the season out.'
One unresolved issue for Los Angeles in the postseason is who will bat leadoff.
Shohei Ohtani, who manned the spot almost exclusively while healthy earlier in the season, led off Friday's 2-0 win over the Giants, going 0-for-4 with three strikeouts.
Roberts moved Betts into the top spot for Saturday's 4-3 victory, and while Betts went just 1-for-5 with a strikeout, his hit was his 23rd home run of the season.
Ohtani, who singled and struck out twice while slotted second on Saturday, has gone just 4-for-18 with just one extra-base hit, a double, since returning from a 16-day absence due to discomfort in his right biceps.
While the Dodgers have not announced a starting pitcher for Sunday's game, the Giants will send right-hander Carson Seymour (0-2, 4.70 ERA) to the mound as an opener. He will make his first start after 24 relief appearances this season.
Seymour does not have a decision in five career outings against the Dodgers. He has a 3.60 ERA, allowing two runs in five innings. He pitched the sixth inning on Saturday, striking out one.
--Field Level Media

item.title: [ocregister.com] Kiké Hernandez’s 9th-inning blast lifts Dodgers past Giants again
item.dc:creator: Bill Plunkett

Pitching for the first time since he left his start in Cincinnati after one inning with groin muscle discomfort, Blake Snell passed his test. He allowed one run on five hits in his four innings Saturday afternoon as the Dodgers beat the San Francisco Giants 4-3 on Kiké Hernandez’s ninth-inning home run. The Dodgers will finish the season with a chance to reach 100 victories for the first time since 2023 – but the fourth time in the past six se
item.content:encoded:
SAN FRANCISCO — It was a four-inning wellness check.
Pitching for the first time since he left his start in Cincinnati after one inning with groin muscle discomfort, Blake Snell passed his test. He allowed one run on five hits in his four innings Saturday afternoon as the Dodgers beat the San Francisco Giants 4-3 on Kiké Hernandez’s ninth-inning home run.
The Dodgers will finish the season with a chance to reach 100 victories for the first time since 2023 – but the fourth time in the past six seasons and sixth time in the past nine full seasons.
Snell was healthy if not efficient. He threw 77 pitches to get through his four innings, allowing hits in each inning.
“Definitely needed to pitch today. Definitely showed that,” Snell said. “I was trying to go up and in, I was missing up and away. Even the last pitch of the game, I try to go up and in and miss right down the middle. I don’t know the last time I did that. It’s been a while. Even the changeup, the speed was up to 88. I gotta fix that as well. Get that to 86. Curveball, the release just has to get better.
“But overall, I learned a lot from it. Really encouraged by it, and just happy to get my legs underneath me and get going and completely move past the groin. I mean, it felt great today, and the velo was good. … I’ve got to figure my body out a little more, but I got a week to do so, and I’m really looking forward to that.”
He stranded runners at the corners in the first inning and at second base in the second. Jonah Cox led off the third with a double into the left-field corner, stole third and scored on a sacrifice fly. Snell gave up a two-out single in the fourth, but Shay Whitcomb was thrown out by left fielder Teoscar Hernandez when he tried to stretch it into a double.
After the game in Cincinnati, Snell expressed confidence that he had avoided serious injury by recognizing the signs early and coming out of the game – something he didn’t do before landing on the injured list four previous times with groin injuries.
Saturday supported that decision. Snell’s fastball averaged 96.8 mph (up slightly from his season average) and he got 10 swings-and-misses (though only three strikeouts). Snell now lines up as the likely Game 3 starter in the National League Division Series, giving him over a week before his next start.
“I thought the fastball was had life. Just some near misses to kind of flip counts,” Dodgers manager Dave Roberts said. “The changeup was okay. The curveball I thought was good. But I think for him overall, he just wasn’t as efficient as he wanted, as we wanted. But again, I thought it was fine for his last tune-up for the postseason.
“I was confident, we were confident (that Snell was healthy). But I think it’s still good to see it. And it’s good also that we got it out of the way, got that rust off, versus whatever game in the postseason, then he’s rusty, and you’ve got to kind of pick up the pieces in a playoff game. So I thought today it was again, really best-case scenario.”
The Dodgers’ offense gave Snell a 3-1 lead.
Mookie Betts hit a solo home run in the third inning – his seventh home run in September as he surges over the final month of the season. Four singles and a walk produced two more runs in the fourth inning.
After a two-hit game including an RBI double Thursday, Shohei Ohtani has gone 1 for 9 with five strikeouts in the two games against the Giants. The lone hit was a ground ball under the glove of Giants first baseman Brett Harris in the fourth inning that was originally ruled an error and later changed.
“I thought today there was just more chase,” Roberts said of Ohtani’s 1 for 5. “And I don’t know if he’s trying to get hits, find his swing, getting a little over-anxious. Everything from Shohei to the training staff, the hitting guys, the work has been great. Looks exactly like it did, like it’s supposed to look.”
Roberts dismissed any suggestion that Ohtani is still not healthy after spending two weeks on the injured list.
“I don’t see any wincing. The bat speed is still (good),” Roberts said. “There’s one thing to just say you could just put him on ice and hope that the performance is there Game One of the postseason, or there’s another camp that says everything looks right and you have to get him (at-bats) and it’s still only – what is it 12, 13 at bats, 14 at bats (since he returned)? So, with a long layoff, that’s not easy either to come back and perform.”
The Dodgers’ bullpen couldn’t hold the 3-1 lead. The Giants came back to tie it with single runs against Brock Stewart in the seventh and Evan Phillips in the eighth before Hernandez put the Dodgers back in the lead with a leadoff home run in the ninth.
The homer was an uplifting moment in a difficult season for Hernandez, who started the season on the IL following elbow surgery, returned for two games, then missed two months with an oblique injury.
“Yeah, I mean it’s been tough, but I mean, it is what it is,” Hernandez said. “That’s the card I’ve drawn this year. It’s nobody’s fault. I was expected to miss the first couple months because of my rehab, and then I was not expecting to miss more time so quickly after coming back. It just happened to be that way. And when you have a team like this one, it’s hard getting in the lineup. So it’s just one of those things where that’s what you have, and you got to make the best of it. I just happened to not have made the best of my opportunities this year.”

Tanner Scott closed out a second straight game, earning his 25th save. Betts homered with two outs in the third inning for hi
item.content:encoded:
SAN FRANCISCO -- - Kiké Hernández hit a tiebreaking home run leading off the ninth inning, Mookie Betts also homered and the Los Angeles Dodgers beat the San Francisco Giants 4-3 on Saturday.
Bo Davidson hit a tying sacrifice fly off Evan Phillips (3-2) with two outs in the eighth for San Francisco before Hernández answered against Trent Harris (0-1) for his fourth homer.
Tanner Scott closed out a second straight game, earning his 25th save.
Betts homered with two outs in the third inning for his team's first hit before Miguel Rojas and Tommy Edman added RBI singles the next two innings.
Betts' blast to the bleachers in left-center sent the large contingent of Dodgers fans in the sellout crowd of 40,124 at Oracle Park into a frenzy on a beautiful sunny afternoon in the Bay Area.
Shohei Ohtani, playing for a fourth straight day following a 13-game absence with right biceps discomfort, went 1 for 5 with two strikeouts after an 0-for-4 showing with three Ks on Friday night.
When Camilo Doval pitched the seventh for San Francisco, he became the 71st player used by the club this season - matching Atlanta's MLB record set last year.
Los Angeles left-hander Blake Snell struck out three and didn't walk a batter, allowing one run on five hits over four innings in his final playoff tune-up.
The Giants lost their fourth straight, seventh of eight and seventh in a row to the rival Dodgers after taking four of five in the series to start the year.
Los Angeles earned its 14th shutout of the season in a 2-0 win Friday, then manager Dave Roberts rested first baseman Freddie Freeman and gave Hernández a start. The Dodgers improved their majors-best road record to 48-32.
Up next
Neither team had announced its starter for Sunday's regular-season finale, when beloved Giants broadcaster Mike Krukow will be celebrated before he retires from the booth after nearly four decades.
------

item.title: [True Blue LA] Blake Snell healthy in final tuneup, Kiké Hernández home run beats Giants
item.dc:creator: Eric Stephen
item.description: Blake Snell looked healthy in his final regular season start and Kiké Hernández homered in the ninth inning to give the Dodgers a 4-3 win over the Giants on Saturday afternoon at Oracle Park in San Francisco. Snell allowed only one run in his four innings and at the very least showed no limitations from leaving his start with left groin tightness on September 16 in Cincinnati. The Dodgers weren’t going to push Snell on Saturday, but more wanted to make sure he got one more start in before the po
item.content:encoded:
Blake Snell looked healthy in his final regular season start and Kiké Hernández homered in the ninth inning to give the Dodgers a 4-3 win over the Giants on Saturday afternoon at Oracle Park in San Francisco.
Snell allowed only one run in his four innings and at the very least showed no limitations from leaving his start with left groin tightness on September 16 in Cincinnati. The Dodgers weren’t going to push Snell on Saturday, but more wanted to make sure he got one more start in before the postseason starts in a week.
“If he can go five innings and come out of it feeling great, that would be fantastic,” manager Dave Roberts told reporters at Oracle Park earlier Saturday, as shown on SportsNet LA. “There’s a balance between getting your work in and making sure you feel good coming out of it.”
Snell threw 77 pitches in his four innings so he wasn’t all that efficient, though he didn’t walk anyone and threw his two fastest pitches of the season — first-inning fastballs at 98.6 mph and 98.2 mph — while averaging 96.8 mph on the fastball on Saturday.
The lone run came when Jonah Cox doubled to open the third inning, stole third base, and scored on a sacrifice fly.
San Francisco swiped two bases Saturday off Snell, who has allowed 10 steals in his nine starts this season. But Snell has limited the damage by simply not allowing many people to reach, with only 25 hits and 14 walks in 39 2/3 innings, a .260 on-base percentage since returning from the injured list.
Snell since returning allowed only five runs, never more than one in any start. On the season he did not allow a home run, his 42 2/3 innings the seventh-most by a Dodgers pitcher in the live-ball era without giving up a long ball.
Most Dodgers innings without allowing a home run
| Pitcher | Season | Innings | ERA |
| Jack Billingham | 1968 | 71 1/3 | 2.14 |
| Brandon League | 2014 | 63 | 2.57 |
| Newt Kimball | 1941 | 52 | 3.63 |
| Joe Beimel | 2008 | 49 | 2.02 |
| Dutch Henry | 1924 | 46 | 5.67 |
| Brandon Morrow | 2017 | 43 2/3 | 2.06 |
| Blake Snell | 2026 | 42 2/3 | 1.90 |
Just like last Sunday at Dodger Stadium, the Dodgers did the bulk of their damage after Matt Wilkinson left. The rookie left-hander, who pitched five scoreless innings in Los Angeles before the Dodgers scored single runs in the next three innings to complete a weekend sweep, on Saturday held the Dodgers without a run until Mookie Betts hit one into the left field seats in the third inning.
Betts has seven home runs in September, after hitting five combined home runs in July and August. It’s been a month to remember for Betts, who raised his seasonal OPS from .701 at the start of September to .783 now, with just one day remaining in the regular season.
Wilkinson was done after three innings, and the Dodgers immediately responded with four singles and a walk in the fourth inning to score two runs.
San Francisco clawed back with single runs in the seventh and eighth innings, before Hernández took Trent Harris deep to open the ninth inning.
Treinen hurt?
Brock Stewart pitched the bottom of the seventh inning but was allotted extra warm-up pitches as he entered the game. He wasn’t warming up in the bullpen before getting called in, but Blake Treinen was before suddenly stopping. In the top of the eighth, the SportsNet LA broadcast showed footage from the Dodgers bullpen, showing bullpen coach Josh Bard embracing Treinen, then of Treinen walking back to the Dodgers dugout and clubhouse with trainer Bernard Li.
Treinen missed two and a half months with elbow inflammation before returning in September, when he has allowed three runs in 6 2/3 innings, with three walks and six strikeouts.
Saturday particulars
Home runs: Mookie Betts (23), Kiké Hernández (4)
WP — Evan Phillips (3-2): 1 IP, 1 hit, 1 run, 1 strikeout
LP — Trent Harris (0-1): 1 IP, 2 hits, 1 run
Sv — Tanner Scott (25): 1 IP, 1 hit, 2 strikeouts

item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers face the San Francisco Giants in the second game of the regular season’s final series.
The Dodgers will rotate in veterans with something to provide heading into the postseason, with Freddie Freeman notably absent for Saturday’s game.
Dodgers Lineup
1. Mookie Betts, SS
2. Shohei Ohtani, DH
3. Will Smith, C
4. Teoscar Hernandez, LF
5. Kyle Tucker, RF
6. Miguel Rojas, 3B
7. Andy Pages, CF
8. Kike Hernandez, 1B
9. Tommy Edman, 2B
The Dodgers are facing lefty Matt Wilkinson, which lets Rojas and Kike Hernandez enter the mix in a favorable matchup with a righty-heavy lineup.
The biggest note of the game is that once again, Mookie Betts is batting leadoff, while Shohei Ohtani is hitting second.
Manager Dave Roberts has made it clear that Ohtani wasn’t guaranteed to hit leadoff against lefties, and with Betts continuing to deliver quality plate appearances, the Dodgers skipper is willing to start the order with Betts.
At-bats from Andy Pages, Kike Hernandez, Miguel Rojas, and Tommy Edman are all worth monitoring. Pages is still somewhat fresh off the injured list, while Tommy Edman has been in a slump.
Rojas and Hernandez feature so inconsistently that they are always worth following whenever they play.
Who is pitching for the Dodgers?
Blake Snell starts against the Giants after being pulled early in his last outing. Snell, who has a history of groin injuries, had some groin soreness surface against the Cincinnati Reds last week.
Initial concern about his postseason viability grew, and as a key member of the rotation, the Dodgers could ill-afford to lose him.
The injury doesn’t seem major, and Snell has a chance to get some pitching work before October kicks into high gear.
In terms of actual pitching production, Snell sits at the top, with elite stuff and sharp command.
If he is fully sharp, Snell can carry a team in the postseason, and while the Dodgers don’t need that this week, next week will be a different story.

item.title: [DodgersBeat] Dave Roberts Praises Tarik Skubal after Dodgers' Shutout Win
item.dc:creator: Steve Webb
item.description: SAN FRANCISCO, CA — Dave Roberts has seen plenty of outstanding pitching performances this season, but Friday night’s masterpiece from Tarik Skubal was something special. The Dodgers manager had little hesitation when asked whether Skubal’s seven shutout innings against the Giants represented his finest outing since joining the club. “That was the best we’ve seen,” Roberts said following the Dodgers’ 2-0 victory at Oracle Park. “He was on a mission tonight. You could see it. Everything was worki
item.content:encoded:
SAN FRANCISCO, CA — Dave Roberts has seen plenty of outstanding pitching performances this season, but Friday night’s masterpiece from Tarik Skubal was something special. The Dodgers manager had little hesitation when asked whether Skubal’s seven shutout innings against the Giants represented his finest outing since joining the club.
“That was the best we’ve seen,” Roberts said following the Dodgers’ 2-0 victory at Oracle Park. “He was on a mission tonight. You could see it. Everything was working, and he just went after those guys and did a fantastic job.”
“Pounded the zone. Everything was working tonight. Efficient. I think he went through seven innings, 75 pitches, something like that. Incredibly good.”
Skubal Had Something to Prove
Skubal had been less than pleased with his previous outing against the Giants, when he surrendered 10 hits and struggled with his fastball command. Roberts believes that disappointment helped fuel Friday’s extraordinary performance.
“I think so, yeah. He wasn’t pleased with his outing the last time, and so to come back and face the same team and do what he did less than a week later is pretty impressive.”
Asked what makes Skubal’s fastball so difficult for hitters, particularly when he’s attacking the strike zone as aggressively as he did Friday, Roberts pointed to the combination of velocity, deception and secondary pitches.
“When it’s right, it’s an explosive fastball. He stays behind it well. He hides it well, and then he’s got the secondaries to go with it.”
“Tonight certainly was really dominant with the fastball and essentially could do whatever he wanted tonight.”
Roberts Sees an Improved, More Confident Roki Sasaki
Skubal’s departure after seven innings provided another opportunity for Roki Sasaki to demonstrate what he can contribute to the Dodgers’ postseason bullpen. The young right-hander struck out two in a scoreless eighth inning, and Roberts believes he’s considerably further along than he was at this point last season.
“Yeah, he is. I think the fastball’s better. I think the split’s better, and it’s also nice that he’s already done it.”
“So just in total, he’s just a better pitcher than he was last year and a lot more confident. Certainly, the stuff was really good the last couple outings.”
Sasaki was followed by Tanner Scott, who struck out two in a perfect ninth inning to record his 24th save. Roberts liked the combination, although he was careful to avoid committing himself to specific bullpen roles for October.
“I liked it tonight. They both did a fantastic job.”
“It’s just better to have as many guys that you have confidence in in leverage. It allows us to deploy guys whenever we need to.”
“I feel comfortable with a lot of guys at the back end, for sure.”
The Offense Needs Contributions Beyond Its Superstars
The Dodgers managed just two runs Friday, both coming on solo home runs in the second inning. Although the offense has struggled to string together hits over the past several games, Roberts remains encouraged by the quality of the team’s at-bats.
“I thought obviously we had two homers tonight. Will had a really good night. I thought Mookie still looks fine.”
“We’re not putting a bunch of hits together, but it doesn’t seem like the results are there. I still like our intent in the batter’s box.”
“Try not to overthink it as far as the production the last few games, because honestly, I like where our offense is at mentally. But I do think, like I said before, this week for our group is going to be a very good thing.”
The manager also emphasized the importance of getting production from the middle and bottom of the batting order. With opposing teams likely to focus their attention on Shohei Ohtani, Mookie Betts and Freddie Freeman, players like Teoscar Hernández and Andy Pages will have opportunities to make a considerable difference.
“It certainly adds length. As we all know, when you get to the postseason, they’re going to try to eliminate Sho and try to make other guys beat you.”
“It always sort of comes to the middle to the bottom of the order, where you’ve either got to get guys on base or get hits, get big hits.”
“The way Teo’s been swinging, Andy’s swinging, we’ve got to get Tommy on track. It’ll certainly be helpful.”
Pages Is Entering October in a Much Different Place
Roberts admitted that he’s been somewhat surprised by how quickly Pages has regained his form after missing approximately five weeks with an injury. Playing in just his fourth game since returning from the injured list, Pages collected two hits Friday, including his 22nd home run.
“I am a little bit, but in the other sense, I’m not surprised because he put in a lot of work before he was active to really hit the ground running.”
“Even the jumps defensively, covering so much ground out there, the at-bat quality. You think that when you take five weeks off, your timing is going to be off a little bit, but he put in a lot of time.”
Asked about Pages’ struggles during last year’s postseason and what might be different this time around, Roberts pointed to the young outfielder’s confidence.
“I think the one thing is the confidence. He went into last October really scuffling, and it sort of bled into October.”
“Right now, he feels really confident, swinging the bat well, and the hope is that this one bleeds into October as well.”
“His headspace is just a lot more confident this year.”
Roberts Still Likes What He Sees From Ohtani
Ohtani went hitless with three strikeouts Friday, but Roberts indicated that he’s continuing to see encouraging signs from the slugger following his return from the injured list.
“Loved them. I liked them. He’s fine.”
“I really think that, just for me, the swing decisions, the bat speed, that’s kind of all that. If that’s in place, then the results will be there.”
With the first-round bye already secured, the Dodgers have the opportunity to use their final regular-season games to sharpen their approach and prepare for the NLDS.
Friday’s performance offered plenty of encouragement on the pitching side, particularly from Skubal and Sasaki. And with Teoscar and Pages continuing to swing the bats well, Roberts has reason to believe his club is moving in the right direction as October approaches.
More Dodgers Coverage:
Have you subscribed to the Bleed Los Podcast YouTube channel? Be sure to ring the notification bell to watch player interviews, participate in shows & promotions, and stay up to date on all Dodgers news and rumors!
A lifelong baseball fan, Webb has been going to Dodger games since he moved to Los Angeles in 1987. His favorite memory was attending the insane Game 3 of the World Series in 2025 and hugging random Dodgers fans after Freddie’s walkoff homer. He has been writing for Dodgersbeat since 2020.

item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers beat the San Francisco Giants, 2-0, on Friday night and improved to 98-62 on the year.
Two-time Cy Young award winner Tarik Skubal unleashed another masterpiece with seven scoreless innings, 10 strikeouts, no walks and just three hits allowed. Offensively, Will Smith had a three-hit evening while two second inning solo home runs were collected by Teoscar Hernández and Andy Pages (his first home run since being activated off the injured list).
Ahead of Friday's game, the Dodgers demoted an infielder to make room on the roster to activate catcher Dalton Rushing. Manager Dave Roberts spoke on the kind of role fans can expect from Rushing down the stretch.
“At the most it would be three pinch-hit at-bats, so just conduct at-bats and see what you got,” Roberts said. “Just the circumstances of his situation, it’s just tough to just be hurt, come back, then be hurt again, and then take three pinch-hit at-bats to potentially then say, ‘Hey, you’re on the roster.’"
Additionally, Roberts had a message for rookie Josue De Paula after he was optioned to Triple-A following a productive first 11 games at the major league level. The reasoning, he revealed, was that De Paula could act as a spark plug while superstar Shohei Ohtani was on the injured list — and during his time on the shelf, it's exactly what the 21-year-old provided.
“This was the original thought, that once Shohei gets back, we’re going to send him out,” Roberts said. “We had a runway to give him, which we gave him and he performed more than admirably. This also, as far as the timing, just gives us an opportunity to potentially have him back for the postseason. He’s a part of the conversation, and he’s earned that, and that’s what I told him last night.”
Finally, there is an update on southpaw Blake Snell after he lasted just one inning due to groin discomfort during his most recent start. Luckily for Dodgers fans, the team announced that Snell will make his next scheduled start on Saturday during the penultimate regular season game.
